charisma.statement: I'd just like to say I admire the thought and consideration of all parties on this bill. It's a shame that we were not able to reach consensus.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, consensus-valuing tone that reaches across party lines.

charisma.statement: The accident compensation scheme was built on a simple promise, and that is: if you are injured, the State will stand beside you, not on top of you.
charisma.explanation: Memorable, principled framing of the no-fault ACC compact.

charisma.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party in total opposition to this bill, a bill that will just cause more harm coming from a Government that clearly does not care about the most vulnerable in our society. This bill is absolutely a disgrace.
charisma.explanation: Condemnatory tone that rallies opponents of the bill rather than persuading the undecided.

charisma.statement: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
charisma.explanation: An applause line aimed at his own side, not persuasion.

charisma.statement: next time someone from the Government gets up and tells us that they care about workers, I urge the public to think, "How much do they care about workers in this country? How much do they care about people?—full stop."
charisma.explanation: Partisan appeal to the public against the Government.

charisma.statement: this law—it's another good reason to change the Government this November.
charisma.explanation: Overt electioneering aimed at her own side.

charisma.statement: The member opposite just talked about fairness, and we all know fairness is too subjective of a term. This is not about fairness; this is about justice.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective reframing, but appeals mainly to her own side.

charisma.statement: Nobody disputes the principle that somebody should not be paid twice for the same income period. But what happens next is the problem. MSD treats the remainder of that back payment as income and seeks to recover it as debt, even though that is often needed for the rehab and living costs that person, themselves, has had to carry
charisma.explanation: Concedes the opponents' valid point before drawing the distinction — seeks common ground.

charisma.statement: Sometimes, some decisions that we have to make are very hard decisions to make, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't be made.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges difficulty and the opponents' concern before defending the decision.

charisma.statement: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
charisma.explanation: Divisive partisan attack.

charisma.statement: we were able to negotiate with the Government—and I thank the Government for their good-faith interactions with us in this respect—to have a short select committee process of around a week.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges cross-party cooperation, modelling constructive engagement.

charisma.statement: the bill mistakes measurement for improvement... No one disagrees with the fact that performance should be visible... but simply writing targets into law isn't going to do anything to create capacity.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the opposing point ('no one disagrees') before rebutting.

authenticity.statement: Labour agrees, though, that the closing of a double-dipping loophole in welfare is important, because we, like everyone, know that Kiwis must feel confident in our welfare system
authenticity.explanation: Concedes the principle while still opposing — a defensible, qualified position rather than a clean flip.

authenticity.statement: Almost 40,000 people have been unlawfully burdened with debts as a result of a practice that has carried on by both National and Labour Governments through decades.
authenticity.explanation: Even-handedly blames Labour as well as National, consistent with the Greens' across-the-aisle critique.

authenticity.statement: I heard from our colleagues that it's a targeted welfare system, no impacts on claimants, clients will not get less under this amendment, and we take them at their word.
authenticity.explanation: Says NZ First want no claimant disadvantage yet accept assurances rather than test them, then vote for the bill.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First do not want any undue hardship or material hardship as a result of these changes; however, we support this bill.
authenticity.explanation: Tension: states a value against hardship while voting for the bill that submitters and the courts say causes that hardship.

authenticity.statement: the Labour Party started in a position of supporting this bill because of what it was told. It was just awake on the job. It found out what was going on. It found out that there was an injustice afoot and it wasn't prepared to tolerate it.
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges Labour's position change and frames it as evidence-driven rather than concealing the shift.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, it's a very important issue. We have to, otherwise we will not be doing justice to those who are going to be affected, because, as days go by, there will be more and more people—those who will be affected.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the 'rushed process' criticism by justifying speed, but only partially addresses the substance of the complaint.

divination.statement: this bill will deepen hardship for survivors of abuse, for survivors of sexual violence and abuse, and for those who suffer most in all of Aotearoa.
divination.explanation: Prediction of worsened hardship; directionally supported by the affected cohort data, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: If people believe that decisions affecting their entitlements can be revisited years later, confidence in the system—confidence in the system—begins to erode.
divination.explanation: Predicts erosion of public confidence from retrospective change; plausible but unmeasured.

divination.statement: Every single person should get, and will get, everything they are entitled to; they just won't get it twice.
divination.explanation: Predicts everyone 'will get' their entitlements; contested by the harm evidence raised.

divination.statement: We know that when people can't afford to see their GP, they delay their care, they get sicker and sicker, they end up in hospitals, and those emergency departments start to overflow.
divination.explanation: Predictive claim about downstream ED pressure; directionally well-supported, magnitude unstated.

rigor.statement: I'll quote directly from paragraph 495 of the royal commission's report: “We consider the failure to ensure that this specific advice reached Ministers and the public was significant.”
rigor.explanation: Cites the report by paragraph and quotes it directly to rebut the Minister's characterisation — evidence-anchored argument.

rigor.statement: Speaking to the point of order, the royal commission finds that, on 22 December 2021, the briefing was made available to the Minister for COVID-19 Response, the Hon Chris Hipkins, of those concerns.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in a date and a named briefing, but selectively reads the report.

rigor.statement: Treasury advised from the outset that pandemic spending should be timely, temporary, and targeted. Despite that advice, the $60 billion COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund spanned 821 programmes, half of which had nothing to do with the pandemic.
rigor.explanation: Sets premise (Treasury advice) against outcome (spending pattern) to support the conclusion that advice was not followed.

rigor.statement: The claim that the level 4 lockdown was extended against public health advice in Auckland is simply factually incorrect. The Director-General of Health attended the Cabinet meeting in which that decisions was taken; the advice he presented on the day was different to the written advice that Cabinet had received several days earlier, and the director-general spoke directly to that at the press conference immediately after the decision was taken.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a claim with a specific evidentiary chain (who attended, what advice differed, public confirmation).

rigor.statement: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
rigor.explanation: Tests a prior claim against an outcome — evidence-based challenge.

rigor.statement: Construction is very contingent upon something called interest rates, because you actually need to borrow money to get developments done and built. How you end up with high interest rates is because of wasteful Government spending leading to high inflation, which leads to high interest rates.
rigor.explanation: Coherent causal chain (spending→inflation→rates→construction), though it elides the specific downturn data.

rigor.statement: This is the guy, when he was Minister of Police, crime went up. When he was Minister of Education, school attendance went down... When he was Prime Minister, Government debt went through the roof.
rigor.explanation: Strings correlations during tenure into an implied causal indictment.

rigor.statement: Could I ask the Minister: how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected as a result of the Government of that time ignoring the advice of people who knew what they were talking about?
rigor.explanation: Leading question that bakes in the contested premise that advice was ignored.

rigor.statement: New Zealand's Government debt rose from 18.6 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 38.7 percent in 2022/2023 fiscal year, obviously a very significant increase.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete data to support the conclusion about reduced fiscal headroom.

rigor.statement: Why is he comfortable expanding defence partnerships with a country that has launched an illegal war with Iran, further destabilised the entire Middle East, and upended global fuel supply?
rigor.explanation: Loads several strong contested premises ('illegal war', 'destabilised') into a single question.

rigor.statement: in 2022, when the Marsden Point refinery was closed down, with the approval of the then Labour Government—
rigor.explanation: Rests an argument on a contested attribution of agency.

rigor.statement: I never said that the Labour Government gave its permission; I said that the Labour Government approved of it in the context of an agreement—i.e., they expressed their agreement... why don't we ask the Clerk to consult the dictionary as to whether “approval” can be an expression of agreement.
rigor.explanation: Retreats to a semantic distinction between 'approval' and 'permission' to defend the original framing.

rigor.statement: Roughly 20 percent of the global oil supply, not exclusively feedstock, does pass through the Strait of Hormuz. But more importantly, two-thirds of the crude used by the refineries in Asia which deliver our fuel does come from the Middle East.
rigor.explanation: Links global supply facts to NZ's exposure to make a coherent point.

rigor.statement: all sides of the House have an interest in fuel security—with the exception of the Greens, who do not believe in fossil fuels.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: equates opposing fossil fuels with having no interest in fuel security.

rigor.statement: The Labour Government did not approve the winding down of Marsden Point; it was a private business.
rigor.explanation: Draws the relevant distinction between a private decision and government approval.

rigor.statement: Was 100 percent of the oil refined at Marsden Point refinery, prior to it being closed, imported?
rigor.explanation: A Socratic question exposing the contradiction in the claim that closure made NZ newly dependent on imported fuel.

rigor.statement: Did his decision to completely remove the Clean Car Discount—which has seen electric vehicle sales plummet from 27 percent in 2023, to 8 percent in 2025—increase or decrease our country's dependence on risky fossil fuels?
rigor.explanation: Ties a specific policy change to a measured outcome to frame a clear question.

rigor.statement: Sorry, but the member, when she was part of a Labour-Greens Government, caused a huge amount of failure in our electricity market. Prices went up to $800 per megawatt hour. That caused mills to shut down and low and middle income working New Zealanders to lose their jobs. I'm sorry, but the member has no credibility in energy.
rigor.explanation: Cites a price spike but pins job losses and mill closures on the opponent without establishing the chain.

rigor.statement: Are wages keeping up, when Radio New Zealand reported that 70 percent of workers received a pay rise that failed to keep up with inflation last year?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a reported figure.

veracity.statement: I'll quote directly from paragraph 495 of the royal commission's report: “We consider the failure to ensure that this specific advice reached Ministers and the public was significant.”
veracity.explanation: Presents a verbatim quotation of the commission's finding; accurate insofar as the text is quoted faithfully.

veracity.statement: Speaking to the point of order, the royal commission finds that, on 22 December 2021, the briefing was made available to the Minister for COVID-19 Response, the Hon Chris Hipkins, of those concerns.
veracity.explanation: A specific factual claim about what the commission found, but directly contested by Hipkins who quotes the opposite finding; representation is partial/disputed.

veracity.statement: Treasury advised from the outset that pandemic spending should be timely, temporary, and targeted. Despite that advice, the $60 billion COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund spanned 821 programmes, half of which had nothing to do with the pandemic.
veracity.explanation: Headline figures are broadly defensible, but “half had nothing to do with the pandemic” is a contestable characterisation.

veracity.statement: The claim that the level 4 lockdown was extended against public health advice in Auckland is simply factually incorrect. The Director-General of Health attended the Cabinet meeting in which that decisions was taken; the advice he presented on the day was different to the written advice that Cabinet had received several days earlier, and the director-general spoke directly to that at the press conference immediately after the decision was taken.
veracity.explanation: Detailed and checkable rebuttal; plausible though not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: Well, I'm very proud of the fact that we actually have seen rents stabilise in this country after having gone up $180 a week under his Government.
veracity.explanation: Claiming rents 'stabilise' sits awkwardly against the unrebutted ~10% rise cited in the question.

veracity.statement: We do have an economic recovery under way. That's evidenced by the GDP growth being 1.1 percent in the last quarter. It's evidenced with inflation being low at 3.1 percent... We've got consumer confidence the highest it's been since 2021... business confidence the highest since 2014... building consents up 20 percent, construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year, job ads up 10 percent in the last year.
veracity.explanation: Cherry-picked but largely real indicators; omits the real-wage point that prompted the question.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders returning back to New Zealand was up 12 percent on the previous year. For the last four months, I'm very pleased to say that New Zealanders leaving is less than in any month in the period that he was Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Specific but selectively framed (returns vs departures) and unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: This is the guy, when he was Minister of Police, crime went up. When he was Minister of Education, school attendance went down... When he was Prime Minister, Government debt went through the roof.
veracity.explanation: Each metric directionally has some basis but causation is asserted, not shown.

veracity.statement: Well, the reality is that there would be tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of young people in that age group, and the reality was—as is outlined in paragraphs 413 and 414 of the report—that a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins. It was then considered by the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall on 7 January 2022.
veracity.explanation: Cites the report, but the claim that the briefing 'reached Ministers' is the very point Hipkins disputes.

veracity.statement: New Zealand's Government debt rose from 18.6 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 38.7 percent in 2022/2023 fiscal year, obviously a very significant increase.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the broad debt trajectory of the period.

veracity.statement: That number has now almost tripled to 36,800 visits. With average visitor spend at $5,800 for Chinese visitors, that's an estimated economic injection of $210 million for Kiwi businesses from those who have visited, with Chinese visitors making up 36,200 visits through the new pathway.
veracity.explanation: Concrete figures, though the $210m is an estimate attributing causation to the visa changes.

veracity.statement: In the December quarter, meat exports increased by a significant 21.4 percent; dairy exports were up 10 percent, tourism... grew by 9.4 percent; transportation exports grew by 7.5 percent; and for our foresters, log exports were up by 3.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Precise, checkable figures presented straightforwardly.

veracity.statement: We do have, however, a reasonable supply of fuel, with 25 days' worth of diesel, 27 days' worth of petrol, and similar amounts safely on its way here.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, plausible operational figures.

veracity.statement: in 2022, when the Marsden Point refinery was closed down, with the approval of the then Labour Government—
veracity.explanation: Frames a private commercial closure as government-approved; misleading as worded, and challenged on point of order.

veracity.statement: Roughly 20 percent of the global oil supply, not exclusively feedstock, does pass through the Strait of Hormuz. But more importantly, two-thirds of the crude used by the refineries in Asia which deliver our fuel does come from the Middle East.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with commonly cited Strait of Hormuz and Asian refinery supply data.

veracity.statement: The Labour Government did not approve the winding down of Marsden Point; it was a private business.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the refinery's conversion was a commercial decision by a private company.

veracity.statement: Did his decision to completely remove the Clean Car Discount—which has seen electric vehicle sales plummet from 27 percent in 2023, to 8 percent in 2025—increase or decrease our country's dependence on risky fossil fuels?
veracity.explanation: EV share figures are checkable; attributing the drop solely to the policy is a simplification.

veracity.statement: the October quarter was the lowest level of emissions generated by this country since 2010. That's good news.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim; plausible but unverified and possibly driven by factors beyond policy.

veracity.statement: There is not and has never been a target for X number of patients being seen through this service... The figure of 1 million, which the member is referring to, was not a projected usage target; it relates to survey findings for access to primary care, not to any target for the Online GP Care service.
veracity.explanation: Asserts there was never a 1m target, but McAnulty notes the figure was verified through the parliamentary process as a stated target.

specificity.statement: Treasury advised from the outset that pandemic spending should be timely, temporary, and targeted. Despite that advice, the $60 billion COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund spanned 821 programmes, half of which had nothing to do with the pandemic.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure ($60b), programme count (821) and a precise proportion.

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure ($2.9b) and a quantified outcome (rents up ~10%).

specificity.statement: We do have an economic recovery under way. That's evidenced by the GDP growth being 1.1 percent in the last quarter. It's evidenced with inflation being low at 3.1 percent... We've got consumer confidence the highest it's been since 2021... business confidence the highest since 2014... building consents up 20 percent, construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year, job ads up 10 percent in the last year.
specificity.explanation: Dense with named figures and timeframes.

specificity.statement: Construction is very contingent upon something called interest rates, because you actually need to borrow money to get developments done and built. How you end up with high interest rates is because of wasteful Government spending leading to high inflation, which leads to high interest rates.
specificity.explanation: Mechanism plus some figures (consents up 20%, jobs up 43%).

specificity.statement: New Zealanders returning back to New Zealand was up 12 percent on the previous year. For the last four months, I'm very pleased to say that New Zealanders leaving is less than in any month in the period that he was Prime Minister.
specificity.explanation: Quantified claims with a comparison window.

specificity.statement: Well, the reality is that there would be tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of young people in that age group, and the reality was—as is outlined in paragraphs 413 and 414 of the report—that a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins. It was then considered by the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall on 7 January 2022.
specificity.explanation: Paragraph references and precise dates.

specificity.statement: New Zealand's Government debt rose from 18.6 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 38.7 percent in 2022/2023 fiscal year, obviously a very significant increase.
specificity.explanation: Exact percentages and a fiscal year.

specificity.statement: Yes, I stand by my statement of 6 March, and I also stand by this Government's decision to unwind proposed petrol tax increases by the previous Government which would have added 12c extra to fuel as well as 10c in a regional fuel tax.
specificity.explanation: Names the 12c and 10c tax figures.

specificity.statement: That number has now almost tripled to 36,800 visits. With average visitor spend at $5,800 for Chinese visitors, that's an estimated economic injection of $210 million for Kiwi businesses from those who have visited, with Chinese visitors making up 36,200 visits through the new pathway.
specificity.explanation: Dense with precise visitor counts, average spend and dollar totals.

specificity.statement: In the December quarter, meat exports increased by a significant 21.4 percent; dairy exports were up 10 percent, tourism... grew by 9.4 percent; transportation exports grew by 7.5 percent; and for our foresters, log exports were up by 3.7 percent.
specificity.explanation: Sector-by-sector percentages for a named quarter.

specificity.statement: We do have, however, a reasonable supply of fuel, with 25 days' worth of diesel, 27 days' worth of petrol, and similar amounts safely on its way here.
specificity.explanation: Exact days-of-supply figures for diesel and petrol.

specificity.statement: Roughly 20 percent of the global oil supply, not exclusively feedstock, does pass through the Strait of Hormuz. But more importantly, two-thirds of the crude used by the refineries in Asia which deliver our fuel does come from the Middle East.
specificity.explanation: Quantified proportions tied to a named geography and supply chain.

specificity.statement: Did his decision to completely remove the Clean Car Discount—which has seen electric vehicle sales plummet from 27 percent in 2023, to 8 percent in 2025—increase or decrease our country's dependence on risky fossil fuels?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and quantifies the EV market-share change with years.

specificity.statement: the risk around the dry year has been costing New Zealand about $5 billion a year since 2017. Building this facility takes that risk premium down, and, as I've said before, this will save Kiwis about $265 million a year, or about $50 a household, and will actually protect 2,000 jobs from higher energy prices.
specificity.explanation: Named dollar savings, per-household figure and jobs number.

specificity.statement: the October quarter was the lowest level of emissions generated by this country since 2010. That's good news.
specificity.explanation: Names a quarter and a benchmark year.

specificity.statement: The Government spent around $138 million on estate regeneration last year, with some $16 million being spent on housing alone. Currently, Defence is planning and constructing a further 77 new homes in Waiōuru, Linton, Ōhakea, and Burnham, with additional homes planned in the coming years.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figures plus a count of homes and named bases.

specificity.statement: Are wages keeping up, when Radio New Zealand reported that 70 percent of workers received a pay rise that failed to keep up with inflation last year?
specificity.explanation: Cites a sourced statistic (70%, RNZ) to frame the question.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge the families, the healthcare workers, the business owners, and the tens of thousands of Kiwis who gave evidence to the commission. This report exists because of them.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, gracious acknowledgement reaching across affected groups rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: I'd like to welcome the second royal commission into the COVID-19 response report that is being presented to the House today and thank the royal commission for the work that they have done.
charisma.explanation: Opens magnanimously, welcoming a report whose findings are contested; inclusive framing.

charisma.statement: I would like to thank all of the front-line workers who were involved in New Zealand's COVID-19 response: our doctors, our nurses, all those in the health system, those who worked at the border, those who managed our quarantine and isolation facilities—all of the essential workers who went to work at a time when there was huge fear and huge uncertainty.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive recognition of a broad range of workers; unifying rather than partisan.

charisma.statement: I'd just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.
charisma.explanation: Combative and dismissive rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: If this guy opened a funeral parlour, nobody would die. He can screw up anything—
charisma.explanation: An applause-line insult that rallies one side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: Denial is not an option. Mistakes were made in the economic response, and these mistakes were costly. Those who choose to minimise these errors are not well placed to learn from them.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically firm but addressed to its own side, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Well, it's always the case that family circumstances vary. While some workers will have received pay rises or moved to jobs with higher pay, others will not have received pay rises in the previous year. What our Government is focused on is increasing opportunities in this economy.
charisma.explanation: Measured and non-combative but appeals to her own framing.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the families, the healthcare workers, the business owners, and the tens of thousands of Kiwis who gave evidence to the commission. This report exists because of them.
civility.explanation: Respectful, dignified tone focused on those affected.

civility.statement: I'd like to welcome the second royal commission into the COVID-19 response report that is being presented to the House today and thank the royal commission for the work that they have done.
civility.explanation: Courteous, constructive tone.

civility.statement: I would like to thank all of the front-line workers who were involved in New Zealand's COVID-19 response: our doctors, our nurses, all those in the health system, those who worked at the border, those who managed our quarantine and isolation facilities—all of the essential workers who went to work at a time when there was huge fear and huge uncertainty.
civility.explanation: Respectful and gracious.

civility.statement: The claim that the level 4 lockdown was extended against public health advice in Auckland is simply factually incorrect. The Director-General of Health attended the Cabinet meeting in which that decisions was taken; the advice he presented on the day was different to the written advice that Cabinet had received several days earlier, and the director-general spoke directly to that at the press conference immediately after the decision was taken.
civility.explanation: Disputes the substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the policy substance.

civility.statement: Well, I'm very proud of the fact that we actually have seen rents stabilise in this country after having gone up $180 a week under his Government.
civility.explanation: Comparative jab but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I'd just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.
civility.explanation: Dismissive, calls the question a 'waste of time' and attacks the questioner's record.

civility.statement: I think it's quite interesting the member is so flippant about the efforts of this Government to help low and middle income working New Zealanders... that member spent too much, borrowed too much, for way too long, caused huge amounts of suffering, and he wants to get a go at doing it all again. Not going to happen.
civility.explanation: Accusatory framing of the questioner; little engagement with the substance.

civility.statement: This is the guy, when he was Minister of Police, crime went up. When he was Minister of Education, school attendance went down... When he was Prime Minister, Government debt went through the roof.
civility.explanation: A personalised tally of failures aimed at the individual ('this guy') rather than engaging a policy.

civility.statement: If this guy opened a funeral parlour, nobody would die. He can screw up anything—
civility.explanation: Pure personal mockery, no policy content.

civility.statement: It is not up to the Chair; it is up to the long, decades-old practice in this House that you have to follow the clock and you've got a certain time to speak. His time has expired. His argument expired a long time before that.
civility.explanation: Procedural point laced with a derisive jab at the opponent's argument.

civility.statement: Could I ask the Minister: how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected as a result of the Government of that time ignoring the advice of people who knew what they were talking about?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory of the former government, though aimed at a policy decision.

civility.statement: Denial is not an option. Mistakes were made in the economic response, and these mistakes were costly. Those who choose to minimise these errors are not well placed to learn from them.
civility.explanation: An implied dig at opponents ('those who minimise') folded into a policy point.

civility.statement: I'd suggest the person doing the most damage to themselves today is Mr Hipkins, who seems to be in a state of fervent denial.
civility.explanation: Personal characterisation of an opponent rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: Why is he comfortable expanding defence partnerships with a country that has launched an illegal war with Iran, further destabilised the entire Middle East, and upended global fuel supply?
civility.explanation: Aggressive framing but directed at a policy/foreign-government, not a personal attack on the PM.

civility.statement: I never said that the Labour Government gave its permission; I said that the Labour Government approved of it in the context of an agreement—i.e., they expressed their agreement... why don't we ask the Clerk to consult the dictionary as to whether “approval” can be an expression of agreement.
civility.explanation: Combative but engages on definitional grounds rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: and when the Government said at that point in time, “I do not believe there is a strong case to support continued refinery operations on fuel security grounds.”—I'm right, you're wrong.
civility.explanation: Triumphal 'I'm right, you're wrong' is a cheap shot rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: all sides of the House have an interest in fuel security—with the exception of the Greens, who do not believe in fossil fuels.
civility.explanation: Caricatures the Greens' position as not caring about fuel security.

civility.statement: Sorry, but the member, when she was part of a Labour-Greens Government, caused a huge amount of failure in our electricity market. Prices went up to $800 per megawatt hour. That caused mills to shut down and low and middle income working New Zealanders to lose their jobs. I'm sorry, but the member has no credibility in energy.
civility.explanation: Ends on a personal credibility attack ('no credibility in energy') rather than the policy question asked.

civility.statement: The Prime Minister, of course, is always right, and, ultimately, the tens of thousands of New Zealanders are using this service, and it will continue to grow, as people become more aware of the service.
civility.explanation: Light deflection ('always right') without attacking the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm very proud of the fact that we actually have seen rents stabilise in this country after having gone up $180 a week under his Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why rents rose ~10%, he asserts they have 'stabilised' and pivots to the previous government's record without addressing the figure.

forthrightness.statement: I'd just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly refuses to engage a clear question about whether a 10% rise signals stabilisation.

forthrightness.statement: We do have an economic recovery under way. That's evidenced by the GDP growth being 1.1 percent in the last quarter. It's evidenced with inflation being low at 3.1 percent... We've got consumer confidence the highest it's been since 2021... business confidence the highest since 2014... building consents up 20 percent, construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year, job ads up 10 percent in the last year.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why people should believe the economy is improving when 70% had below-inflation pay rises, he marshals macro stats but does not address real wages.

forthrightness.statement: Construction is very contingent upon something called interest rates, because you actually need to borrow money to get developments done and built. How you end up with high interest rates is because of wasteful Government spending leading to high inflation, which leads to high interest rates.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about $5b less activity and 751 liquidations, he explains causes and cites consents/jobs but does not engage the liquidation figure.

forthrightness.statement: New Zealanders returning back to New Zealand was up 12 percent on the previous year. For the last four months, I'm very pleased to say that New Zealanders leaving is less than in any month in the period that he was Prime Minister.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses migration with counter-figures rather than the 2,000-a-week emigration framing of the question.

forthrightness.statement: I think it's quite interesting the member is so flippant about the efforts of this Government to help low and middle income working New Zealanders... that member spent too much, borrowed too much, for way too long, caused huge amounts of suffering, and he wants to get a go at doing it all again. Not going to happen.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name one family that received the full $250/fortnight promised, he names none and pivots to attack.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the reality is that there would be tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of young people in that age group, and the reality was—as is outlined in paragraphs 413 and 414 of the report—that a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins. It was then considered by the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall on 7 January 2022.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the question, naming paragraphs, dates and the Ministers involved.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I stand by my statement of 6 March, and I also stand by this Government's decision to unwind proposed petrol tax increases by the previous Government which would have added 12c extra to fuel as well as 10c in a regional fuel tax.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms standing by the cited statement and adds substance.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, that was a very wise statement from Nicola Willis, who I also recall at the time was pointing out while we can't control global factors, the Government can always control its own response, including the spending decision it makes.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms the prior statement and reaffirms it, though pivots to attack the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it's always the case that family circumstances vary. While some workers will have received pay rises or moved to jobs with higher pay, others will not have received pay rises in the previous year. What our Government is focused on is increasing opportunities in this economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether wages are keeping up given 70% had below-inflation rises, she diffuses with 'circumstances vary' and pivots to opportunities.

forthrightness.statement: I reject the characterisation and the assumptions that are inherent in that question.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to engage the substance of whether he is comfortable expanding the partnership; rejects framing without answering.

forthrightness.statement: We've canvassed these issues before. As I've said, any intelligence that is collected and shared is done in accordance with New Zealand law.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out providing resources/intelligence to the US-Israel campaign, he gives a process answer ('in accordance with law') rather than ruling it out.

forthrightness.statement: the risk around the dry year has been costing New Zealand about $5 billion a year since 2017. Building this facility takes that risk premium down, and, as I've said before, this will save Kiwis about $265 million a year, or about $50 a household, and will actually protect 2,000 jobs from higher energy prices.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the LNG terminal increases or decreases fossil-fuel dependence, he reframes around dry-year risk and savings rather than answering the dependence question.

forthrightness.statement: There is not and has never been a target for X number of patients being seen through this service... The figure of 1 million, which the member is referring to, was not a projected usage target; it relates to survey findings for access to primary care, not to any target for the Online GP Care service.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers by disputing the premise of the question rather than confirming/denying progress to a figure; partially responsive.

forthrightness.statement: The Prime Minister, of course, is always right, and, ultimately, the tens of thousands of New Zealanders are using this service, and it will continue to grow, as people become more aware of the service.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile the PM's optimism with data showing 5% of the promised reach, he quips and asserts growth rather than addressing the gap.

forthrightness.statement: We haven't been asked. We are not central to the region, we are not central to the issue, and we are a long way away. We haven't been asked and we don't expect we will be.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to categorically rule out military support for the US/Israel, he explains NZ is unlikely to be asked but stops short of a categorical ruling-out.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I stand by my statement of 6 March, and I also stand by this Government's decision to unwind proposed petrol tax increases by the previous Government which would have added 12c extra to fuel as well as 10c in a regional fuel tax.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts her words match her government's action (unwinding the fuel tax), consistent with her stated cost-of-living stance.

authenticity.statement: Yes, that was a very wise statement from Nicola Willis, who I also recall at the time was pointing out while we can't control global factors, the Government can always control its own response, including the spending decision it makes.
authenticity.explanation: Pressed on whether her 2022 demands of the previous government apply to her now, she affirms a consistent position; defensible but self-serving.

strength.statement: That number has now almost tripled to 36,800 visits. With average visitor spend at $5,800 for Chinese visitors, that's an estimated economic injection of $210 million for Kiwi businesses from those who have visited, with Chinese visitors making up 36,200 visits through the new pathway.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered policy change with measurable uptake, though benefit is partly projected.

strength.statement: The Government spent around $138 million on estate regeneration last year, with some $16 million being spent on housing alone. Currently, Defence is planning and constructing a further 77 new homes in Waiōuru, Linton, Ōhakea, and Burnham, with additional homes planned in the coming years.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete, in-progress delivery (spend made, homes under construction) rather than mere aspiration.

divination.statement: the risk around the dry year has been costing New Zealand about $5 billion a year since 2017. Building this facility takes that risk premium down, and, as I've said before, this will save Kiwis about $265 million a year, or about $50 a household, and will actually protect 2,000 jobs from higher energy prices.
divination.explanation: Forecasts $265m/year savings and 2,000 jobs protected — a projected benefit whose accuracy is uncertain.

civility.statement: congratulations to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) for the new website, which I hope we’ve all gone and had a good look at. Good work there. It actually does seem to work quite well. It’s a great example of technical modernisation by this Parliament, in fact.
civility.explanation: Gracious, constructive praise of officials and the institution; no attack.

civility.statement: I’d be curious if the Minister could explain to this committee why we didn’t simply put the relevant definitions and provisions in the Legislation Act for all of the legislation, rather than having general provisions in a specific Act, and having essentially a big red legislative hand going, “And if you want to know about this, you’ve got to go all the way over there”, which is strikes me as kind of poor drafting and just, frankly, hard to read.
civility.explanation: Critiques drafting structure, not any person.

civility.statement: an “instrument of the Crown” is not a department but might otherwise describe—I’m trying not to use the word “entity”, because a Crown entity is different again. An example of the instrument of the Crown, I’m told, is PCO, the Parliamentary Counsel Office
civility.explanation: Good-humoured, respectful follow-up to a colleague's query.

civility.statement: the definition of “minimum legislative information” would have inserted after it “ ‘or MLI’ ”, effectively defining that term, albeit that it’s an acronym that is, at least as yet, not as well known as, for example, “PCO”. I take his point around that.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance and acknowledges the member's point.

civility.statement: To rework the bill in the way that I think he’s proposing would have taken more policy work and time. I think that’s possibly as far as you’ll get from me as an acknowledgment that he makes a very jolly good point and that’s maybe something that could be looked at further.
civility.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of an opposition member's argument.

civility.statement: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
civility.explanation: Disagrees on the substance respectfully.

civility.statement: Thank you in advance to the Minister for his, no doubt, very thoughtful responses on this significant piece of legislation, which has huge constitutional importance.
civility.explanation: Courteous, collegial framing of the exchange.

civility.statement: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
civility.explanation: Constructive, policy-focused engagement with the Minister's amendment.

civility.statement: thinking about either malicious attacks or just mistakes or just data being lost: can I be reassured that there is some way that there will be paper? I’m not requiring any stone tablets to be produced by this Government or any other.
civility.explanation: Good-humoured and non-adversarial.

civility.statement: I always find the committee of the whole House stage with the particular Minister in the chair to be extremely enjoyable and engaging.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful tone toward the Minister.

civility.statement: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
civility.explanation: Disagrees respectfully and defers a broader discussion to 'another day'.

civility.statement: I’d invite Dr Xu-Nan to maybe just reframe that question in the next call, because I was nodding in understanding of his position, not necessarily in response.
civility.explanation: Courteous, honest clarification that avoids letting a misread nod stand as agreement.

charisma.statement: congratulations to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) for the new website, which I hope we’ve all gone and had a good look at. Good work there. It actually does seem to work quite well. It’s a great example of technical modernisation by this Parliament, in fact.
charisma.explanation: Positive, non-partisan tone crediting a shared parliamentary achievement.

charisma.statement: To rework the bill in the way that I think he’s proposing would have taken more policy work and time. I think that’s possibly as far as you’ll get from me as an acknowledgment that he makes a very jolly good point and that’s maybe something that could be looked at further.
charisma.explanation: Concedes merit across the aisle and signals openness to future work — consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I always find the committee of the whole House stage with the particular Minister in the chair to be extremely enjoyable and engaging.
charisma.explanation: Friendly cross-party rapport-building.

charisma.statement: will there be ways for us to be accessible from a disability lens, particularly when we’re looking at the ability for the new legislation website to have better ways for, I guess, speech transcription for those who are blind, in particular?
charisma.explanation: Advocates inclusion of an under-served group in a constructive way.

rigor.statement: I’d be curious if the Minister could explain to this committee why we didn’t simply put the relevant definitions and provisions in the Legislation Act for all of the legislation, rather than having general provisions in a specific Act, and having essentially a big red legislative hand going, “And if you want to know about this, you’ve got to go all the way over there”, which is strikes me as kind of poor drafting and just, frankly, hard to read.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that cross-cutting definitions belong in the Legislation Act rather than a specific Act; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: Whilst New Zealand might not fall if we can’t read our legislation, it still is important that it be sovereign, right? I’d be interested to know when you say hosted on behalf, by or on behalf of PCO, whether it’s in fact hosted in New Zealand, and if it’s on behalf, whether there is any kind of sovereign risk in that?
rigor.explanation: Raises a legitimate data-sovereignty/hosting risk; self-aware hedging ('might not fall') tempers hyperbole.

rigor.statement: what we are providing is not a handy reference, it is the definitive source of what the law is in New Zealand. If that’s the case, saying, “It wasn’t practicable for me to provide the law. The website’s down for a week and we can’t actually get it back up because it’s tricky.”—that’s actually not good enough.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion: because the website is now the definitive legal source, a 'practicable' threshold is too low.

rigor.statement: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
rigor.explanation: Plausible interpretive argument that 'possible' would be read as 'reasonably possible'; some assertion rather than authority cited.

rigor.statement: in the absence of any particular consequence being outlined for non-compliance with the particular requirements of new section 68A in terms of how law is to be published, I wouldn’t have thought there was any different outcome to that which would currently be the case.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference from the bill's silence on consequences, though no external authority cited.

rigor.statement: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete failure mode (law in force but inaccessible) and proposes a targeted fix; conclusion follows from premise.

rigor.statement: if you are able to download secondary legislation, then you may well have the tools to be able to apply a voice system or to increase the size of the print, etc., and so that could be quite an effective way of addressing the accessibility issue by simply changing the word “or” in that paragraph, to the word “and”.
rigor.explanation: Links a download right to practical accessibility tooling; reasoned and concrete.

rigor.statement: We have seen that ManageMyHealth, and also other health data that’s held by private companies, has been subject to malicious attacks. What reassurance can the public have that legislation—including regulations—that is held and is more available to the public and now more vulnerable to attack will be protected from being undermined?
rigor.explanation: Reasons by analogy from health-data breaches to a single-point-of-access legislation site; plausible but the analogy carries the argument.

rigor.statement: thinking about either malicious attacks or just mistakes or just data being lost: can I be reassured that there is some way that there will be paper? I’m not requiring any stone tablets to be produced by this Government or any other.
rigor.explanation: Raises a legitimate redundancy/data-loss concern, but the case is made colourfully/rhetorically rather than with evidence.

rigor.statement: we are seeing, for example, in Canada, legislation is published in both English and French; and, for example, in Wales, legislation is published in both English and Welsh.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete comparative precedents to support a bilingual-drafting proposal.

rigor.statement: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point about reconciling cross-language interpretation, though asserted generally rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: I’m not convinced that that change would make a material difference. Of course, there are probably arguments that as soon as you’re accessing something online, through a device, you have actually downloaded that data, anyway, so there may well be some technical interpretation questions as to why you have “accessed… or downloaded” as being the option.
rigor.explanation: Plausible technical point that accessing online entails downloading, but somewhat asserted rather than established.

specificity.statement: I’d be curious if the Minister could explain to this committee why we didn’t simply put the relevant definitions and provisions in the Legislation Act for all of the legislation, rather than having general provisions in a specific Act, and having essentially a big red legislative hand going, “And if you want to know about this, you’ve got to go all the way over there”, which is strikes me as kind of poor drafting and just, frankly, hard to read.
specificity.explanation: Names specific instruments (Legislation Act, Contract and Commercial Law Act, electronic signature definitions, clause 8/section 16B).

specificity.statement: Whilst New Zealand might not fall if we can’t read our legislation, it still is important that it be sovereign, right? I’d be interested to know when you say hosted on behalf, by or on behalf of PCO, whether it’s in fact hosted in New Zealand, and if it’s on behalf, whether there is any kind of sovereign risk in that?
specificity.explanation: Targets a concrete issue (where the site is hosted) but no figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: what we are providing is not a handy reference, it is the definitive source of what the law is in New Zealand. If that’s the case, saying, “It wasn’t practicable for me to provide the law. The website’s down for a week and we can’t actually get it back up because it’s tricky.”—that’s actually not good enough.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to clause 17 / replacement section 72(2) and the exact words 'as far as practicable'.

specificity.statement: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
specificity.explanation: Names exact mechanism and concrete options (20 or 40 day rectification window).

specificity.statement: if you are able to download secondary legislation, then you may well have the tools to be able to apply a voice system or to increase the size of the print, etc., and so that could be quite an effective way of addressing the accessibility issue by simply changing the word “or” in that paragraph, to the word “and”.
specificity.explanation: Precise textual amendment ('or' to 'and') tied to replacement section 75(2)(a).

specificity.statement: The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
specificity.explanation: Broad value statement with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: will there be ways for us to be accessible from a disability lens, particularly when we’re looking at the ability for the new legislation website to have better ways for, I guess, speech transcription for those who are blind, in particular?
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete feature (speech transcription / screen-reader access for blind users).

specificity.statement: we are seeing, for example, in Canada, legislation is published in both English and French; and, for example, in Wales, legislation is published in both English and Welsh.
specificity.explanation: Cites named jurisdictions and language pairs.

specificity.statement: Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in. We anticipate that this will require publication of secondary legislation in machine-readable formats, and so that means that people who are supported by screen readers will be able to use them to read published legislation. The new website will also aim to comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Level AA
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms: machine-readable formats, screen-reader support, and the WCAG 2.2 Level AA standard.

forthrightness.statement: As for the instrument of the Crown, I might benefit from some advice on that point and would look forward to coming back to him.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to Webb's direct question on what an 'instrument of the Crown' is, he honestly admits he cannot answer yet and defers.

forthrightness.statement: an “instrument of the Crown” is not a department but might otherwise describe—I’m trying not to use the word “entity”, because a Crown entity is different again. An example of the instrument of the Crown, I’m told, is PCO, the Parliamentary Counsel Office
forthrightness.explanation: Returns to Webb's earlier question and gives a direct, concrete answer with an example.

forthrightness.statement: the definition of “minimum legislative information” would have inserted after it “ ‘or MLI’ ”, effectively defining that term, albeit that it’s an acronym that is, at least as yet, not as well known as, for example, “PCO”. I take his point around that.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Webb's MLI question directly (it is now being defined) and concedes the acronym-clarity concern.

forthrightness.statement: those various repealed definitions may relate to a part of the bill that is no longer required because there is an intersection between what this legislation had proposed to do with the Regulatory Standards Act, as it now is. I’ll confirm and let her know if that’s not the case
forthrightness.explanation: Partial, hedged answer to Walters's question on repealed definitions; offers a probable reason but promises to confirm.

forthrightness.statement: I would say that cybersecurity and other considerations are of course important, but I think properly outside the remit of the legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages Webb's security question but answers by deflecting it as out of the bill's scope rather than addressing sovereign-hosting risk substantively.

forthrightness.statement: To rework the bill in the way that I think he’s proposing would have taken more policy work and time. I think that’s possibly as far as you’ll get from me as an acknowledgment that he makes a very jolly good point and that’s maybe something that could be looked at further.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a reason (more policy work/time) but stops short of fully resolving the drafting question.

forthrightness.statement: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages Webb's 'practicable vs possible' question and states a view.

forthrightness.statement: in the absence of any particular consequence being outlined for non-compliance with the particular requirements of new section 68A in terms of how law is to be published, I wouldn’t have thought there was any different outcome to that which would currently be the case.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a cautious but direct answer to Xu-Nan's question on consequences for non-compliance.

forthrightness.statement: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives Xu-Nan a clear 'no' to bilingual drafting in this bill, with a stated reason.

forthrightness.statement: Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in. We anticipate that this will require publication of secondary legislation in machine-readable formats, and so that means that people who are supported by screen readers will be able to use them to read published legislation. The new website will also aim to comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Level AA
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the disability-access questions with specific detail.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not convinced that that change would make a material difference. Of course, there are probably arguments that as soon as you’re accessing something online, through a device, you have actually downloaded that data, anyway, so there may well be some technical interpretation questions as to why you have “accessed… or downloaded” as being the option.
forthrightness.explanation: States a clear view on Walters's 'or' vs 'and' proposal.

forthrightness.statement: I’d invite Dr Xu-Nan to maybe just reframe that question in the next call, because I was nodding in understanding of his position, not necessarily in response.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly admits he has not actually answered and asks for the question to be restated.

veracity.statement: New Zealand law includes the Bill of Rights 1688, which is New Zealand law that predates New Zealand in terms of New Zealand
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Bill of Rights 1688 is retained as part of New Zealand law (via the Imperial Laws Application Act 1988) and predates the modern NZ state.

veracity.statement: while the Edward VII and then King George VI were both born in November and December, respectively, their birthdays were celebrated in the middle of the year to allow for that.
veracity.explanation: Edward VII (Nov) and George VI (Dec) birth months are accurate, and the official mid-year birthday tradition is broadly attributed to weather, though the precise origin is contestable.

veracity.statement: We have seen that ManageMyHealth, and also other health data that’s held by private companies, has been subject to malicious attacks. What reassurance can the public have that legislation—including regulations—that is held and is more available to the public and now more vulnerable to attack will be protected from being undermined?
veracity.explanation: Health-data systems including ManageMyHealth have been subject to security incidents; broadly accurate though stated generally.

veracity.statement: we are seeing, for example, in Canada, legislation is published in both English and French; and, for example, in Wales, legislation is published in both English and Welsh.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Canadian federal legislation is bilingual (English/French) and Welsh legislation is published in English and Welsh.

veracity.statement: even in British or English legislation, they currently still use Normandy French because Law French goes back to the courts in the 13 th century.
veracity.explanation: Law French is genuine and dates to the Norman period; 'currently still use' is accurate only for a few residual formulae (e.g. royal assent phrases), so partly overstated.

authenticity.statement: The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the Greens' stated accessibility/transparency positioning, but no action shown either way in the text.

divination.statement: Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in. We anticipate that this will require publication of secondary legislation in machine-readable formats, and so that means that people who are supported by screen readers will be able to use them to read published legislation. The new website will also aim to comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Level AA
divination.explanation: Forecast that the regulations 'will require' machine-readable formats; plausible given the stated policy intent, but contingent on future regulations.

forthrightness.statement: the fact that the secondary legislation doesn't come into force until it's published kind of takes care of that. If the regulator wants the rule to be enforced or regulatable, they should publish it and bring it into force.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses Walters' earlier question about whether there should be a mandatory publication date, pointing to clause 20's mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: my instinct would be that the legal status of any secondary legislation or, in fact, legislation, would be that the Order in Council or the regulation which is signed off by the Minister or the Governor-General is the one that is the final version and has legal force
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Walters' question on legal status but expressly hedges ('I'll stand to be corrected') and offers an instinct rather than a settled answer.

forthrightness.statement: If it was "must include", then, therefore, the report would be legally required to include recommendations on something that it might not have a recommendation on. A report has the option of including a recommendation, but it doesn't have to do it
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Walters' question about why the annual report's repeal recommendations are 'may' not 'must'.

forthrightness.statement: The term "official versions" means that a printout of the website is taken to state the law. That makes it easier to use in court proceedings. If you are presenting the court with a printout of the website, that will be accepted as what is the law.
forthrightness.explanation: Squarely answers Walters' question on the effect and legal status of 'official versions'.

forthrightness.statement: I'll have to think about the interaction between the powerful Regulations Review Committee and the Parliamentary Counsel Office's editorial ability—editorial change ability... I can't exactly comment on that at the moment, but I will get some advice from officials.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly admits he cannot answer Xu-Nan's question now and defers to official advice — honest but not a substantive answer.

forthrightness.statement: I acknowledge the member's amendments, but we wouldn't support them for the reasons that I've outlined.
forthrightness.explanation: Clear, unambiguous statement of the Government's position on Xu-Nan's amendments.

forthrightness.statement: It is the case that if a piece of secondary legislation is needing to be published, which provides a consolidation of all secondary legislation that incorporates all of the amendments made by every amending instrument—if it doesn't meet the requirements of publication, it is all repealed. So I have to correct that: it is all repealed.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives the corrected substantive answer rather than glossing over the change.

forthrightness.statement: Despite my intense passion and love of that particular piece of legislation, I haven't yet committed them all to memory, so I'll take a chance to look it up.
forthrightness.explanation: Honestly admits he cannot answer the Civil Aviation Act point now and defers to looking it up.

forthrightness.statement: You've got, essentially, a default provision in clause 2(1), which is the "Act comes into force on a date or dates set by Order in Council."... except for, in subclause (2), the specific sections... they'll come into force on the day after Royal assent.
forthrightness.explanation: Fully and directly explains the commencement provisions on request.

forthrightness.statement: the transitional provisions require all existing agencies' secondary legislation to be republished. So everything needs to be republished. If an agency fails to republish, regulations can be made under the Legislation Act, which can provide the possibility that the legislation is revoked.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's question about what happens to secondary legislation not updated by the deadline.

forthrightness.statement: My understanding is that the current website won't require retrospectivity... They're expensive to create and they're expensive to maintain, and I'd be surprised if we go for a whole new one again.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's second question on whether retrospectivity is needed for the new legislation website.

forthrightness.statement: I have done a bit of work in the past on the Incorporated Societies Act when that came into force. forthrightness.explanation: Engages Xu-Nan's question about the five-year fallback with a relevant example, but qualified as recollection rather than a confirmed answer.

specificity.statement: the fact that the secondary legislation doesn't come into force until it's published kind of takes care of that. If the regulator wants the rule to be enforced or regulatable, they should publish it and bring it into force.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific clause and the operative mechanism (no force until published), though no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: should that secondary piece of legislation fall off a website, it would still be law, regardless of people not being able to access it.
specificity.explanation: Concrete scenario tied to her proposed amendment, though no precise drafting offered here.

specificity.statement: while this has been in place since the 1990s, that was at a time when PCO may not have had the capacity to do some of the drafting, which is not necessarily the case nowadays.
specificity.explanation: References the 1990s origin and the select committee recommendation, though without dates or figures.

specificity.statement: The term "official versions" means that a printout of the website is taken to state the law. That makes it easier to use in court proceedings. If you are presenting the court with a printout of the website, that will be accepted as what is the law.
specificity.explanation: Concrete explanation of the practical effect in court proceedings.

specificity.statement: there is a risk, on one analysis, that you can do sweeping reforms. It's clearly not intended... particularly those first three—could look like a reform programme. But we know that that's not what revision bills actually are about.

specificity.statement: To have two bills go through in 14 years since the system's been available is probably not a great reflection of its accessibility and usability.

specificity.statement: You've got, essentially, a default provision in clause 2(1), which is the "Act comes into force on a date or dates set by Order in Council."... except for, in subclause (2), the specific sections... they'll come into force on the day after Royal assent.

specificity.statement: the transitional provisions require all existing agencies' secondary legislation to be republished. So everything needs to be republished. specificity.statement: My understanding is that the current website won't require retrospectivity... They're expensive to create and they're expensive to maintain, and I'd be surprised if we go for a whole new one again.
