Sadly, that CEO has confirmed to me that such a proposal could never work because of the regulatory unwillingness of the last Government to make it easier for such a thing to be developed, and the only reason that the member is talking about 70 million litres of storage is because she closed 700 million litres down.
civility.explanation: Repeats the 'she closed 700 million litres' personal-blame line.

civility.statement: Why did he tell the House yesterday there was no budget for a diesel reserve, when officials had identified a surplus of almost $50 million in the fuel levy fund, rising to around $110 million by 2025, specifically there to pay for fuel resilience measures like the diesel reserve?
civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive, focused on the factual record.

civility.statement: this is a finance Minister who has borrowed more we did when we were in Government, and the only strategy that she seems to have is hope, and that has been no more evident than what we've seen over the last three or four weeks as New Zealand has navigated a cost of living crisis.
civility.explanation: 'Only strategy is hope' is a sharp characterisation but aimed at strategy, not person.

civility.statement: Well, by Shane Jones' logic, Oji Fibre Solutions, Smithfield meatworks, Winstone Pulp, Carter Holt Harvey, Heinz Wattie's, and McCain Foods have all been allowed to be shut down by this Government.
civility.explanation: Combative but engages the logic of the opponent's argument.

civility.statement: the fact that the Government of the day considered a report on the implications of Marsden Point being closed by its private sector owners does not mean the Government approved of it... But lack of intervention to prop up a business that was closing anyway does not mean the Government approved of that business closing.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the dispute without personal attack.

civility.statement: how does this temporary brief oversight for a few minutes compare with the over $52 million bribe through the Public Interest Journalism Fund?
civility.explanation: Levels an allegation of bribery, an imputation of corruption rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: I know that the member is very excited about her very first question as education spokesperson and would love a great conspiracy, but unfortunately there is not one here. But I look forward to her next question abut something that is relevant to achievement.
civility.explanation: Condescending personal framing of the questioner ('excited', 'would love a conspiracy').

civility.statement: Has the Minister considered engaging a private detective to get to the bottom of this weighty matter—who did it, who took it off the YouTube channel, and how do we make sure it never happens again?
civility.explanation: Sarcasm mocking the opposition's line of questioning rather than engaging it, though not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I also want to note that it is a very difficult time for anyone affected by these proposals—workers, growers, and contractors alike—and my thoughts are with those involved. Support is available from the Ministry of Social Development, including help with finding new employment and income support for those who are eligible.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges those affected respectfully and points to concrete support.

civility.statement: I think the member is confused; he's referring to a quarterly growth rate for the fourth quarter of the year... I would refer the member to the Statistics New Zealand website—it's easy to find on Google—which shows that the economy grew in the last calendar year.
civility.explanation: 'The member is confused' and 'easy to find on Google' are belittling asides.

civility.statement: Is $12 extra enough to meet the additional costs of fuel and other living expenses, or does she expect people living in poverty to get further into debt simply to survive?
civility.explanation: Pointed and loaded, but targets the policy's adequacy rather than the Minister personally.

civility.statement: Other parties, as we have heard, opposed all savings—opposed all savings. They want to bring back expensive programmes and spend and borrow more.
civility.explanation: Caricatures opponents' position rather than engaging specific objections.

civility.statement: when you have just agreed with the point of order made by Chris Hipkins that the assertion that the previous Government closed Marsden Point is incorrect, and he then turns around and ignores that and says it anyway, we are going to express concern about that.
civility.explanation: A measured procedural objection focused on accuracy, distinguishing legitimate political answers from false assertions.

forthrightness.statement: I don't have that number right at hand today, but I just say to you that, yes, there is no doubt about it, LNG prices have increased around the world.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the specific increase in global LNG price; admits he lacks the figure but confirms the direction.

forthrightness.statement: Well, no disrespect, but that is a member who delivered a failed energy policy—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the LNG terminal makes NZ more or less reliant on imports; pivots immediately to attacking the questioner's record.

forthrightness.statement: It had a Lake Onslow project at $17 billion—$8,000 for every single household in the country—that led to an $800 megawatt per hour price in wholesale electricity prices. What we are doing, as I've previously explained, is we're dealing with the dry-year risk, lowering the risk premium, and therefore wanting to lower power bills by $50 for every household.
forthrightness.explanation: Eventually describes his own plan but only after deflecting the asked question onto the opponent.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it meant that New Zealand is the only country I know of that's making the rather unique transition from domestic gas to international coal, and, in the process, worsening emissions. But that is a function of a failed Labour-Greens energy policy.
forthrightness.explanation: Friendly question on import dependence; broadly answers but wraps it in blame.

forthrightness.statement: As I just said to the member, the phases of our National Fuel Plan and how they will be considered will be discussed on Friday.
forthrightness.explanation: One of several specific operational questions on the fuel emergency framework deferred wholesale to a future announcement.

forthrightness.statement: Because, unlike what we observed under a previous Government, we have learnt the lessons of COVID mismanagement. We are making sure that we are doing it appropriately and with industry on board, and we will deliver that, as I said, on Friday, as we foreshadowed last week.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why basic questions about a two-year-old framework can't be answered; deflects with a COVID jab and another deferral.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that is true. The conflict is hurting Kiwis with higher fuel prices.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he won't condemn the perpetrators; concedes the harm but doesn't address the condemnation point.

forthrightness.statement: We have not been asked or there have been no proposals put to us about any military engagement. We are very focused on actually responding to this conflict and the impact that it has on Kiwis. That's where our focus is.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to categorically rule out military support; states no proposals exist but stops short of ruling it out.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, these are independent actions by the US and Israel, and it's up to them to explain the basis for their attacks.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to condemn 'Operation Epic Fury'; sidesteps by passing responsibility for explanation back to the US and Israel.

forthrightness.statement: Fitch Ratings has confirmed New Zealand's foreign currency rating at AA+ but revised the outlook from “stable” to “negative”. Fitch is concerned about delays in fiscal consolidation and debt reduction, due to weaker than expected economic growth.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what reports she has seen on the fiscal position.

forthrightness.statement: Net core Crown debt rose markedly as a proportion of GDP, and forecasts made before the Middle East conflict show debt getting close to the debt ceiling of 50 percent of GDP—that is the debt ceiling recommended by Treasury.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses how prepared NZ is for a shock.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, the former Minster did leave some squiggles on a Cabinet paper. There was, however, no well-developed proposal and, I just want to remind the House, that it was September 2021 when the Labour Cabinet approved the closure of the refinery, and then it took until—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a $50m levy surplus for a diesel reserve; minimises ('squiggles') rather than addressing the funds.

forthrightness.statement: That account is dedicated to a range of expenses, and if the member would like to write me a letter without squiggles, I shall provide a detailed answer.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a precise figure (the levy account balance) and refuses to give one, deflecting with a quip.

forthrightness.statement: Sadly, New Zealand is labouring under a shortage of capacity to store fuel. You cannot lay that problem at any other place than the feet of that woman, who approved the closure of the refinery.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about storage at Marsden Point today; deflects entirely into blame.

forthrightness.statement: As night fell on the last Labour Government and as they fled from their Cabinet offices, there was a half-baked proposal—unfunded, incomplete—and in the interests of good constitutional Government, I couldn't take that forward in that incomplete state.
forthrightness.explanation: Does offer a reason for not proceeding, amid the rhetoric.

forthrightness.statement: I have taken the liberty of speaking to the CEO of Port Taranaki, one of the entities that was involved with what the Hon Megan Woods is referring to. Sadly, that CEO has confirmed to me that such a proposal could never work because of the regulatory unwillingness of the last Government to make it easier for such a thing to be developed, and the only reason that the member is talking about 70 million litres of storage is because she closed 700 million litres down.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the diesel-reserve question but routes it back into blame.

forthrightness.statement: The ministerial video was mistakenly uploaded to the wrong site. When brought to my attention it was resolved within about 15 minutes, and an email to the sector was sent this morning with the correct link to the same video.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains the error and the remedy in response to the question.

forthrightness.statement: It was human error. Of course, I take responsibility for all of the things that happen in my office, as you would expect.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the responsibility question, though leaves the 'who authorised' specifics unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: I know that the member is very excited about her very first question as education spokesperson and would love a great conspiracy, but unfortunately there is not one here. But I look forward to her next question abut something that is relevant to achievement.
forthrightness.explanation: Dodges the 'pattern of behaviour' question by dismissing it.

forthrightness.statement: It is worth remembering that 2.9 million New Zealanders are working in jobs across the country, and that this rose by 15,000 in the last quarter. While the last few years have been challenging for many manufacturers, the Performance of Manufacturing Index has shown the manufacturing sector, as a whole, expanding each month since the middle of last year.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the closures contribute to growth; answers obliquely via aggregate framing.

forthrightness.statement: the unemployment figure reflects both new jobs that are created and jobs that are lost, and it is the case, in any modern developed economy, that while some firms close, other firms open... It is the overall balance of these factors that determines the unemployment rate.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the mechanism rather than directly conceding the closures raise unemployment.

forthrightness.statement: I think the member is confused; he's referring to a quarterly growth rate for the fourth quarter of the year... I would refer the member to the Statistics New Zealand website—it's easy to find on Google—which shows that the economy grew in the last calendar year.
forthrightness.explanation: Defends her record and cites a source, though dismissively.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, it is $20, not $50.
forthrightness.explanation: A direct, concrete correction of the figure put to her.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government is very clear about the fact that what is happening in the Middle East is having an impact on many New Zealanders, with the fuel-price pressure that they are facing. We are also very clear that any response needs to be targeted, timely, and temporary, otherwise every single person in New Zealand would be affected by inflation going up again.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether $12 is enough for those in poverty; pivots to the 'targeted, timely, temporary' rationale without answering.

rigor.statement: It had a Lake Onslow project at $17 billion—$8,000 for every single household in the country—that led to an $800 megawatt per hour price in wholesale electricity prices. What we are doing, as I've previously explained, is we're dealing with the dry-year risk, lowering the risk premium, and therefore wanting to lower power bills by $50 for every household.
rigor.explanation: Marshals figures and a mechanism (dry-year risk premium) but blends in contestable causal claims.

rigor.statement: What I do know is that this conflict won't result in a windfall gain of hundreds of millions of dollars in extra GST, as some have alleged; that is simply economic illiteracy.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the conclusion without spelling out the offsetting-spending reasoning.

rigor.statement: The bill limits objections to those who live or work in the local council area or within 1 kilometre of the proposed licence... In one case, a venue spent $45,000 preparing for a hearing that the objector didn't even turn up for.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote ($45,000 case) to justify a general rule.

rigor.statement: I have taken the liberty of speaking to the CEO of Port Taranaki, one of the entities that was involved with what the Hon Megan Woods is referring to. Sadly, that CEO has confirmed to me that such a proposal could never work because of the regulatory unwillingness of the last Government to make it easier for such a thing to be developed, and the only reason that the member is talking about 70 million litres of storage is because she closed 700 million litres down.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an unnamed-detail appeal to authority (the CEO 'confirmed') rather than documentary evidence.

rigor.statement: Why did he tell the House yesterday there was no budget for a diesel reserve, when officials had identified a surplus of almost $50 million in the fuel levy fund, rising to around $110 million by 2025, specifically there to pay for fuel resilience measures like the diesel reserve?
rigor.explanation: Builds a documented contradiction between yesterday's claim and identified funds.

rigor.statement: How can he claim there was no budget, no proposal for Labour's diesel reserve that had not only tens of millions of dollars available for funding it but also had a legislated change to make the levy available and a Cabinet decision to start work on procurement?
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the 'unfunded, incomplete' characterisation with concrete steps taken.

rigor.statement: We have GDP that is lower than it was two years ago. That will be a context for the delivery of this year's Budget. We have unemployment that is higher now than it was two years ago. We have business liquidations higher now than they were two years ago. We have the number of children in poverty higher now than it was two years ago. And our economic outlook from our credit agency, Fitch, has been downgraded under this Government.
rigor.explanation: Marshals multiple indicators to frame the fiscal context coherently.

rigor.statement: Well, by Shane Jones' logic, Oji Fibre Solutions, Smithfield meatworks, Winstone Pulp, Carter Holt Harvey, Heinz Wattie's, and McCain Foods have all been allowed to be shut down by this Government.
rigor.explanation: A reductio that exposes the inconsistency in applying 'allowed to close' as government approval.

rigor.statement: The only difference is that in Government, when we saw something shutting down, as a Cabinet, we discussed it; we took a paper to Cabinet, and we said, “What are the implications for New Zealand? We need to put a plan in place to respond to that.” Have we seen this Government do that? No, we have not.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clear distinction but the contrast claim is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: When you actually drill down to what the Treasury projections were, it's 1 percent growth. That is what is meant to be feeding New Zealanders' hope.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the Minister's 'anecdata' with cited projections.

rigor.statement: the fact that the Government of the day considered a report on the implications of Marsden Point being closed by its private sector owners does not mean the Government approved of it... But lack of intervention to prop up a business that was closing anyway does not mean the Government approved of that business closing.
rigor.explanation: Clean logical distinction between considering a report and approving an outcome.

rigor.statement: On the definition that Shane Jones is now creating, the McCain Foods factory, the Wattie's factory, the Kinleith factory, the Winstone factory have all been closed— —by this Government.
rigor.explanation: Mirrors Jones's logic to expose it, though deliberately adopts the same flawed inference to make the point.

rigor.statement: how does this temporary brief oversight for a few minutes compare with the over $52 million bribe through the Public Interest Journalism Fund?
rigor.explanation: False equivalence plus a loaded 'bribe' framing rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: if you read the document in 2021 it is as plain as daylight they are being asked “What are the consequences if we make this decision? Will it be a crisis for this country?” or words to that effect, and they said no. That's an approval of closure and we're not going to stand by here and turn a document of evidence into something that we can't use.
rigor.explanation: An interpretive reading of a document; the inference from 'no crisis' to 'approval of closure' is a stretch.

rigor.statement: 62.2 percent of patients are now receiving their first specialist assessment within four months, up from 60.6 percent the same time the year before; while 64.5 percent of patients are receiving their elective treatment within four months, up from 59.2 percent the same time the year before... 179,816 first specialist assessments carried out in this quarter, up by more than 11,000 compared to the same time the year before; and 51,513 elective treatments, up by more than 4,500 compared to the same time the year before.
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in concrete, comparable data.

rigor.statement: On average, it's taking 128 working days for decisions on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in scope... Green Steel... said it would have taken a minimum of six years to take the project through the Resource Management Act (RMA) consenting process; under fast track, just seven months. Kings Quarry said that using fast track instead of the RMA saved them three years in consenting time. Their project was approved in just over six months.
rigor.explanation: Uses named project examples to support the time-saving claim.

rigor.statement: It is worth remembering that 2.9 million New Zealanders are working in jobs across the country, and that this rose by 15,000 in the last quarter. While the last few years have been challenging for many manufacturers, the Performance of Manufacturing Index has shown the manufacturing sector, as a whole, expanding each month since the middle of last year.
rigor.explanation: Reframes individual firm closures within macro context — logically sound.

rigor.statement: the unemployment figure reflects both new jobs that are created and jobs that are lost, and it is the case, in any modern developed economy, that while some firms close, other firms open... It is the overall balance of these factors that determines the unemployment rate.
rigor.explanation: Accurate, generally-applicable economic reasoning about net job flows.

rigor.statement: Our Government is very clear about the fact that what is happening in the Middle East is having an impact on many New Zealanders, with the fuel-price pressure that they are facing. We are also very clear that any response needs to be targeted, timely, and temporary, otherwise every single person in New Zealand would be affected by inflation going up again.
rigor.explanation: Offers an inflation-based reason for limiting relief, though it sidesteps the adequacy question.

rigor.statement: In contrast, over the last two Budgets, the Government has made cumulative ongoing savings of over $11 billion a year... $60 billion was borrowed and spent during COVID-19, and $30 billion of that was on non-direct COVID expenditure—half of it not directly related to COVID.
rigor.explanation: References Treasury and a royal commission report to support the figures, but the 'non-direct' framing is interpretive.

rigor.statement: when you have just agreed with the point of order made by Chris Hipkins that the assertion that the previous Government closed Marsden Point is incorrect, and he then turns around and ignores that and says it anyway, we are going to express concern about that.
rigor.explanation: Clearly articulates the inconsistency between a conceded point and the Minister's repeated claim.

strength.statement: we're in the process of approving a project in Southland that will deliver renewable energy to 100,000 homes, which the Labour-Greens Government didn't approve.
strength.explanation: 'In the process of approving' is announcement/intent, not delivered renewable capacity.

strength.statement: This bill makes a series of changes which will free New Zealanders and businesses from the stranglehold of red tape and support economic growth.
strength.explanation: Introduction of a bill is action-in-progress, not delivered reform.

strength.statement: From term 2 this year, parents will have access to clearer, more useful information about how their child's school is performing... The new ERO reports will focus on student achievement, progress, and engagement, with clear measures, visual summaries, as well as more detail in the back end.
strength.explanation: An announced overhaul not yet implemented — intent with delivery pending.

strength.statement: 62.2 percent of patients are now receiving their first specialist assessment within four months, up from 60.6 percent the same time the year before; while 64.5 percent of patients are receiving their elective treatment within four months, up from 59.2 percent the same time the year before... 179,816 first specialist assessments carried out in this quarter, up by more than 11,000 compared to the same time the year before; and 51,513 elective treatments, up by more than 4,500 compared to the same time the year before.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for measurable improvements actually being delivered.

strength.statement: Faster cancer treatment has improved, with 87 percent of patients now receiving treatment within 31 days of a decision to treat, up from 85.9 percent... Childhood immunisation rates have also lifted to 82.9 percent, up from 77 percent... Shorter stays in emergency departments... 74.2 percent of patients being admitted, discharged, or transferred within six hours, up from 72.1 percent.
strength.explanation: Points to delivered, measured gains across health targets.

strength.statement: On average, it's taking 128 working days for decisions on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in scope... Green Steel... said it would have taken a minimum of six years to take the project through the Resource Management Act (RMA) consenting process; under fast track, just seven months. Kings Quarry said that using fast track instead of the RMA saved them three years in consenting time. Their project was approved in just over six months.
strength.explanation: Points to actual approvals delivered under the fast-track regime.

charisma.statement: we're in the process of approving a project in Southland that will deliver renewable energy to 100,000 homes, which the Labour-Greens Government didn't approve.
charisma.explanation: Frames an achievement against the opposition rather than building common ground.

charisma.statement: We have GDP that is lower than it was two years ago. That will be a context for the delivery of this year's Budget. We have unemployment that is higher now than it was two years ago. We have business liquidations higher now than they were two years ago. We have the number of children in poverty higher now than it was two years ago. And our economic outlook from our credit agency, Fitch, has been downgraded under this Government.
charisma.explanation: Effective for her own side but framed as an indictment, not bridge-building.

charisma.statement: Has the Minister considered engaging a private detective to get to the bottom of this weighty matter—who did it, who took it off the YouTube channel, and how do we make sure it never happens again?
charisma.explanation: A partisan applause line aimed at deflating opponents, not persuading them.

charisma.statement: I also want to note that it is a very difficult time for anyone affected by these proposals—workers, growers, and contractors alike—and my thoughts are with those involved. Support is available from the Ministry of Social Development, including help with finding new employment and income support for those who are eligible.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic and inclusive in tone before the political argument.

charisma.statement: Other parties, as we have heard, opposed all savings—opposed all savings. They want to bring back expensive programmes and spend and borrow more.
charisma.explanation: Rallying his own side via a blanket characterisation of opponents.

authenticity.statement: In total, we have made $43 billion worth of savings across the last two Budgets, with further savings planned in Budget 2026. Any slippage in our fiscal targets has occurred because of forecast revisions outside the Government's immediate control, not because of discretionary spending or revenue decisions. Unlike the last finance Minister, I stick to my operating allowances.
authenticity.explanation: 'I stick to my operating allowances' is a self-consistency claim directly challenged later (borrowing more than the prior government).

authenticity.statement: The only difference is that in Government, when we saw something shutting down, as a Cabinet, we discussed it; we took a paper to Cabinet, and we said, “What are the implications for New Zealand? We need to put a plan in place to respond to that.” Have we seen this Government do that? No, we have not.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent process for her own former government; plausible but self-serving and unverified here.

authenticity.statement: It was human error. Of course, I take responsibility for all of the things that happen in my office, as you would expect.
authenticity.explanation: Owns the mistake rather than deflecting; words align with accepting accountability.

divination.statement: instead what we'd see are New Zealand – trained graduate nurses getting on the plane with the tens of thousands of other young New Zealanders who are leaving the country because they do not see a future here. We are in danger of becoming a training ground for Australia when it comes to our medical professionals.
divination.explanation: Predicts continued emigration of NZ-trained nurses; directionally consistent with current outflow trends but magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: Take the Green Steel project... they expect it will create about 200 skilled jobs in the region. Arataki, the new housing development in Hawke's Bay—200 new residential allotments—estimates it will create over 630 jobs over the five-year development period during construction.
divination.explanation: Forecasts of job creation ('expect ~200', 'over 630') over multi-year horizons — plausible but unproven.

civility.statement: if you're the architect of a plan to build 100,000 homes and you build less than 1,000, then you'd talk that sort of trash, wouldn't you?
civility.explanation: Sneering jab at Twyford ('talk that sort of trash') framed as a personal put-down rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: I'm just sitting in here listening to insults and snaps and barbs being traded and personal insults being made; it always leaves out the actual human people's realities who are at the centre of the violence of an illegal war, and those real lives and the harm on them is quickly forgotten in a tit-for-tat political debate. I abhor that.
civility.explanation: Explicitly deplores personal insults and refocuses on substance and human impact.

civility.statement: he has had to correct himself at least twice because he doesn't even know what his own ministries are doing to provide some practical support to the very people who are living under stress and fear right now.
civility.explanation: Criticism edges into the personal ('doesn't even know') rather than focusing purely on the policy gap.

civility.statement: I'd like to talk about the way that people are being affected at home by this conflict, but I want to first respond to some of the amoral tripe that I've heard from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' arguments as 'amoral tripe' — insult rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: Some people are so blinded by their hatred of Israel, and perhaps the type of people that live there, and their hatred of America that they can't see the moral dimension of this conflict.
civility.explanation: Imputes bigotry and hatred to opponents — a strawman of their position rather than addressing it.

civility.statement: I mean, as for Christopher "Bambi" Hipkins, who I now call "No-eye deer", who said he literally has no idea what should be done about it, well, this Government does.
civility.explanation: Mocking nicknames aimed at an opponent — pure personal ridicule.

civility.statement: Even today, there are people, sadly—and I see one of them is in this House—who think that Mr Putin's really quite a nice bloke, if only he wasn't provoked by that nasty NATO, aka our allies.
civility.explanation: Mocks a named colleague's position via caricature rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: 47 years of oppression of its own people, 30,000 Iranians who happened to wish to protest their Government murdered in January this year, and there's not a peep from the human rights proponents on the other side.
civility.explanation: Legitimate point about the regime, but the 'not a peep from the human rights proponents' jab targets opponents' motives.

civility.statement: I can tell those members on the other side who has to fight those fights; it's actually our Defence Force. Frankly, I'm not putting them forward if we don't have to do something, because it's their lives while people on the other side are talking from their very, very excited position of holier than thou.
civility.explanation: Substantive concern undercut by the 'holier than thou' characterisation of opponents.

civility.statement: when she doesn't even pronounce Mark Rutte's name correctly. For goodness' sake, get these things right. If you're going to start quoting the secretary-general of NATO, for goodness' sake, give the man his name.
civility.explanation: Belittles an opponent over pronunciation, though softened by prior praise of her; more cheap shot than substance.

civility.statement: This is hypocrisy. I didn't call anybody a hypocrite, Mr Speaker, but this is hypocrisy.
civility.explanation: Charges the government with hypocrisy while pointedly avoiding naming an individual — accusatory but procedurally careful.

civility.statement: The principle is this: don't say anything that might attract a late night tweet from the White House. New Zealand's once proud, independent foreign policy has under this Government... been reduced to abject servility to the Trump White House.
civility.explanation: Mocking characterisation ('abject servility') aimed at impugning the government rather than its policy reasoning.

civility.statement: I want to, first of all, acknowledge the Iranian people... any family in a conflict zone is in a horrific place, but, of course, the brutal regime that they have had to survive under for some decades is terrible as well.
civility.explanation: Respectful, measured tone that engages the humanitarian substance.

civility.statement: Words matter, and we need to dial it back a notch from some of the rhetoric that we've heard on the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Calls for restraint and lower temperature, though directed pointedly at 'the other side'.

civility.statement: What we've seen from the Government and from the Minister of Foreign Affairs today is an incoherent and rambling knee-jerk approach. They are making it up as they go along.
civility.explanation: Harsh characterisation of the government's competence; criticism of conduct but bordering on dismissive.

civility.statement: Now, I agree with much of what has been said on the other side: the Iranian regime is a despicable regime that has an atrocious human rights record. We rightly recognise the people of Iran, both resident in Iran and the communities in New Zealand and around the world.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the other side's case.

civility.statement: I do want to acknowledge the Finance and Expenditure Committee's work on this. We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough... I do want to also acknowledge the 275 individuals and groups who submitted on this bill.
civility.explanation: Constructive, acknowledges cross-party committee work and public submitters with respect.

civility.statement: Now, there is one good measure, and I want to front-foot it because I'm a positive guy. I like to start by saying positive things. One good measure that this bill does that we do support is the change to exempt income from selling electricity to the grid. That is a good change.
civility.explanation: Constructive, acknowledges merit in an opponent's bill.

civility.statement: It's emblematic of what this Government has done through the entire term: giving tax cuts to big landlords, big fossil, and big tobacco.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical 'big landlords/fossil/tobacco' framing characterises motives rather than engaging specifics.

civility.statement: The so-called digital nomad tax exemption stems from some fantasy that this Government has that the way to create a modern, resilient, productive economy is to sell our country to foreign investors. It is selling to them our conservation land, allowing them to buy our houses, and now, apparently, exempting them from the tax regimes in this country.
civility.explanation: Attributes a 'fantasy' motive to the government rather than engaging the policy's stated rationale.

rigor.statement: if you're the architect of a plan to build 100,000 homes and you build less than 1,000, then you'd talk that sort of trash, wouldn't you?
rigor.explanation: Has a factual core (KiwiBuild's target-vs-delivery gap) but deployed as an ad hominem to dismiss the opponent.

rigor.statement: Some people are so blinded by their hatred of Israel, and perhaps the type of people that live there, and their hatred of America that they can't see the moral dimension of this conflict.
rigor.explanation: Strawman/ad hominem; substitutes an imputed motive for an argument.

rigor.statement: There were people about 80 years ago who said that maybe Mr Hitler could be worked with and seen sense with—if only we could keep the economy preserved during that time.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to historical analogy (appeasement of Hitler) to discredit opponents rather than evidence about the present case.

rigor.statement: Even today, there are people, sadly—and I see one of them is in this House—who think that Mr Putin's really quite a nice bloke, if only he wasn't provoked by that nasty NATO, aka our allies.
rigor.explanation: Strawmans the opponent's view ('Putin's really quite a nice bloke') to dismiss it.

rigor.statement: I give you, then, international law on the law of the sea and the rights for this country and other countries to be able to have commercial shipping, and we call on Iran to comply with the United Nations Security Council Resolution 2817.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the position in a concrete legal instrument rather than rhetoric.

rigor.statement: I can tell those members on the other side who has to fight those fights; it's actually our Defence Force. Frankly, I'm not putting them forward if we don't have to do something, because it's their lives while people on the other side are talking from their very, very excited position of holier than thou.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point that real personnel bear the risk, but leans on an emotive 'holier than thou' framing.

rigor.statement: Those of you that would have read The Lancet scientific journal would know that it reported that USA sanctions on other countries between 1971 and 2021 have murdered over 38 million people.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the authority of a journal but the cited statistic is contested and the causal link asserted, not shown.

rigor.statement: This particular letter reminds me of a rugby game. You get punched in the face, and then you retaliate. Who gets the yellow card? The guy who retaliated.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a rugby analogy that simplifies the conflict's causation rather than arguing from evidence.

rigor.statement: Where is the consistency from this Government? You cannot condemn one without the other.
rigor.explanation: A coherent consistency argument: condemning one set of attacks but not the other is logically inconsistent.

rigor.statement: Will you rule out sending New Zealand personnel and New Zealand defence assets to the Strait of Hormuz?
rigor.explanation: A pointed question grounded in the specific wording of the joint statement he just quoted.

rigor.statement: There is a way to clear the Strait of Hormuz and get the oil flowing again, and it's very simple. It's stop the war; stop the war.
rigor.explanation: Identifies the root cause but presents an oversimplified single solution as 'very simple'.

rigor.statement: It's endorsed and cosigned by many countries that we would typically have strong and close partnerships with—the United Kingdom, France, Netherlands, Canada, Japan. They've all signed on because they also understand the importance of the international rules-based system.
rigor.explanation: Supports the case with the fact of broad co-signing, but partly an appeal to the company kept rather than the statement's merits.

rigor.statement: The statement, which was clearly hurriedly put together, is itself internally inconsistent. We see in its last paragraph that it talks about upholding the principles of international law and freedom of navigation, but in the immediately preceding paragraph it says... rigor.explanation: Builds a specific textual argument quoting adjacent paragraphs to show an internal tension.

rigor.statement: The fiscal cost of this is so small. Therefore, it points to the fact that this is not a significant change. We're not going to get much more. It's not going to incentivise those really highly skilled, capable new immigrants to New Zealand or expatriates back to New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the low fiscal cost to the conclusion that the measure is marginal — a sound evidence-to-conclusion chain.

rigor.statement: the New Zealand Law Society suggested there should be proportionality or necessity tests as part of this... there is no mandatory privacy impact assessments, there's short review cycles for these agreements, there's no requirement for independent audits, and stronger transparency was needed.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the objection in authoritative submissions (Law Society, Privacy Commissioner) with specific deficiencies.

rigor.statement: We know that 311 of the wealthiest families in Aotearoa already hold more wealth than the bottom 50 percent.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete statistic to support the inequality argument, though cited loosely.

rigor.statement: The so-called digital nomad tax exemption stems from some fantasy that this Government has that the way to create a modern, resilient, productive economy is to sell our country to foreign investors. rigor.explanation: Bundles distinct policies into a single 'selling our country' narrative — hyperbole that conflates separate measures.

rigor.statement: That was a provision within this bill that encourages residential solar uptake, ensuring residents up and down this country who export excess power back to the grid... won't face income tax, recognising that the compliance burden would outweigh any benefit and it will encourage solar and battery uptake.

veracity.explanation: Claim that the PM corrected himself twice is plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: This is a regime that was machine-gunning its own people by the tens of thousands just a few weeks ago.

veracity.statement: We can't even send anybody over there; we've got a naval frigate underneath the ocean at the moment in the Pacific that needs to be dealt with.
veracity.explanation: Refers to the NZ navy vessel lost in the Pacific (HMNZS Manawanui) — substantially accurate.

veracity.statement: Those of you that would have read The Lancet scientific journal would know that it reported that USA sanctions on other countries between 1971 and 2021 have murdered over 38 million people.
veracity.explanation: Misrepresents the source; the 38-million figure is a loose, heavily-derived estimate, and 'murdered' overstates the causal claim.

veracity.explanation: Precise casualty figures cited as fact in an active conflict; not independently verifiable and contestable.

veracity.explanation: Fuel price spikes are plausible given the Strait disruption, but 'directly led' is a simplified single-cause attribution.

veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ did not join the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

veracity.statement: We know that 311 of the wealthiest families in Aotearoa already hold more wealth than the bottom 50 percent.

charisma.statement: There were people about 80 years ago who said that maybe Mr Hitler could be worked with and seen sense with—if only we could keep the economy preserved during that time.

charisma.statement: Words matter, and we need to dial it back a notch from some of the rhetoric that we've heard on the other side of the House.

charisma.statement: I do want to acknowledge the Finance and Expenditure Committee's work on this. We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough... I do want to also acknowledge the 275 individuals and groups who submitted on this bill.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, bridge-building tone that credits collaborative process.

charisma.statement: Now, there is one good measure, and I want to front-foot it because I'm a positive guy. I like to start by saying positive things. One good measure that this bill does that we do support is the change to exempt income from selling electricity to the grid. That is a good change.
charisma.explanation: Credits the government's measure and leads with the positive — a consensus-building gesture across the aisle.

charisma.statement: the residential solar power tweaks that we did was a sensible addition among many in this bill, which make practical changes to make this system more effective. rigor.statement: The structure of the way we've taxed capital gains has actually encouraged people to invest in rental properties, which is unproductive investment.
rigor.explanation: Plausible incentive argument consistent with mainstream economic view, but 'unproductive' is asserted without data and is itself contestable.

rigor.statement: someone who sits on an asset and gets the value in it just out of it sitting there pays much less tax on their economic income than our cleaners, our baristas, our supermarket checkout clerks, and so on.
rigor.explanation: Sound fairness argument that follows from the untaxed-capital-gains premise established earlier.

rigor.statement: The Minister asserted that we have a broad based – low rate tax, but I do not see how that can be consistent with his assertion that we should not have capital gains. If we're not taxing capital gains, it is not a broad-base system
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine internal contradiction: 'broad base' is incompatible with excluding capital gains; logically tight.

rigor.statement: We know that the Inland Revenue Department hasn't collected the data yet, because the income tax year hasn't ended, so there is no data available from the Inland Revenue Department. On what grounds can the Minister say that that policy is a success
rigor.explanation: Evidence-focused challenge: success claims require data, and she explains why no data can yet exist (tax year not ended).

rigor.statement: Why have we not considered a capital gains tax? Well, we don't want to tax capital, because of the surprising fact that capital assists us to grow our economy. If you tax capital, you do not grow your economy.
rigor.explanation: Absolute claim ('if you tax capital, you do not grow your economy') stated as a 'fact' without evidence; a false dichotomy ignoring that most comparable economies tax capital gains.

rigor.statement: We don't have a policy to tax people's homes. We don't have a policy to tax people's farms or their baches—which I appreciate the member is keen to do all that, or a 66 percent tax rate, which seems to be on the agenda; we're not doing any of that.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a strawman of the opponent's position rather than engaging her actual argument.

rigor.statement: amending section BB1 to introduce a tax-free income bracket would be a really good way to deliver immediate, quick, targeted relief for families.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable claim linking a tax-free threshold to low-income relief, but 'targeted' is asserted (a universal threshold also benefits higher earners, which he partly acknowledges elsewhere).

civility.statement: someone who sits on an asset and gets the value in it just out of it sitting there pays much less tax on their economic income than our cleaners, our baristas, our supermarket checkout clerks, and so on.
civility.explanation: Makes a substantive equity point about workers vs asset-holders without personal attack.

civility.statement: The Minister asserted that we have a broad based – low rate tax, but I do not see how that can be consistent with his assertion that we should not have capital gains. If we're not taxing capital gains, it is not a broad-base system
civility.explanation: Sharp but engages the Minister's actual claim on the substance; no personal attack.

civility.statement: We know that the Inland Revenue Department hasn't collected the data yet, because the income tax year hasn't ended, so there is no data available from the Inland Revenue Department. On what grounds can the Minister say that that policy is a success
civility.explanation: Demands evidence and engages the claim's basis rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: this is a Government that has chosen to decrease spending, and that's having a significant on health, homes, and jobs.
civility.explanation: Partisan criticism of the Government's choices, but framed around policy areas rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: when he ruled out the taxes that the Government had ruled out, he, of course, didn't list a gas tax, which the Government has gone on to implement
civility.explanation: Points out an omission/inconsistency in the Minister's framing, but does so on substance without insult.

civility.statement: We don't have a policy to tax people's homes. We don't have a policy to tax people's farms or their baches—which I appreciate the member is keen to do all that, or a 66 percent tax rate, which seems to be on the agenda; we're not doing any of that.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents Russell's position ('keen to do all that', '66 percent... on the agenda') when she raised 66% only as historical context; a strawman attributing intentions she did not state.

authenticity.statement: It was deeply inconvenient to us as a Government at the time, but I'm looking at it now and thinking, actually, it's really worth looking at.
authenticity.explanation: Candid admission that her own former government found the 2022 IR briefing inconvenient; self-aware rather than self-serving, a consistent-with-record acknowledgement.

authenticity.statement: We are a broad based – low rate party. We are not looking to increase tax. We are looking to increase economic growth, and that is the priority on this side of the Chamber.
authenticity.explanation: The 'broad based' label sits in tension with the Government's refusal to tax capital gains, a contradiction Russell directly highlights; words and the stated policy don't fully cohere.

forthrightness.statement: Yeah, a lot of consideration in regards to revenue methods. The primary method that we're focused on is growing our economy so that we can grow the revenue of every business and every household in this country. That's been a major focus of this Government, and one of the ways we achieve that is through a broad based - low rate tax system. I receive a wide range of advice from Treasury as part of my role.
forthrightness.explanation: Woods asked specifically what consideration he gave to broadening the base / taxing things other than income; he pivots to economic growth and offers no substance on base-broadening.

forthrightness.statement: Has the Government considered a land value tax? No. Has the Government considered a capital gains tax? No. Has the Government considered a death tax? No. Has the Government considered a whole lot of taxes that one wants to make up off the cuff? No.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives clear, unambiguous 'No' answers to Russell's questions about whether specific taxes were considered, though he avoids the corporate-rate/2022-briefing question.

forthrightness.statement: In regard to the corporate tax rate, yes, we did consider, as part of the assessment when we put in place Investment Boost, whether we would be better to reduce the corporate tax rate or do another alternative. We selected to do Investment Boost, because Investment Boost is a targeted mechanism in order to ensure that the benefit goes to those who most need it.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially answers: confirms a corporate-rate cut was weighed against Investment Boost, but doesn't address Russell's specific question about the 2022 IR long-term insights briefing.

forthrightness.statement: The answer in regards to asset sales is no. The Government has not considered that and is not considering that at this point.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, complete answer to Woods' specific question about whether asset-sale revenue was considered.

forthrightness.statement: The context in the question around Investment Boost—again, it provides a targeted intervention which, in effect, has an overarching effect to reduce the broader rate of tax that businesses pay, which is important.
forthrightness.explanation: Russell asked specifically what evidence supports calling Investment Boost a 'success'; he restates the mechanism and never supplies any evidence.

forthrightness.statement: No. Quite simply, the Government is not considering increasing taxes for hard-working Kiwis; quite the opposite. We're wanting to create a broad based - low rate tax system to encourage economic growth.
forthrightness.explanation: A clear blanket 'No' to Hernandez, but it sidesteps his specific questions about scope (new top brackets, super levies, a tax-free threshold under section BB1).

charisma.statement: Has the Government considered a land value tax? No. Has the Government considered a capital gains tax? No. Has the Government considered a death tax? No. Has the Government considered a whole lot of taxes that one wants to make up off the cuff? No.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side around 'points of difference between the sides of the House'; effective but us-vs-them, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: We are a party and a Government of fiscal discipline. We think about where we spend taxpayer money—because it's not our money; it's taxpayer money
charisma.explanation: A confident framing aimed at his own base ('taxpayer money'); rhetorically tidy but not consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: No. Quite simply, the Government is not considering increasing taxes for hard-working Kiwis; quite the opposite. We're wanting to create a broad based - low rate tax system to encourage economic growth.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to 'hard-working Kiwis' for his own side; not aimed at persuading opponents or finding common ground.

authenticity.statement: In answer to question No. 6 yesterday, I said that vaccine mandates and workplace settings for the 12- to 17-year age group remained in place until late January 2022. This was based on written Ministry of Health advice which the ministry has since acknowledged was incorrect as it related to booster mandates rather than the primary two-dose series. The correct position is that these mandates remained in place until 4 April 2022.
authenticity.explanation: Voluntarily corrects his own prior statement to the House; words brought into line with the record.

authenticity.statement: Well, as we know, the unemployment rate is where Treasury forecast it would be, and, as I accept, it is higher than anyone would like. For any individual who finds themselves without a job, it’s incredibly difficult for them and their family.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges an unwelcome reality rather than denying it.

authenticity.statement: I’m not aware of why this briefing was not publicly released. That would be a question for the Ministry of Health or the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins.
authenticity.explanation: Admits the limits of his own knowledge rather than overclaiming.

authenticity.statement: The sector has been calling out for this change since 2022. We heard their calls, and we have delivered.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the action as matching what the sector requested.

veracity.statement: In answer to question No. 6 yesterday, I said that vaccine mandates and workplace settings for the 12- to 17-year age group remained in place until late January 2022. This was based on written Ministry of Health advice which the ministry has since acknowledged was incorrect as it related to booster mandates rather than the primary two-dose series. The correct position is that these mandates remained in place until 4 April 2022.
veracity.explanation: Issues a factual correction of dates, attributing the earlier error to incorrect ministry advice.

veracity.statement: at that point there were close to 190,000 people on jobseeker support. Those numbers have been steadily rising since 2022, which is before we took office. The COVID-19 royal commission inquiry has found the previous Government’s increased spending drove up debt, inflation, and interest rates, which leads to higher unemployment... As of December, the quarterly figures show 223,500 people on jobseeker support
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures (190,000; 223,500) plausibly, but the causal chain pinned on prior spending is contestable and selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Are we really seeing the “green shoots of economic recovery”, as she claimed yesterday, when 7 percent of New Zealand’s working-age population are now on jobseeker support—a new record?
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual claim of 7 percent / a new record; plausible figure used to challenge the Minister.

veracity.statement: Yes. If you look at the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research report that came out in January this year, it shows that business confidence is at the highest it’s been since 2014.
veracity.explanation: Cites a named NZIER report and a specific claim; cherry-picks a favourable indicator.

veracity.statement: Is it a sign of green shoots when the number of young people—18- to 24-year-olds—on jobseeker has grown by 32 percent on her watch, as reported by Radio New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced figure (32 percent, RNZ) used as a factual challenge.

veracity.statement: we’ve got 70,000 people in case management, some of those over the phone; we have introduced a traffic light system so more people know what their obligations are; 90 percent of those on the jobseeker benefit say that is helpful to them.
veracity.explanation: Operational figures plausible; the '90 percent say helpful' is an unverifiable self-cited stat.

veracity.statement: Was the Prime Minister wrong when he said in May last year that “Unemployment is just almost peaking and about to come down.”, given there are now more people on jobseeker support than at the height of COVID-19?
veracity.explanation: Quotes a prior PM statement and contrasts it with current jobseeker numbers; the COVID-height comparison is broadly defensible.

veracity.statement: When you think about more than 50 percent of the Government’s spending during the years of COVID-19, having nothing to do with COVID-19... I am really proud that despite those challenges, 83,000 New Zealanders left welfare for a job, in the last year. That’s something worth celebrating.
veracity.explanation: 'More than 50 percent of spending had nothing to do with COVID' is a contestable framing; 83,000 figure presented favourably without the offsetting inflow.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with economist Brad Olsen that “we know that the number of jobs being advertised in the economy are still 25 percent lower than pre-pandemic”, and if so, how does she expect more beneficiaries to fill fewer jobs?
veracity.explanation: Cites a named economist and a specific figure (25 percent lower job ads).

veracity.statement: In answer to the first arm of the question, yes. In answer to the second, I would note that in the enumerated 2023 Census, administrative data significantly improved the under-count in Māori descent.
veracity.explanation: Claim that admin data improved Māori under-count in 2023 is plausible but cited without figures.

veracity.statement: Yes, whether it’s Minister Brown leading improved Māori two-year-old immunisation rates, from the terrible 64 percent it was in October 2023 to 68 percent now... or Minister Goldsmith cracking on with law and order policies that have reduced the 12-month levels of Māori victims of crime from 43,733 to 4,650. We don’t speak from the podium of truth but from the crucible of outcomes.
veracity.explanation: Some figures plausible (immunisation 64%→68%), but the crime drop from 43,733 to 4,650 is an implausibly large fall that looks like a misstatement or misleading comparison.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister accept that his track record in terms of cutting Māori and targeted funding in areas like Māori housing, Māori broadcasting, and Māori trade training has resulted in a record 10-year high of Māori unemployment, and if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Embedded claim of a 10-year high in Māori unemployment plus funding cuts; specific but the causal link is asserted.

veracity.statement: Yes, my ministry is involved and responsible for advocating for the increased employment of Māori, but it wasn’t too long ago under a Labour Government that the number of Māori unemployed was around 25 percent.
veracity.explanation: The 'around 25 percent under Labour' figure is offered without timeframe and likely refers to a much earlier/specific period—potentially misleading.

veracity.statement: Great progress. Restoring law and order is a core focus of our plan to fix the basics. We banned gang patches, reintroduced tougher sentences for serious offending, and made stalking an illegal and imprisonable offence... in two years, we’ve made great progress with 49,000 fewer victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Reforms are real; the '49,000 fewer victims' headline is a self-cited survey-based figure presented favourably.

veracity.statement: The Government’s initiative to clamp and seize cars of people not paying court fines has been highly successful, returning more than $700,000 and seizing 236 vehicles... Between July 2025 and February 2026, bailiffs scanned 147,000 number plates and identified 2,866 people with overdue court fines and reparations. Six hundred of those paid on the spot. Eighty vehicles have been sold at auction
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable figures presented as administrative data; framed as success.

veracity.statement: The royal commission found that the Hon Chris Hipkins was informed of the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group’s concerns in a briefing on 22 December 2021, and this briefing was considered by the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall on 7 January 2022. The briefing stated in paragraph 23, “In November 2021, CV TAG has raised concerns about vaccine mandates requiring younger age groups (e.g. [those under] 18 years) to be fully vaccinated.
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific findings to the royal commission with direct quotation; verifiable.

veracity.statement: No, but 15,000 more people in work compared to three months ago does.
veracity.explanation: Cites a 15,000 quarterly jobs gain against a 32,000 two-year fall the question raised—true but selectively timed.

veracity.statement: I want to extend my sympathies to the Heinz-Wattie’s team at this tough time... In the latest ANZ Business Outlook survey, manufacturing is leading business confidence at 77 points. The latest BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index also shows the sector expanding, with a reading of 55.2—above the level that indicates overall growth.
veracity.explanation: Cites real indices accurately, but uses sector-wide optimism to offset a specific local job-loss event.

veracity.statement: Is it a sign of growth when 17,000 people attend a jobs fair in Auckland, when only 100 employers were looking for workers?
veracity.explanation: Embedded figures (17,000 attendees vs 100 employers) used to dramatise the imbalance; the ratio framing may strip context.

veracity.statement: The latest Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) forecasts show that food and fibre exports remain at historically high levels, with horticulture alone expected to reach $9.2 billion in revenue this year.
veracity.explanation: Cites MPI forecasts with a specific number; presented as official forecast.

veracity.statement: we’ve taken strong steps to restore law and order, with 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime; ram raids are down 85 percent; and repeat youth offending is down 22 percent... lifting childhood immunisations to 82.6 percent... We are seeing progress in education, with phonics proficiency lifting from 36 percent to 58 percent.
veracity.explanation: Figures are presented favourably and some (e.g. ram raids down 85%) depend heavily on baseline choice; broad cross-portfolio claims hard to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: Is he delivering the brighter future he promised Pasifika, when almost 10,000 more Pasifika children are living in hardship now, under his watch?
veracity.explanation: Embedded claim of ~10,000 more Pasifika children in hardship; specific figure used as challenge.
