forthrightness.statement: Our Government is committed to taking action to reduce child poverty by fixing the basics and building the future for all young New Zealanders. … We have made a number of changes to improve the lives of Kiwi families, including increasing the in-work tax credit, lifting the threshold for Working for Families, providing working families with tax relief, and introducing FamilyBoost.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what 'immediate actions' she is taking; lists past/ongoing measures rather than new immediate steps for the escalating numbers.

forthrightness.statement: I accept that there are many families who are doing it tough right now. While it would be nice to have said that we had inherited a set of economic circumstances that made it easier for people and families to get ahead, that is not the case. In Budget 2024, our Government prioritised reducing the number of children in poverty with the measures that I outlined before to lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to urgent pre-Budget actions for Te Tai Tokerau and, if not, why not; does not commit and points back to Budget 2024.

forthrightness.statement: Well, yes. That is why we need to have a growing economy so that there are more job opportunities and there are more opportunities for families to get ahead under their own steam. That is how we reduce harm and we reduce hardship—by reducing the number of children who are growing up in benefit-dependent households.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she maintains the current approach is sufficient; she says 'yes' directly, then gives a general rationale rather than addressing the Canterbury figure cited.

forthrightness.statement: This bill will ensure that there is equitable treatment across all people who received ACC payments, whether ongoing, weekly, or backdated. Everyone will have their supplementary assistance assessed by the same rules. The bill is confirming the current policy intent, so this will not change the way people are treated from previous practice.
forthrightness.explanation: The primary question (on notice) asked whether and how many sexual-violence, abuse-in-care and head-injury survivors are affected; none of those groups or numbers are addressed.

forthrightness.statement: In the legislation that has been introduced and had its second reading in the House, it referred to 37,000 people who had an ACC-related debt established related to supplementary assistance. The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) does not have the specific reason for each ACC claim, nor should they. It is private information.
forthrightness.explanation: After a point of order, gives a concrete figure (37,000) and explains why the breakdown-by-reason cannot be provided, though still not the requested group counts.

forthrightness.statement: I'm the Minister for Social Development and Employment. I'm not the Minister for ACC and I wasn't in the select committee when the ACC appeared this morning.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she accepts the ACC briefing showing survivors are the largest affected group; deflects on portfolio grounds rather than engaging the substance.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I refute that. I've never used that expression in terms of the recipients or the people affected by this bill. There is no change in terms of what currently happens. … They have a responsibility to taxpayers to repay that debt, and MSD, when they have conversations about when a debt has been created, they talk to the person about how that debt can be repaid and over what period.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she has not acknowledged the debts for survivors and instead described 'double dipping'; she directly denies using that phrase but does not engage the underlying impact claim.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. The Government expects all organisations that handle New Zealanders' health information, including private providers, to meet the highest standards to keep that information safe. Following recent incidents involving private digital health providers, I asked the Director-General of Health and the chief executive of Health New Zealand to write to providers across the sector reminding them of their obligations … That's why we invested an additional $9 million in Budget 2024 and a further $10 million in Budget 2025 to strengthen cyber-security capability within Health New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'yes' and details the specific steps taken to get assurance, as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we have inherited a system, and we are working with the system that the last Government put together when they amalgamated 20 DHBs into Health New Zealand and forgot to actually fix the basics. We're fixing the basics, we're increasing the monitoring, and, as I said, we're now taking a number of actions to ensure improved oversight of our data and digital systems across New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a specific Tracy Watkins quote on government oversight; pivots immediately to blaming the previous Government, prompting a point of order.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the question was in relation to Tracy Watkins' piece in the papers on the weekend. I agree that there is a need for increased oversight. … Is the system perfect? No. Is there more work to do? Yes. That is across Government that we need to do that, and we're committed to doing just that.
forthrightness.explanation: After the point of order, does engage the quote ('I agree there is a need for increased oversight') and candidly concedes the system is imperfect.

forthrightness.statement: The answer is that obligations sit in a number of places including, under the Privacy Act, on private companies, and, ultimately, the penalty regime in New Zealand is woeful, and it needs to be fixed. … It's all well and good for the former Minister on the other side of the House to sit there and complain, but we inherited a system from her, which we are now fixing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he keeps deflecting blame when responsibilities lie with his Government; partly engages (obligations sit in multiple places) but again ends on blaming the former Minister.

forthrightness.statement: Well, this Government hasn't failed on the Prime Minister's commitment to make New Zealand a safer place, and New Zealand is a safer place. We don't have gang members taking over provincial towns. We don't have gang members taking over public spaces and public roads. We don't have gang members intimidating members of the public with their gang patches. All of that has changed under this Government. That was the commitment the Prime Minister made, and we've delivered on it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he failed the specific 'fewer gang members than police officers' commitment; reframes the commitment to a broader 'safer place' claim and avoids the numbers.

forthrightness.statement: In relation to gang members, yep, you're right: there's three more gang members in New Zealand than there are police officers. But the good news is this: help is on its way. Next Thursday, 59 police officers will graduate, and there'll be 56 more police officers than gang members.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the unfavourable fact ('you're right: there's three more gang members') and gives specific figures rather than dodging.

forthrightness.statement: I can clear that up and be categorical and say that, no, I did not contact any member at TVNZ, including a board member. I was contacted by a senior member of TVNZ—not board member. I could name them but I won't.
forthrightness.explanation: After a point of order, gives a categorical, direct answer to the specific question about contacting a TVNZ board member.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I just answered, and I've been very clear about the fact that I was contacted by a member of TVNZ with an apology, because it appears the only ones in this country that don't realise that crime is improving is Labour and TVNZ.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he is aware it would be illegal to direct TVNZ content; does not address the legality point and instead restates the apology and takes a swipe.

forthrightness.statement: The Government has agreed to amend the Summary Offences Act to allow police to issue move-on orders that will require a person to leave a specified area for a specified amount of time and to move on a reasonable distance from the area if they are displaying disorderly, disruptive, threatening, or intimidation behaviours. They will also apply to those who are obstructing and impeding someone entering a business, breaching peace, all forms of begging, and those who are intending to inhabit a public place.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how move-on orders will work; gives a clear, mechanism-level answer.

specificity.statement: Well, international commodity prices rise and fall. That's inevitable. You don't change your approach or strategy just because of that. What I can say is that banning oil and gas put a chilling effect on this country. The Lake Onslow project, at $17 billion—to be delivered in 2037 at $8,000 a household—and $800 megawatt per hour wholesale electricity prices means that we have a failed energy policy. We have dry-year risk, and, as a result, this has actually been a good move, because it has lowered the forward electricity prices by about $25 since we made that announcement.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures: $17bn, 2037, $8,000/household, $800/MWh, ~$25 forward-price fall.

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister has consistently made a causal connection between the ban to offshore oil and gas exploration, and the prices of energy, yet all of the data and evidence shows that the average time it takes to go from exploration to production is 16 years.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (16 years) and ties it to the 2018 timeline.

specificity.statement: Why does the Prime Minister accept the Trump administration's word for the legality of its attack on Iran, stating, "It's up for them to provide the legal evidence and justification for these strikes." when Russia made exactly the same argument under Article 51 of the UN Charter when it invaded Ukraine and we, correctly, did not accept that justification?
specificity.explanation: Cites Article 51 and a specific quoted statement to anchor the challenge.

specificity.statement: It is a little early to say whether the conflict is having a significant impact on the economy yet. As I said yesterday, there is likely to be an impact, but what that is and how quickly things get back to normal will depend on the nature, severity, and duration of the disruption arising from this conflict. … Key channels by which events in the Middle East could affect New Zealand are an increase in oil prices, shipping and air disruptions and freight costs, demand for New Zealand exports, and risk aversion in financial markets that affects the New Zealand dollar and global growth. To what extent those channels operate is yet to be seen. The Government is monitoring events closely.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete channels (oil, freight, exports, FX) though without figures at this point.

specificity.statement: Brent crude oil ended the day at US$82 a barrel, up from around $72 before the weekend. Global equity markets fell, with the S&P 500 down 0.7 percent and the Nikkei down 3.1 percent. We are observing volatility in these numbers during the course of trading hours. The New Zealand dollar is 0.5c lower against the US dollar compared to yesterday.
specificity.explanation: Exact prices and percentage moves: Brent $82 vs $72, S&P −0.7%, Nikkei −3.1%, NZD −0.5c.

specificity.statement: New Zealand is well placed. We have sound fundamentals: a resilient banking sector and a floating exchange rate that helps buffer shocks. … Right now, the terms of trade is at record highs in a series that goes all the way back to 1957. New Zealand's current account deficit has narrowed considerably. It was 3.5 percent of GDP in the September 2025 quarter compared with 9 percent in December 2022.
specificity.explanation: Concrete data points: record terms of trade since 1957, current account 3.5% vs 9% of GDP.

specificity.statement: In the video the member refers to, there are five things I said a National Government would do. We would stop adding costs to farmers: tick—achieved. We would make sure they had the workers they need: tick—achieved. We would bring Government spending under control: tick—that's what we're doing. We would focus the Reserve Bank on fighting inflation: tick—that's what we've done. We would let you keep more of what you earn with our plan for tax reduction: tick—we delivered tax relief.
specificity.explanation: Itemises five named commitments, but the central question (grocery prices) is answered only in vague counterfactual terms.

specificity.statement: One statement which the Government made very emphatically and which we have delivered on, where we said that we would deliver a tax package which would deliver up to $250 of tax relief for families—delivered. … I want to thank the member for joining the National Party in voting for the legislation which we introduced to expand the generosity of that scheme to ensure that thousands more families would receive that level of support.
specificity.explanation: Names the tax figure, the $150/fortnight FamilyBoost payment, and the legislative expansion.

specificity.statement: Last week, the Government announced we will remove barriers that prevent many farm and other rural workers from using their KiwiSaver accounts to buy their first home. … We're making a technical change to the KiwiSaver Act that will enable service tenancy workers to buy a first home while living in employer-provided housing. … Legislation is expected to be introduced in the middle of this year.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism (KiwiSaver Act change, trust/partnership eligibility) and a rough timeframe (legislation mid-year).

specificity.statement: When can Kiwis "expect to pay less for home-grown food at the checkout" as she has promised them since 2023, given the price of butter is up 78 percent, mince is up 32 percent, and milk is up 22 percent from two years ago?
specificity.explanation: Pins the challenge to precise price increases: butter +78%, mince +32%, milk +22% over two years.

specificity.statement: What immediate actions is the Minister taking to stop the escalation of the 170,000 tamariki experiencing child poverty and hardship, particularly for Māori, who make up a quarter of this number across Aotearoa?
specificity.explanation: Frames the question with concrete figures: 170,000 children and Māori as a quarter of that number.

specificity.statement: Our Government is committed to taking action to reduce child poverty by fixing the basics and building the future for all young New Zealanders. … We have made a number of changes to improve the lives of Kiwi families, including increasing the in-work tax credit, lifting the threshold for Working for Families, providing working families with tax relief, and introducing FamilyBoost.
specificity.explanation: Names specific levers (in-work tax credit, Working for Families threshold, FamilyBoost) though without amounts or timing.

specificity.statement: In the legislation that has been introduced and had its second reading in the House, it referred to 37,000 people who had an ACC-related debt established related to supplementary assistance. The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) does not have the specific reason for each ACC claim, nor should they. It is private information.
specificity.explanation: Provides the 37,000 figure and a clear reason (MSD does not hold the claim cause).

specificity.statement: Yes. The Government expects all organisations that handle New Zealanders' health information, including private providers, to meet the highest standards to keep that information safe. Following recent incidents involving private digital health providers, I asked the Director-General of Health and the chief executive of Health New Zealand to write to providers across the sector reminding them of their obligations … That's why we invested an additional $9 million in Budget 2024 and a further $10 million in Budget 2025 to strengthen cyber-security capability within Health New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions and figures: provider letters, a security review, $9m (2024) and $10m (2025) investments.

specificity.statement: Artificial intelligence (AI) scribe technology is now live in all emergency departments (ED) across New Zealand with the rapid roll out making it available to 1,250 ED doctors and front-line staff complete—250 more than originally announced following a successful pilot last year. This places New Zealand among the fastest health systems in the world to move from pilot to nationwide front-line use in our emergency departments of AI scribes.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: live in all EDs, 1,250 staff, 250 above the original announcement.

specificity.statement: After just one month of use at Middlemore emergency department, 80 percent of surveyed staff said the AI scribe improved productivity or efficiency and 84 percent said it had a positive impact on their overall experience and wellbeing during shifts.
specificity.explanation: Precise survey figures with location and timeframe: Middlemore, one month, 80% and 84%.

specificity.statement: In relation to gang members, yep, you're right: there's three more gang members in New Zealand than there are police officers. But the good news is this: help is on its way. Next Thursday, 59 police officers will graduate, and there'll be 56 more police officers than gang members.
specificity.explanation: Exact numbers and date: three more gang members now, 59 graduating next Thursday, 56 net more officers.

specificity.statement: Let me give you some of the numbers: in 2025, there were over 100,000 police foot patrols—that is nearly double on 2023. This number here—that wasn't reported on 1News, but is a very important figure—is there are 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime and there is a 22 percent reduction in serious repeat offenders. Ram raids have also dropped by 85 percent.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures: 100,000+ foot patrols, 49,000 fewer victims, 22% fewer serious repeat offenders, 85% fewer ram raids.

specificity.statement: The Government has agreed to amend the Summary Offences Act to allow police to issue move-on orders that will require a person to leave a specified area for a specified amount of time and to move on a reasonable distance from the area if they are displaying disorderly, disruptive, threatening, or intimidation behaviours. They will also apply to those who are obstructing and impeding someone entering a business, breaching peace, all forms of begging, and those who are intending to inhabit a public place.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute (Summary Offences Act) and the precise behaviours and conditions the orders cover.

specificity.statement: A survey conducted late last year found that 91 percent of operators in Auckland CBD were being negatively affected by rough sleeping and begging, and 81 percent believed the CBD was not in a good state to attract more people and more investment.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages tied to a defined population (Auckland CBD operators) and timeframe.

specificity.statement: Today I announced a major increase in compliance activity which supports the law changes we made last year to ban disposable vapes and increase penalties for sales to under-18-year-olds. Health New Zealand more than doubled store visits and controlled purchase operations, targeting illegal sales to minors in the last year. Compliance is strong with upwards of 90 percent of retailers doing the right thing … infringement notices more than double over the last year. The infringement efforts have been boosted with the recruitment of an additional 18 compliance officers.
specificity.explanation: Concrete measures and figures: doubled store visits, 90%+ compliance, doubled infringement notices, 18 extra compliance officers.

specificity.statement: Last year, the Government passed the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill, which banned disposable vapes, increased penalties for selling to minors, and tightened retail visibility and proximity routes. The great news is that youth smoking rates are very low and vaping rates are declining … This funding of $550,000 a year is part of a $5.3 million investment towards marketing and quit-smoking campaigns.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and exact figures ($550,000/year within $5.3m).

veracity.statement: Well, international commodity prices rise and fall. That's inevitable. You don't change your approach or strategy just because of that. What I can say is that banning oil and gas put a chilling effect on this country. The Lake Onslow project, at $17 billion—to be delivered in 2037 at $8,000 a household—and $800 megawatt per hour wholesale electricity prices means that we have a failed energy policy. We have dry-year risk, and, as a result, this has actually been a good move, because it has lowered the forward electricity prices by about $25 since we made that announcement.
veracity.explanation: Cites contested Lake Onslow costings and attributes a $25 forward-price fall to his own announcement; the causal attribution is unverified and selectively framed.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister has consistently made a causal connection between the ban to offshore oil and gas exploration, and the prices of energy, yet all of the data and evidence shows that the average time it takes to go from exploration to production is 16 years.
veracity.explanation: The long lead-time claim is broadly supported by industry data, though '16 years average' is a single figure offered without citation.

veracity.statement: Brent crude oil ended the day at US$82 a barrel, up from around $72 before the weekend. Global equity markets fell, with the S&P 500 down 0.7 percent and the Nikkei down 3.1 percent. We are observing volatility in these numbers during the course of trading hours. The New Zealand dollar is 0.5c lower against the US dollar compared to yesterday.
veracity.explanation: Presents concrete, checkable market figures as facts; consistent with how such data is reported.

veracity.statement: New Zealand is well placed. We have sound fundamentals: a resilient banking sector and a floating exchange rate that helps buffer shocks. … Right now, the terms of trade is at record highs in a series that goes all the way back to 1957. New Zealand's current account deficit has narrowed considerably. It was 3.5 percent of GDP in the September 2025 quarter compared with 9 percent in December 2022.
veracity.explanation: Cites Stats NZ terms-of-trade and current-account figures; specific and checkable, though framed favourably.

veracity.statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given, including my statement yesterday that the member "wishes to return to the monetary policy framework that resulted in New Zealand's highest period of inflation in recent history". At a time of heightened global instability, proposing to dilute the Reserve Bank's focus on inflation is the last thing New Zealand needs.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the opponent's monetary-policy position as causing the 'highest period of inflation'; a partisan characterisation rather than an established fact.

veracity.statement: When can Kiwis "expect to pay less for home-grown food at the checkout" as she has promised them since 2023, given the price of butter is up 78 percent, mince is up 32 percent, and milk is up 22 percent from two years ago?
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable grocery price claims; plausible and likely sourced, though presented to maximise the contrast.

veracity.statement: What immediate actions is the Minister taking to stop the escalation of the 170,000 tamariki experiencing child poverty and hardship, particularly for Māori, who make up a quarter of this number across Aotearoa?
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific hardship figure and Māori share; broadly consistent with poverty statistics, though the exact basis is unstated.

veracity.statement: Artificial intelligence (AI) scribe technology is now live in all emergency departments (ED) across New Zealand with the rapid roll out making it available to 1,250 ED doctors and front-line staff complete—250 more than originally announced following a successful pilot last year. This places New Zealand among the fastest health systems in the world to move from pilot to nationwide front-line use in our emergency departments of AI scribes.
veracity.explanation: Rollout numbers are precise, but 'among the fastest health systems in the world' is an unverifiable superlative.

veracity.statement: After just one month of use at Middlemore emergency department, 80 percent of surveyed staff said the AI scribe improved productivity or efficiency and 84 percent said it had a positive impact on their overall experience and wellbeing during shifts.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific internal survey; plausible but self-reported satisfaction data presented favourably.

veracity.statement: Let me give you some of the numbers: in 2025, there were over 100,000 police foot patrols—that is nearly double on 2023. This number here—that wasn't reported on 1News, but is a very important figure—is there are 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime and there is a 22 percent reduction in serious repeat offenders. Ram raids have also dropped by 85 percent.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific official-sounding statistics favourable to the Government; presented without source and selected to support the case.

veracity.statement: A survey conducted late last year found that 91 percent of operators in Auckland CBD were being negatively affected by rough sleeping and begging, and 81 percent believed the CBD was not in a good state to attract more people and more investment.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific survey figures (91% / 81%); checkable in principle, though the survey's source and methodology are unstated.

veracity.statement: Today I announced a major increase in compliance activity which supports the law changes we made last year to ban disposable vapes and increase penalties for sales to under-18-year-olds. Health New Zealand more than doubled store visits and controlled purchase operations, targeting illegal sales to minors in the last year. Compliance is strong with upwards of 90 percent of retailers doing the right thing … infringement notices more than double over the last year. The infringement efforts have been boosted with the recruitment of an additional 18 compliance officers.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific compliance statistics presented favourably; plausible but self-reported.

veracity.statement: Last year, the Government passed the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill, which banned disposable vapes, increased penalties for selling to minors, and tightened retail visibility and proximity routes. The great news is that youth smoking rates are very low and vaping rates are declining … This funding of $550,000 a year is part of a $5.3 million investment towards marketing and quit-smoking campaigns.
veracity.explanation: Claims youth smoking very low and vaping declining; directionally consistent with NZ trends, asserted without the underlying data.

veracity.statement: I am actively working on the regulatory environment with officials. … There is currently a tougher regime for vapes than there is for cigarettes, and we have seen the adverse effects manifest in Australia, where illicit tobacco is the largest part of the market. The wrong settings can and will create unintended outcomes, and we will fix it.
veracity.explanation: Claim that illicit tobacco is the 'largest part' of the Australian market is broadly directionally supported but likely overstated as a flat assertion.

rigor.statement: Well, international commodity prices rise and fall. That's inevitable. You don't change your approach or strategy just because of that. What I can say is that banning oil and gas put a chilling effect on this country. The Lake Onslow project, at $17 billion—to be delivered in 2037 at $8,000 a household—and $800 megawatt per hour wholesale electricity prices means that we have a failed energy policy. We have dry-year risk, and, as a result, this has actually been a good move, because it has lowered the forward electricity prices by about $25 since we made that announcement.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link between the announcement and falling forward prices without evidence ruling out other factors.

rigor.statement: He ended up banning oil and gas, and, as a result, we import Indonesian coal, and we actually are reliant on others rather than being reliant on ourselves. So I don't take lectures from that member, because it was an abject failure. The Labour-Greens energy policy was a total failure—he knows it, he's trying to gaslight his way through it, and we're not having it.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the oil-and-gas ban directly caused coal imports without addressing the long lead times for gas production.

rigor.statement: Well, I think it's a bit disgraceful and embarrassing for the member to compare Ukraine with Iran. But, again, as I said yesterday, it is up for the Israelis and the Americans to give justification for the legality of their strikes. We are not party to the information or intelligence that they have received. It would be wrong of New Zealand, either way, to jump to conclusions. We need fact and evidence to be produced, and that's what we would reasonably expect.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable appeal to lacking the intelligence, but dismisses the Ukraine/Iran parallel without explaining the relevant difference.

rigor.statement: The Prime Minister has consistently made a causal connection between the ban to offshore oil and gas exploration, and the prices of energy, yet all of the data and evidence shows that the average time it takes to go from exploration to production is 16 years.
rigor.explanation: Marshals a specific evidentiary point — the ~16-year exploration-to-production lag — to challenge the asserted causal link between the 2018 ban and current prices.

rigor.statement: Why does the Prime Minister accept the Trump administration's word for the legality of its attack on Iran, stating, "It's up for them to provide the legal evidence and justification for these strikes." when Russia made exactly the same argument under Article 51 of the UN Charter when it invaded Ukraine and we, correctly, did not accept that justification?
rigor.explanation: Constructs a consistency argument by analogy to the Russia/Ukraine Article 51 case; reasoned, though the two situations may differ materially.

rigor.statement: It is a little early to say whether the conflict is having a significant impact on the economy yet. As I said yesterday, there is likely to be an impact, but what that is and how quickly things get back to normal will depend on the nature, severity, and duration of the disruption arising from this conflict. … Key channels by which events in the Middle East could affect New Zealand are an increase in oil prices, shipping and air disruptions and freight costs, demand for New Zealand exports, and risk aversion in financial markets that affects the New Zealand dollar and global growth. To what extent those channels operate is yet to be seen. The Government is monitoring events closely.
rigor.explanation: Identifies specific transmission channels and conditions impact on severity/duration rather than overclaiming.

rigor.statement: New Zealand is well placed. We have sound fundamentals: a resilient banking sector and a floating exchange rate that helps buffer shocks. … Right now, the terms of trade is at record highs in a series that goes all the way back to 1957. New Zealand's current account deficit has narrowed considerably. It was 3.5 percent of GDP in the September 2025 quarter compared with 9 percent in December 2022.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'well placed' conclusion with relevant data, though it selects favourable indicators.

rigor.statement: Well, yes. That is why we need to have a growing economy so that there are more job opportunities and there are more opportunities for families to get ahead under their own steam. That is how we reduce harm and we reduce hardship—by reducing the number of children who are growing up in benefit-dependent households.
rigor.explanation: Relies on the general premise that growth and fewer benefit-dependent households reduce hardship, without evidence linking it to the specific rising numbers raised.

rigor.statement: A survey conducted late last year found that 91 percent of operators in Auckland CBD were being negatively affected by rough sleeping and begging, and 81 percent believed the CBD was not in a good state to attract more people and more investment.
rigor.explanation: Backs the policy rationale with survey evidence, an improvement on bare assertion, though it leans on a single unsourced survey.

rigor.statement: Our main streets and public places have been blighted by disruption and disturbance, leading to our communities becoming places of intimidation and dysfunction. Now, that has been obvious to anybody that's visited our main streets in recent times.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to common sense ('obvious to anybody') rather than evidence for the scale of the problem.

rigor.statement: I am actively working on the regulatory environment with officials. … There is currently a tougher regime for vapes than there is for cigarettes, and we have seen the adverse effects manifest in Australia, where illicit tobacco is the largest part of the market. The wrong settings can and will create unintended outcomes, and we will fix it.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Australian illicit-tobacco experience as cautionary evidence; a relevant comparison, though presented as a single analogy.

civility.statement: Look, no disrespect, but I'm not taking lectures from that member on energy policy. I saw some wonderful comments that we should be more independent and have an independent energy policy. Well, actually, the actions of that member's Government created an importation of Indonesian coal and didn't actually create the independent energy policy that we are creating through an "and, and, and" approach of lots of initiatives.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'not taking lectures' framing, but attacks the opponent's record rather than the person.

civility.statement: Yes, he was, because, actually, we have taken a policy in our Government that we table the advice, and then we make some decisions. What we don't do is create an $800 megawatt per hour cost that ends up shutting down mills, and low and middle income working New Zealanders lose their jobs. That's exactly what that member did—economic vandal, arsonist, now complaining about the fire that we're putting out that you created.
civility.explanation: Personal epithets — 'economic vandal, arsonist' — aimed at the opponent.

civility.statement: He ended up banning oil and gas, and, as a result, we import Indonesian coal, and we actually are reliant on others rather than being reliant on ourselves. So I don't take lectures from that member, because it was an abject failure. The Labour-Greens energy policy was a total failure—he knows it, he's trying to gaslight his way through it, and we're not having it.
civility.explanation: 'Abject failure', 'total failure', accusation he is trying to 'gaslight' — heated and accusatory.

civility.statement: Well, I think it's a bit disgraceful and embarrassing for the member to compare Ukraine with Iran. But, again, as I said yesterday, it is up for the Israelis and the Americans to give justification for the legality of their strikes. We are not party to the information or intelligence that they have received. It would be wrong of New Zealand, either way, to jump to conclusions. We need fact and evidence to be produced, and that's what we would reasonably expect.
civility.explanation: Opens by calling the comparison 'disgraceful and embarrassing' rather than engaging the analogy on substance.

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, I just draw your attention—I'm sure you have many longer memories than mine—of the way Speakers have held order in the House by shutting down such ridiculous debating points masquerading as points of order, before a member was able to disrupt the House making them.
civility.explanation: Characterises another member's point as 'ridiculous' and 'masquerading', dismissive but aimed at the procedural conduct rather than the person.

civility.statement: The member is being, I think, quite disingenuous. It is clear from my statement and the work that the Government is doing that our plan is about ensuring that prices in the future would be lower than would otherwise be the case. … I stand by this Government's view that increasing retail competition in the grocery sector could result in a situation in which prices are lower than would otherwise be the case.
civility.explanation: Labels the questioner 'disingenuous' rather than answering, but otherwise engages the policy substance.

civility.statement: For example, I did see some quotes from one member of this House today that suggested that if we had lower interest rates and lower unemployment, there would be no effect on inflation. I suggest that member read an economics textbook.
civility.explanation: 'I suggest that member read an economics textbook' is a condescending personal jab rather than substantive rebuttal.

civility.statement: Is the reason she gets so defensive when confronted with her own broken promise to reduce food prices because she knows she will never ever deliver on it?
civility.explanation: Loaded, rhetorical question imputing motive ('so defensive', 'never ever deliver') rather than engaging policy substance.

civility.statement: Well, we have inherited a system, and we are working with the system that the last Government put together when they amalgamated 20 DHBs into Health New Zealand and forgot to actually fix the basics. We're fixing the basics, we're increasing the monitoring, and, as I said, we're now taking a number of actions to ensure improved oversight of our data and digital systems across New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Critique aimed at the prior Government's structural decision rather than a personal attack, but uses the 'forgot to fix the basics' jab.

civility.statement: The answer is that obligations sit in a number of places including, under the Privacy Act, on private companies, and, ultimately, the penalty regime in New Zealand is woeful, and it needs to be fixed. … It's all well and good for the former Minister on the other side of the House to sit there and complain, but we inherited a system from her, which we are now fixing.
civility.explanation: Pointed dig at the 'former Minister' but framed around the policy/legislative inheritance.

civility.statement: Well, I just answered, and I've been very clear about the fact that I was contacted by a member of TVNZ with an apology, because it appears the only ones in this country that don't realise that crime is improving is Labour and TVNZ.
civility.explanation: Closing jab lumping 'Labour and TVNZ' together as oblivious rather than engaging the legal question.

civility.statement: Why are gangs better at recruiting members than he is at recruiting police officers?
civility.explanation: A pointed rhetorical jibe at the Minister's performance; barbed but tied to the policy record on recruitment numbers.

charisma.statement: Yes, he was, because, actually, we have taken a policy in our Government that we table the advice, and then we make some decisions. What we don't do is create an $800 megawatt per hour cost that ends up shutting down mills, and low and middle income working New Zealanders lose their jobs. That's exactly what that member did—economic vandal, arsonist, now complaining about the fire that we're putting out that you created.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them framing; no attempt to persuade or build consensus.

charisma.statement: He ended up banning oil and gas, and, as a result, we import Indonesian coal, and we actually are reliant on others rather than being reliant on ourselves. So I don't take lectures from that member, because it was an abject failure. The Labour-Greens energy policy was a total failure—he knows it, he's trying to gaslight his way through it, and we're not having it.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side against the Opposition; no bridge-building.

charisma.statement: For example, I did see some quotes from one member of this House today that suggested that if we had lower interest rates and lower unemployment, there would be no effect on inflation. I suggest that member read an economics textbook.
charisma.explanation: Belittling an opponent rather than persuading; alienating rather than consensus-building.

strength.statement: In the video the member refers to, there are five things I said a National Government would do. We would stop adding costs to farmers: tick—achieved. We would make sure they had the workers they need: tick—achieved. We would bring Government spending under control: tick—that's what we're doing. We would focus the Reserve Bank on fighting inflation: tick—that's what we've done. We would let you keep more of what you earn with our plan for tax reduction: tick—we delivered tax relief.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivering five commitments, some genuinely enacted (tax relief), but 'bring spending under control' is conceded as in-progress.

strength.statement: One statement which the Government made very emphatically and which we have delivered on, where we said that we would deliver a tax package which would deliver up to $250 of tax relief for families—delivered. … I want to thank the member for joining the National Party in voting for the legislation which we introduced to expand the generosity of that scheme to ensure that thousands more families would receive that level of support.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of a tax package ('up to $250') and FamilyBoost expansion; the 'up to' framing hedges how many families actually received the maximum.

strength.statement: Last week, the Government announced we will remove barriers that prevent many farm and other rural workers from using their KiwiSaver accounts to buy their first home. … We're making a technical change to the KiwiSaver Act that will enable service tenancy workers to buy a first home while living in employer-provided housing. … Legislation is expected to be introduced in the middle of this year.
strength.explanation: An announcement with legislation not yet introduced; intent stated but delivery still pending.

strength.statement: I accept that there are many families who are doing it tough right now. While it would be nice to have said that we had inherited a set of economic circumstances that made it easier for people and families to get ahead, that is not the case. In Budget 2024, our Government prioritised reducing the number of children in poverty with the measures that I outlined before to lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
strength.explanation: Claims Budget 2024 measures to 'lift 17,000 children out of poverty'; a stated outcome target whose delivery is asserted but not demonstrated here.

strength.statement: Yes. The Government expects all organisations that handle New Zealanders' health information, including private providers, to meet the highest standards to keep that information safe. Following recent incidents involving private digital health providers, I asked the Director-General of Health and the chief executive of Health New Zealand to write to providers across the sector reminding them of their obligations … That's why we invested an additional $9 million in Budget 2024 and a further $10 million in Budget 2025 to strengthen cyber-security capability within Health New Zealand.
strength.explanation: Describes commissioned reviews and funding allocations; concrete steps under way, though outcomes not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Artificial intelligence (AI) scribe technology is now live in all emergency departments (ED) across New Zealand with the rapid roll out making it available to 1,250 ED doctors and front-line staff complete—250 more than originally announced following a successful pilot last year. This places New Zealand among the fastest health systems in the world to move from pilot to nationwide front-line use in our emergency departments of AI scribes.
strength.explanation: Describes a delivered, nationwide rollout exceeding the original target (1,250 vs 1,000), not merely an announcement.

strength.statement: Well, this Government hasn't failed on the Prime Minister's commitment to make New Zealand a safer place, and New Zealand is a safer place. We don't have gang members taking over provincial towns. We don't have gang members taking over public spaces and public roads. We don't have gang members intimidating members of the public with their gang patches. All of that has changed under this Government. That was the commitment the Prime Minister made, and we've delivered on it.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on a re-characterised commitment; concedes the original numeric pledge only later.

strength.statement: Let me give you some of the numbers: in 2025, there were over 100,000 police foot patrols—that is nearly double on 2023. This number here—that wasn't reported on 1News, but is a very important figure—is there are 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime and there is a 22 percent reduction in serious repeat offenders. Ram raids have also dropped by 85 percent.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for measurable crime reductions as delivered results, though the question was about the gang/police ratio.

strength.statement: Today I announced a major increase in compliance activity which supports the law changes we made last year to ban disposable vapes and increase penalties for sales to under-18-year-olds. Health New Zealand more than doubled store visits and controlled purchase operations, targeting illegal sales to minors in the last year. Compliance is strong with upwards of 90 percent of retailers doing the right thing … infringement notices more than double over the last year. The infringement efforts have been boosted with the recruitment of an additional 18 compliance officers.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted law changes and delivered enforcement increases, not just intentions.

strength.statement: Last year, the Government passed the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill, which banned disposable vapes, increased penalties for selling to minors, and tightened retail visibility and proximity routes. The great news is that youth smoking rates are very low and vaping rates are declining … This funding of $550,000 a year is part of a $5.3 million investment towards marketing and quit-smoking campaigns.
strength.explanation: Names a bill actually passed and specific funding committed — delivered legislation plus investment, not mere announcement.

authenticity.statement: Well, I refute that. I've never used that expression in terms of the recipients or the people affected by this bill. There is no change in terms of what currently happens. … They have a responsibility to taxpayers to repay that debt, and MSD, when they have conversations about when a debt has been created, they talk to the person about how that debt can be repaid and over what period.
authenticity.explanation: Denies ever using 'double dipping'; from the text alone the consistency of this denial cannot be verified.

divination.statement: In relation to gang members, yep, you're right: there's three more gang members in New Zealand than there are police officers. But the good news is this: help is on its way. Next Thursday, 59 police officers will graduate, and there'll be 56 more police officers than gang members.
divination.explanation: Predicts that after next Thursday's graduation there will be 56 more police officers than gang members; near-term and concrete, likely accurate barring offsetting changes.

forthrightness.statement: As the Hon Chris Penk well outlined on behalf of the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery yesterday, work is ongoing and well under way to consider any hypothetical future shortages. Any future settings in this area will be developed. … I'm not sure it's helpful to presuppose any changes in settings at this point.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether 'critical customer' status guarantees enough fuel for police; deflects to 'work is ongoing' and declines to engage the question.

forthrightness.statement: As the Police have done on a range of issues throughout the history of policing, they will continue to prioritise to ensure that emergency services are maintained. Prioritisation is a matter of operational police performance.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a specific yes/no on whether P4/P5 callouts continue at level 4; gives a generic prioritisation answer without saying yes or no.

forthrightness.statement: As we've stipulated repeatedly, hypothetical discussions around what will or will not happen in future settings is not helpful to the public, or reassuring.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Police Eagle helicopter could operate under level 3/4; refuses to answer by labelling the question unhelpful.

forthrightness.statement: Police prioritisation will be an operation issue for Police to resolve. As the settings are changed, those settings will be communicated to Police leadership, and prioritisation, as has always been the case for policing, will be dealt with by the police system.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether area/district commanders or National HQ decide; partially answers — settings come centrally, prioritisation is operational — but doesn't name the decision level asked about.

forthrightness.statement: The specific fuel levels, I think, are really unhelpful to reassure the public that policing services are being maintained. … At this point, we do not have issues with supply, and, therefore, future settings and discussions at this time are not helpful.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked how many days of reserve police hold; declines to give any figure.

forthrightness.statement: Planning is ongoing and continuing. We have a fuel plan in place. … this Government is supporting that by ensuring supply is maintained, as according to the announcements that we've made around increasing storage that was secured by Minister Jones and announced by Minister Jones this morning.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how police can plan with no operational detail; rebuts the premise and points to a concrete storage announcement but gives no operational detail.

forthrightness.statement: We make substantial investments in public transport services across the country, including in our regional towns. … I have been advised that public transport authorities are not yet facing capacity concerns. We are open to further investment to ensure capacity, if shown to be necessary…
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether funding will be made available for frequent regional bus services; offers conditional openness rather than a yes/no commitment.

forthrightness.statement: That second assertion in that member's question is not borne out by the facts. The public transport activity class funding range rose between 2021 and 2024 and 2027. There are hundreds of millions of dollars more flowing through to public transport under this Government as compared to the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise and signals he won't invite reapplications, focusing instead on existing services.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm proud of the record of past National Governments in electrifying the rail network in Auckland, for example, so the member's general point that electrification at the moment is lowering costs is, of course, correct. We have to weigh up funding those sort of things…
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the merit but neither commits to nor rules out reversing the cuts.

forthrightness.statement: The Government provides, through SuperGold Card and community services card concessions, quite extensive and generous subsidies already for public transport. I'm not ruling out further extensions, but nor am I ruling it in…
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reverse cuts to youth fares; explains the targeting rationale but explicitly neither rules in nor out.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it's important—as I think the member knows—not to confuse capital and operating costs. … We are giving due consideration to all of the funding pressures on transport… It's a very tricky situation for the country, and transport is at the epicentre of that funding challenge.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically to pause highway planning funds to fund buses; deflects on a capital/operating distinction without answering.

forthrightness.statement: Fuel continues to flow and there is no immediate supply disruption, with 59 days of petrol, 52 days of diesel, and 46 days of jet fuel in-country—within our exclusive economic zone or in the water heading here… we are acting on three fronts: providing temporary targeted support to the squeezed middle; strengthening fuel resilience…; and working closely with industry…
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers how the Government is responding, with structure.

forthrightness.statement: Yesterday, Ministers signed off on a proposal through the Regional Infrastructure Fund to increase New Zealand's diesel storage capacity through a commercial arrangement with Channel Infrastructure at Marsden Point. This will provide up to an additional 93 million litres of diesel storage, which is around a 20 percent increase in current capacity…
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what further actions are being taken.

forthrightness.statement: I absolutely stand by all of the Government's statements and actions, and in particular, the measured and careful approach that we are taking to the situation with fuel shortage. We are being careful to preserve New Zealand's future options, including our fiscal room and our children's education, while also preparing for worse scenarios…
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the stock 'do you stand by' question affirmatively and elaborates the approach.

forthrightness.statement: I am advised that 22 renewable generation projects are currently going through the fast-track process—a process that member opposed. In fact, I am advised that more renewable energy has been commissioned in this term of Government than in the previous 10 years combined.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the report question by pointing to overlapping work rather than addressing the $22bn figure directly.

forthrightness.statement: Just in the past fortnight, I stood alongside other Ministers as we announced the extension of our investment into the electric vehicle (EV) charging network for the country… I've also been advised that registrations for EVs have surged…
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether scrapping transition support left businesses exposed; pivots to EV charging announcements rather than addressing the claim.

forthrightness.statement: …rather than science funding being spent on projects about singing to kauri trees, we will be investing in projects that actually can generate future economic growth. And I note that in the middle of this year, the Government will release its new Science Investment Plan…
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why funding was axed causing science-sector redundancies; never addresses the redundancies, pivots to reform framing.

forthrightness.statement: That's why, today, we've announced that the mileage rates for home and community support workers will increase by 30 percent. Many workers will receive an extra $19 per 100 kilometres of travel to help offset the cost of rising fuel prices.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what was announced.

forthrightness.statement: This is a timely, temporary, and targeted response with the increase remaining in place for up to 12 months or until the price of 91 octane petrol falls below $3 per litre for four consecutive weeks. It will apply to home and community support workers who work for providers contracted by Health New Zealand, the Ministry of Social Development, and ACC.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers how long the rate will remain.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do. I thank the member for asking that question. Indeed, it's the first question she's asked me in 2½ years on agriculture. … farmers being worth $60 billion worth of exports and up to 360,000 jobs in the economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms he stands by the statement, then elaborates.

forthrightness.statement: I'm informed that we have enough fertiliser now to get us through the winter. We're working very closely with fertiliser importers to make sure that spring will also be good.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially answers how he'll support farmers on input costs — addresses supply but not the cost question directly.

forthrightness.statement: …when we came to Government 2½ years ago, they did a survey and they came out and they said very openly and widely that confidence in the farming sector was the lowest it's ever been—at minus-66 percent. On January 2026, results since we'd come to Government had improved to plus-37 percent; that's an increase of 100 points.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a named Federated Farmers president's warning is wrong; sidesteps to confidence-survey figures.

forthrightness.statement: That is a very challenging issue and it's something that we're working through. … An example of some of the things we've had to change is we had to take away a ute tax, there was going to be a fertiliser tax, a capital gains tax, a water tax, tax, tax, tax—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for a jobs-lost estimate from named plant closures; gives no number and pivots to attacking previous-government taxes.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there's no direct evidence that farmers will be producing less. In fact, we produce enough food to feed 40 million people around the world. … There will always be enough food for New Zealanders to eat because we're not a population of 40 million people.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the import-reliance question by disputing the premise of reduced production.

forthrightness.statement: No. The Public Service already has a clear and flexible policy that allows agencies to manage working from home arrangements as required. … While we acknowledge the increase in fuel prices, we do not currently face a fuel shortage. If that situation were to change, then we would consider whether further measures were required.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question with a clear 'No' and gives the reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: …New Zealand's situation has, I understand, been mentioned at the OECD, I think it was, just recently in Paris as the exemplar of how a country should manage this fuel situation and, at the same time, keep their economy going. … The Government's doing well. The Public Service is doing well. The public is doing very well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why not follow IEA peers like Australia; asserts difference but glides into general praise.

forthrightness.statement: …a lot of those, for instance, Fonterra staff employees cannot work from home, because they're working in factories. … Certainly, if we look in the public sector, New Zealand Police front-line staff, Corrections front-line staff, probation officers, nurses, doctors, and teachers do not have that luxury.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the comparison but reframes rather than addressing the WFH-where-possible thrust.

forthrightness.statement: there are people with some concerns about disestablishing the ministry, but, again, let's just look at the facts. There are no substantive changes to the functions, there is no reduction in environmental protection, and the changes are structural.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why her view differs from official advice; gives her position but doesn't engage the cited advice directly.

forthrightness.statement: What I can say is that environmental outcomes always depend on good evidence, and from that good evidence, good decisions. Regardless of any structural changes to Government agencies, the statutory environmental reporting will continue…
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically how disestablishment would help Te Tai Tokerau resilience; answers generically about reporting continuing.

forthrightness.statement: The Ministry for the Environment gives advice to the Minister, and decisions are made based on that advice and based on the information that comes, so there is no thought that a structural change will change the standard of that advice, the level of that advice—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for specific replacement safeguards; gives no specifics, prompting a point of order that the question was unanswered.

specificity.statement: Planning is ongoing and continuing. We have a fuel plan in place. … this Government is supporting that by ensuring supply is maintained, as according to the announcements that we've made around increasing storage that was secured by Minister Jones and announced by Minister Jones this morning.
specificity.explanation: References a real storage announcement but gives no figures, mechanism or timeframe in this answer.

specificity.statement: We have every confidence in Police management and capability to plan. This is why the police Minister does not need to speculate about that level of detail, because we have full confidence in the Police executive management to deal with these issues.
specificity.explanation: A general expression of confidence with no detail, figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Revenue into the National Land Transport Fund is actually forecast to decline because people are driving less … We are also facing rising costs because 80 percent of our buses are diesel buses, and the price of diesel in particular is rising quickly…
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (80% diesel buses) and named mechanisms, though no dollar amounts.

specificity.statement: As I often say to the Greens: there is no magic money tree, and to the extent that there is one, the leaves just got clipped off.
specificity.explanation: A slogan committing to nothing concrete.

specificity.statement: Fuel continues to flow and there is no immediate supply disruption, with 59 days of petrol, 52 days of diesel, and 46 days of jet fuel in-country—within our exclusive economic zone or in the water heading here… we are acting on three fronts: providing temporary targeted support to the squeezed middle; strengthening fuel resilience…; and working closely with industry…
specificity.explanation: Names precise day-counts of fuel stocks and three concrete fronts of action.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, Ministers signed off on a proposal through the Regional Infrastructure Fund to increase New Zealand's diesel storage capacity through a commercial arrangement with Channel Infrastructure at Marsden Point. This will provide up to an additional 93 million litres of diesel storage, which is around a 20 percent increase in current capacity…
specificity.explanation: Names the fund, the partner, the site, the volume (93m litres) and the percentage increase.

specificity.statement: When we released the framework last week, we were clear that phases three and four would not be locked in without our working alongside industry. These decisions need to be made with industry, not to industry. … we have engaged with more than 800 businesses and have received more than 830 submissions through our priority bands channel…
specificity.explanation: Concrete engagement figures (800+ businesses, 830+ submissions) and named process.

specificity.statement: The Government has moved quickly to provide extra support for low to middle income working families by increasing the in-work tax credit for up to a year. … It gives about 143,000 families an extra $50 a week, and another 14,000 families an abated amount of relief. … It is funded from the Budget 2026 operating allowance, and so it will not add to forecast debt or inflationary pressures.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, beneficiary counts (143,000 + 14,000), the $50/week amount, the duration and the funding source.

specificity.statement: We come into this situation with $191.4 billion of debt, half of that was borrowed, not throughout New Zealand's long history but just in three or four years of COVID response.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise debt figure and timeframe.

specificity.statement: That is why we have decided to give an increase in mileage rates to those people who travel for work; not those people who travel to work. It's those health and support workers that have, often, quite low incomes, they travel from home to home helping vulnerable New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the target group and rationale but no rate figure in this passage.

specificity.statement: these extra 90 million litres delivered in the next eight weeks, for a $21 million commitment by the Government, represents excellent value by any standard, including that of the regional investment fund.
specificity.explanation: Names volume (90m litres), timeframe (eight weeks) and cost ($21m).

specificity.statement: I am advised that 22 renewable generation projects are currently going through the fast-track process—a process that member opposed. In fact, I am advised that more renewable energy has been commissioned in this term of Government than in the previous 10 years combined.
specificity.explanation: Gives a project count and a comparative claim, though no capacity figures.

specificity.statement: It is supporting thousands of jobs across the country… It is a job-supporting, job-rich policy that the members opposite opposed. What a shame they opposed more job opportunities for Kiwis.
specificity.explanation: 'Thousands of jobs' is asserted without figures or named projects.

specificity.statement: That's why, today, we've announced that the mileage rates for home and community support workers will increase by 30 percent. Many workers will receive an extra $19 per 100 kilometres of travel to help offset the cost of rising fuel prices.
specificity.explanation: States the exact increase (30%) and dollar effect ($19 per 100km).

specificity.statement: …in practical terms that means for every 100 kilometres travelled, these workers will receive an extra $19, which covers the current rise in fuel costs, which is around $8.50 for the average petrol vehicle and $11.80 for the average diesel vehicle.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures tied to vehicle types.

specificity.statement: This is a timely, temporary, and targeted response with the increase remaining in place for up to 12 months or until the price of 91 octane petrol falls below $3 per litre for four consecutive weeks. It will apply to home and community support workers who work for providers contracted by Health New Zealand, the Ministry of Social Development, and ACC.
specificity.explanation: States exact duration, the price trigger ($3/L for four weeks) and the eligible cohort.

specificity.statement: I'm informed that we have enough fertiliser now to get us through the winter. We're working very closely with fertiliser importers to make sure that spring will also be good.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete near-term assurance (winter supply) but no costs, volumes or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: Over the last two years, this Government has invested an extra $343 million into the aged-care sector to provide stability while we work on changes to the system. Health New Zealand has introduced a new Casemix funding model and framework across the South Island…
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure ($343m), a named funding model and a region.

specificity.statement: Quite simply, we want older New Zealanders to be able to access the right care at the right time and in the right place. … supporting people to age in the place that is right for them is better for their care and quality of life…
specificity.explanation: Aspirational 'right care, right time, right place' framing with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: …I can confirm that 515 rough-sleeping households have been housed in social housing through the Housing First programme up until 25 March 2026. This includes 237 whānau housed so far in the additional 300 places that this Government funded, plus a further 278 households…
specificity.explanation: Precise counts (515; 237; 300; 278) and a cut-off date.

charisma.statement: Would the Minister anticipate severe scrutiny from the Opposition if a Government was to start interfering in Police independence, right down to the level of detail of when they fill up their petrol tanks?
charisma.explanation: A supportive set-up question framing the Opposition's line as over-reach; rhetorically effective but appeals to its own side.

charisma.statement: Well, I'm proud of the record of past National Governments in electrifying the rail network in Auckland, for example, so the member's general point that electrification at the moment is lowering costs is, of course, correct. We have to weigh up funding those sort of things…
charisma.explanation: Concedes the opponent's point as correct and frames a genuine trade-off rather than dismissing her — bridge-building tone.

charisma.statement: As I often say to the Greens: there is no magic money tree, and to the extent that there is one, the leaves just got clipped off.
charisma.explanation: An applause line aimed at the Greens; rhetorically sharp but partisan, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Every day in Government is better than even the best day in Opposition, Kieran.
charisma.explanation: A partisan jibe directed at a named opponent; rallies own side, not unifying.

charisma.statement: When we released the framework last week, we were clear that phases three and four would not be locked in without our working alongside industry. These decisions need to be made with industry, not to industry. … we have engaged with more than 800 businesses and have received more than 830 submissions through our priority bands channel…
charisma.explanation: 'With industry, not to industry' frames a collaborative, consensus-seeking approach.

charisma.statement: That's 22 projects which he voted against being able to happen faster. He thought they should be tied up in court. … We'll be judged on action, not rhetoric.
charisma.explanation: Confident and combative; appeals to own side rather than seeking common ground despite the report's call for bipartisanship.

charisma.statement: It is supporting thousands of jobs across the country… It is a job-supporting, job-rich policy that the members opposite opposed. What a shame they opposed more job opportunities for Kiwis.
charisma.explanation: Ends a patsy answer with a partisan dig rather than persuasion.

charisma.statement: …if she really wants us to be as rich as Australia, I suggest that she supports the Resource Management Act reforms and she also supports fast track and she supports mining. If she does that, we will be richer than Australia.
charisma.explanation: Partisan challenge to an opponent rather than persuasion or common ground.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge that there have been people who are concerned about this disestablishment, and that hasn't been helped by perhaps some of the misinformation about it. If we keep coming back to what is actually happening, there are no substantive changes to the functions under the Environment Act…
charisma.explanation: Attempts a reassuring tone but frames dissent as misinformed rather than inviting it in.

veracity.statement: There is no public transport in Levin.
veracity.explanation: Dismissive interjection; Levin/Horowhenua does have bus services, so the absolute claim is misleading.

veracity.statement: Revenue into the National Land Transport Fund is actually forecast to decline because people are driving less … We are also facing rising costs because 80 percent of our buses are diesel buses, and the price of diesel in particular is rising quickly…
veracity.explanation: Claims about diesel bus share and NLTF revenue dynamics are broadly plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: That second assertion in that member's question is not borne out by the facts. The public transport activity class funding range rose between 2021 and 2024 and 2027. There are hundreds of millions of dollars more flowing through to public transport under this Government as compared to the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts higher PT funding than the previous Government; plausible but figures unverified and contested by the questioner.

veracity.statement: The Government provides, through SuperGold Card and community services card concessions, quite extensive and generous subsidies already for public transport. I'm not ruling out further extensions, but nor am I ruling it in…
veracity.explanation: SuperGold and community services card PT concessions do exist; 'generous' is a characterisation.

veracity.statement: Fuel continues to flow and there is no immediate supply disruption, with 59 days of petrol, 52 days of diesel, and 46 days of jet fuel in-country—within our exclusive economic zone or in the water heading here… we are acting on three fronts: providing temporary targeted support to the squeezed middle; strengthening fuel resilience…; and working closely with industry…
veracity.explanation: Specific stock figures presented as fact; plausible but not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: The Government has moved quickly to provide extra support for low to middle income working families by increasing the in-work tax credit for up to a year. … It gives about 143,000 families an extra $50 a week, and another 14,000 families an abated amount of relief. … It is funded from the Budget 2026 operating allowance, and so it will not add to forecast debt or inflationary pressures.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures stated as fact; plausible but unverified, and the no-inflation claim is a contestable assertion.

veracity.statement: We come into this situation with $191.4 billion of debt, half of that was borrowed, not throughout New Zealand's long history but just in three or four years of COVID response.
veracity.explanation: Debt figure is specific; 'half borrowed in three or four years of COVID' is a defensible but selectively framed characterisation of debt accumulation.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders are moving to public transport at current fares in order to preserve fuel, and that is what prices do. That is how markets work, and that is the opposite of how communism works.
veracity.explanation: Earlier claim that PT users 'are not actually affected by fuel prices' is undercut by his own point that fuel prices drive the shift; partly misleading.

veracity.statement: I am advised that 22 renewable generation projects are currently going through the fast-track process—a process that member opposed. In fact, I am advised that more renewable energy has been commissioned in this term of Government than in the previous 10 years combined.
veracity.explanation: Two specific claims (22 projects; more renewables than prior decade) stated as advised fact; plausible but unverified and rhetorically strong.

veracity.statement: Just in the past fortnight, I stood alongside other Ministers as we announced the extension of our investment into the electric vehicle (EV) charging network for the country… I've also been advised that registrations for EVs have surged…
veracity.explanation: EV registration 'surge' stated as advised; plausible but unquantified.

veracity.statement: …our ability to access our own security, in the form of our own natural gas and oil, was completely curtailed by the actions of the last Government, who made us more dependent on imported energy because they couldn't count
veracity.explanation: References the 2018 offshore exploration ban but overstates ('completely curtailed', 'couldn't count') in a misleading, polemical way.

veracity.statement: Yes, I do. I thank the member for asking that question. Indeed, it's the first question she's asked me in 2½ years on agriculture. … farmers being worth $60 billion worth of exports and up to 360,000 jobs in the economy.
veracity.explanation: $60bn exports and 'up to 360,000 jobs' are broadly in line with sector estimates, though 'up to' hedges the upper figure.

veracity.statement: …when we came to Government 2½ years ago, they did a survey and they came out and they said very openly and widely that confidence in the farming sector was the lowest it's ever been—at minus-66 percent. On January 2026, results since we'd come to Government had improved to plus-37 percent; that's an increase of 100 points.
veracity.explanation: Specific confidence figures cited; plausible but unverified and selectively favourable.

veracity.statement: That is a very challenging issue and it's something that we're working through. … An example of some of the things we've had to change is we had to take away a ute tax, there was going to be a fertiliser tax, a capital gains tax, a water tax, tax, tax, tax—
veracity.explanation: Lists a 'capital gains tax' among policies removed, though no such tax was enacted — misleading.

veracity.statement: Well, there's no direct evidence that farmers will be producing less. In fact, we produce enough food to feed 40 million people around the world. … There will always be enough food for New Zealanders to eat because we're not a population of 40 million people.
veracity.explanation: NZ's food-export-to-population framing is broadly accurate as a generalisation.

veracity.statement: …I can confirm that 515 rough-sleeping households have been housed in social housing through the Housing First programme up until 25 March 2026. This includes 237 whānau housed so far in the additional 300 places that this Government funded, plus a further 278 households…
veracity.explanation: Specific operational figures stated as confirmed; plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: …New Zealand's situation has, I understand, been mentioned at the OECD, I think it was, just recently in Paris as the exemplar of how a country should manage this fuel situation and, at the same time, keep their economy going. … The Government's doing well. The Public Service is doing well. The public is doing very well.
veracity.explanation: Heavily hedged ('I understand', 'I think it was') claim of being an OECD 'exemplar'; vague sourcing and self-congratulatory, hard to verify.
