veracity.statement: there are people with some concerns about disestablishing the ministry, but, again, let's just look at the facts. There are no substantive changes to the functions, there is no reduction in environmental protection, and the changes are structural.
veracity.explanation: 'No reduction in environmental protection' is an assertion contested by officials referenced in the question; presented as settled fact.

civility.statement: There is no public transport in Levin.
civility.explanation: A factual heckle aimed at the question rather than a person; minor.

civility.statement: Hey, mate! You've got to get into Government to be reshuffled, and that won't be happening to you anytime soon.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a colleague that engages no policy substance.

civility.statement: Every day in Government is better than even the best day in Opposition, Kieran.
civility.explanation: A mild taunt rather than a personal attack on character.

civility.statement: Let me just get something straight: the money belongs to the people. The Government takes it off them in taxes. … If you think the Government owns all the money, Damien O'Connor, then you really are—not joking—a communist.
civility.explanation: Names a colleague and labels him a 'communist' — a personal attack rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: We've seen other initiatives—such as unions, who are supposed to represent workers, actually campaigning for workers not to go to work and even taking legal action to avoid going into work.
civility.explanation: Characterises unions in a derisive 'supposed to' framing rather than engaging the substance of their position.

civility.statement: …rather than science funding being spent on projects about singing to kauri trees, we will be investing in projects that actually can generate future economic growth. And I note that in the middle of this year, the Government will release its new Science Investment Plan…
civility.explanation: 'Singing to kauri trees' caricatures prior research to mock it rather than engage substance.

civility.statement: That's 22 projects which he voted against being able to happen faster. He thought they should be tied up in court. … We'll be judged on action, not rhetoric.
civility.explanation: Attributes 'tied up in court' motives to the member; pointed but aimed at his voting record.

civility.statement: …our ability to access our own security, in the form of our own natural gas and oil, was completely curtailed by the actions of the last Government, who made us more dependent on imported energy because they couldn't count
civility.explanation: 'Because they couldn't count' is a derisive characterisation of opponents rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: Yes, I do. I thank the member for asking that question. Indeed, it's the first question she's asked me in 2½ years on agriculture. … farmers being worth $60 billion worth of exports and up to 360,000 jobs in the economy.
civility.explanation: The '2½ years' jab is a mild dig at the questioner rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, what I have on my paper, it says "It looks like a tax, it smells like a tax, it's a tax."
civility.explanation: Flippant response to a point of order; a slogan rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Ginny Andersen used to be so much nicer when she'd turn up in my office trying to be nice to me. I don't know what's happened to her since then, but anyway, if she doesn't want an answer, she won't get one.
civility.explanation: A personal, belittling remark about a named colleague that engages no substance.

civility.statement: I acknowledge that there have been people who are concerned about this disestablishment, and that hasn't been helped by perhaps some of the misinformation about it. If we keep coming back to what is actually happening, there are no substantive changes to the functions under the Environment Act…
civility.explanation: Acknowledges concern but attributes it partly to 'misinformation', implicitly faulting critics rather than only addressing substance.

rigor.statement: Revenue into the National Land Transport Fund is actually forecast to decline because people are driving less … We are also facing rising costs because 80 percent of our buses are diesel buses, and the price of diesel in particular is rising quickly…
rigor.explanation: Coherent causal argument linking high fuel prices to falling fund revenue and rising operating costs; conclusion follows from premises.

rigor.statement: We come into this situation with $191.4 billion of debt, half of that was borrowed, not throughout New Zealand's long history but just in three or four years of COVID response.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete figure to justify fiscal caution, but the causal attribution to COVID alone simplifies.

rigor.statement: That is why we have decided to give an increase in mileage rates to those people who travel for work; not those people who travel to work. It's those health and support workers that have, often, quite low incomes, they travel from home to home helping vulnerable New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clear 'travel for vs to work' distinction to justify targeting; coherent rationale.

rigor.statement: Let me just get something straight: the money belongs to the people. The Government takes it off them in taxes. … If you think the Government owns all the money, Damien O'Connor, then you really are—not joking—a communist.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a false dichotomy (either tax cuts or 'the Government owns all the money') and resolves it with ad hominem.

rigor.statement: We've seen other initiatives—such as unions, who are supposed to represent workers, actually campaigning for workers not to go to work and even taking legal action to avoid going into work.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a strawman characterisation of unions' aims rather than evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: New Zealanders are moving to public transport at current fares in order to preserve fuel, and that is what prices do. That is how markets work, and that is the opposite of how communism works.
rigor.explanation: A valid price-signal point, but the partisan 'opposite of communism' flourish substitutes rhetoric for analysis.

rigor.statement: …in practical terms that means for every 100 kilometres travelled, these workers will receive an extra $19, which covers the current rise in fuel costs, which is around $8.50 for the average petrol vehicle and $11.80 for the average diesel vehicle.
rigor.explanation: Backs the rate with concrete cost figures showing the uplift exceeds the modelled fuel-cost rise; numbers support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: Well, there's no direct evidence that farmers will be producing less. In fact, we produce enough food to feed 40 million people around the world. … There will always be enough food for New Zealanders to eat because we're not a population of 40 million people.
rigor.explanation: The 'feed 40 million' point is relevant to domestic supply but doesn't actually address import substitution for specific produce.

rigor.statement: They have told me directly that the investment announced in September is making a huge and material difference to whānau rough sleeping. My officials shared with me this week an example about a gentleman they met who, through Government tautoko, a provider has supported through immediate access into a warm home.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote and provider testimony rather than outcome data to evidence 'huge and material difference'.

rigor.statement: …a lot of those, for instance, Fonterra staff employees cannot work from home, because they're working in factories. … Certainly, if we look in the public sector, New Zealand Police front-line staff, Corrections front-line staff, probation officers, nurses, doctors, and teachers do not have that luxury.
rigor.explanation: Counters the private-sector analogy with relevant examples of roles that cannot work remotely; reasonable point.

rigor.statement: …if she really wants us to be as rich as Australia, I suggest that she supports the Resource Management Act reforms and she also supports fast track and she supports mining. If she does that, we will be richer than Australia.
rigor.explanation: Overstated causal claim that backing three policies would make NZ 'richer than Australia' — unsupported leap.

strength.statement: Yesterday, Ministers signed off on a proposal through the Regional Infrastructure Fund to increase New Zealand's diesel storage capacity through a commercial arrangement with Channel Infrastructure at Marsden Point. This will provide up to an additional 93 million litres of diesel storage, which is around a 20 percent increase in current capacity…
strength.explanation: A concrete decision signed off, not just aspiration; delivery is committed but storage not yet built.

strength.statement: The Government has moved quickly to provide extra support for low to middle income working families by increasing the in-work tax credit for up to a year. … It gives about 143,000 families an extra $50 a week, and another 14,000 families an abated amount of relief. … It is funded from the Budget 2026 operating allowance, and so it will not add to forecast debt or inflationary pressures.
strength.explanation: A concrete delivered fiscal measure, though impact unfolds over the coming year.

strength.statement: these extra 90 million litres delivered in the next eight weeks, for a $21 million commitment by the Government, represents excellent value by any standard, including that of the regional investment fund.
strength.explanation: A committed spend with a near-term delivery window, though storage not yet delivered.

strength.statement: That's why, today, we've announced that the mileage rates for home and community support workers will increase by 30 percent. Many workers will receive an extra $19 per 100 kilometres of travel to help offset the cost of rising fuel prices.
strength.explanation: An announced, dated delivery of a concrete measure.

strength.statement: Over the last two years, this Government has invested an extra $343 million into the aged-care sector to provide stability while we work on changes to the system. Health New Zealand has introduced a new Casemix funding model and framework across the South Island…
strength.explanation: Describes concrete delivered investment and a rolled-out funding model.

strength.statement: …I can confirm that 515 rough-sleeping households have been housed in social housing through the Housing First programme up until 25 March 2026. This includes 237 whānau housed so far in the additional 300 places that this Government funded, plus a further 278 households…
strength.explanation: Reports concrete delivered outcomes against a funded commitment.

veracity.statement: My question is: in Budget 2024, the actual proof is that we saw a lot of cuts to front-line services, so does the Minister stand by her statement that there will be no cuts to front-line services?
veracity.explanation: Claims Budget 2024 cut front-line services; partly supportable but turns on the contested definition of 'front-line service', which the response disputes.

veracity.statement: It is the case that this Government has delivered $43 billion in savings in public expenditure across two Budgets.
veracity.explanation: A specific fiscal figure stated as fact; plausible as a cumulative savings total though 'savings' framing can be contestable.

veracity.statement: They are health, where we have committed increases in funding for front-line health services above and beyond population and inflationary pressures.
veracity.explanation: Claim of real-terms increases is plausible but unverified and depends on baseline definitions.

veracity.statement: one of the bits of advice I’ve had is that if the member hadn’t banned oil and gas exploration for New Zealand, we would most likely have more sufficient gas supply and not the acute electricity price increases that we were left with.
veracity.explanation: Causal link between the 2018 exploration ban and present electricity prices is contested; long lead times for new supply complicate the claim.

veracity.statement: I can confirm that 87,444 unique families have received the FamilyBoost childcare tax credit so far, and I do want to thank the member and her party for supporting the most recent legislation, which expanded that scheme and which has seen that, in the December quarter, at least 11,068 families received at least $150 a fortnight—
veracity.explanation: Detailed statistics stated as fact; precise but answers a different metric than the '$250 a fortnight to how many families' asked.

veracity.statement: instead she referred to how a Government Budget was akin to a household budget—a longstanding metaphor that has been proven incorrect time and time again.
veracity.explanation: The claim that the household-budget metaphor is economically misleading is broadly supported by mainstream macroeconomics.

veracity.statement: We’ve ended up with record-high unemployment—the highest in 10 years. We’ve also ended up with, by some figures, 15,000 construction sector jobs lost, and, obviously, as we all well know, this Government waving goodbye to the 200-plus New Zealanders leaving the country every single day.
veracity.explanation: Mixes a hedged claim ('by some figures') with specific numbers; directionally plausible but the unemployment 'highest in 10 years' and net-migration framing need verification.

veracity.statement: they have made decisions to cut flood protection funding across this country by 41 percent compared to the former Government.
veracity.explanation: Specific 41% cut attributed to an OIA response from the Ministry for the Environment; sourced but unverified here.

veracity.statement: The Government has decided to also cut, and did in its initial Budget, $6 billion from climate emergency response funding and from resilience—from the likes of that flood protection and otherwise—which has not only undermined our ability to mitigate climate-changing emissions but also to adapt to the impacts of climate change.

charisma.explanation: Cross-party thanks to Labour for supporting the expansion is a genuine bridge-building note.

charisma.statement: I thank the Minister for answering some of the questions put forward by colleagues.
charisma.explanation: Gracious opening, though it precedes partisan questioning.

charisma.statement: who do you trust? The people who can give you the numbers and show they’ve delivered, or that lot over there, who raise petty points of order about something as small as a pin?
charisma.explanation: A rallying us-vs-them appeal that energises his own side while dismissing opponents rather than persuading them.

charisma.statement: no one is wildly satisfied with the status quo, but changing the system is a big call and is something that requires quite a bit of consideration... One thing I think that would be useful to do is move to 10-year windows for transport funding. The three-year thing works for no one.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges shared dissatisfaction across central and local government, finding common ground.

charisma.statement: the member raises an interesting issue. We don’t have any active policy work under way on it, but it is definitely true that we need to make some improvements over time and I’m very aware of the problems the member raises.
charisma.explanation: Validates the opponent's point and concedes the problem is real.

rigor.statement: What the member is actually saying is that, in her book, the way to grow an economy is to suck more money out of the pockets of working people.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts the opponent's argument about Government spending as a claim about taxing workers more.

rigor.statement: one of the bits of advice I’ve had is that if the member hadn’t banned oil and gas exploration for New Zealand, we would most likely have more sufficient gas supply and not the acute electricity price increases that we were left with.
rigor.explanation: Cites unnamed advice; plausible mechanism but a strongly causal conclusion from a single attributed factor.

rigor.statement: our Government has taken the same advice from the Auditor-General and the Treasury that the member took when she was the Associate Minister of Finance, which is to recognise that there is no constructive obligation unless the Government commits that it will sign a cheque.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the answer in Auditor-General/Treasury advice, though it leans on the 'you did the same' point.

rigor.statement: instead she referred to how a Government Budget was akin to a household budget—a longstanding metaphor that has been proven incorrect time and time again.
rigor.explanation: Correctly flags the household-budget analogy as a flawed comparison, though asserts it without citing the economics.

rigor.statement: The Government has decided to also cut, and did in its initial Budget, $6 billion from climate emergency response funding and from resilience—from the likes of that flood protection and otherwise—which has not only undermined our ability to mitigate climate-changing emissions but also to adapt to the impacts of climate change.
rigor.explanation: Links the cut to weakened mitigation and adaptation, a reasonable chain but asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Can the Minister of Finance clearly articulate for us how exactly this Government has apparently increased our resilience while actively subsidising new fossil-fuel production and cutting investment in renewable energy generation?
rigor.explanation: Points to an alleged inconsistency (subsidising fossil fuels while claiming resilience), though states the premises as given.

rigor.statement: you do not grow when you starve. That is the approach that this Government has taken to our economy.
rigor.explanation: Relies on the 'starve' metaphor as argument; rhetorically vivid but light on the evidentiary mechanism.

rigor.statement: Budget 2024 cut $178 million from the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority’s budget. This was money that was largely to reduce household electricity bills... In a year when the Government had $790 million - odd in tax cuts for landlords, $178 million was sliced from initiatives that could have directly helped families with the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts a cut with a tax concession to argue misplaced priorities; effective but the two are not directly fungible.

rigor.statement: sometimes you meet people who grab on to one fact and hold it so tightly they squeeze out any relevance it had. That is what’s happened in this case.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the opponent's fact (15-year well lead time) but argues it is being misapplied; a fair logical move stated without much evidence.

rigor.statement: It is not because there are no new wells allowed; it’s because of the old wells that don’t produce... because they destroyed all the confidence required to keep producing in the old ones.
rigor.explanation: Offers a confidence/investment mechanism to rebut the lead-time objection; coherent but evidence is anecdotal.

rigor.statement: Perhaps it is the focus also of a small man and a small mind, but, as I was saying, this year that we’re talking about—
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem, no reasoning content.

rigor.statement: The proportion of the economy that was taken by Government went down over this year from 33.1 percent to 32.5 percent. That may not sound like a lot, but 0.6 of a percent of the whole economy is about $2.5 billion.
rigor.explanation: Quantifies the change and translates it into dollars to make the point land.

rigor.statement: We reduced violent crime from 185,000 crimes at the end of 2023 down to 135,000 by October 2025, when this financial year was under way. That is a massive, 50,000 decrease in violent crimes that people are a victim of, because we put the money... into law and order. We actually got results with it.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the spending caused the fall without isolating other factors — a causal leap.

rigor.statement: when the Government takes less, people eat more. It takes pressure off inflation... with lower inflation, we don’t have the high interest rates that people suffered for many years... And, with lower interest rates, you actually get jobs created and possibility for people in their lives
rigor.explanation: Lays out a causal chain (less spending → lower inflation → lower rates → jobs) that is plausible but presented as automatic with no evidence.

rigor.statement: The member claims there have been “billions of dollars”—this is a direct quote—“billions of dollars of blow-out on roads.” Well, I’d like the member to actually provide some evidence for that... Yes, there are some overruns, but not to the extent of billions of dollars.
rigor.explanation: Demands evidence for the opponent's figure and concedes some overruns while disputing the scale — a reasoned rebuttal.

rigor.statement: well, I thought the member supported the Treaty settlement process!... Yes, the iwi have profited from that, but I thought the member was for rangatiratanga and economic development.
rigor.explanation: A 'gotcha' consistency argument rather than addressing the member's actual point about price, which she explicitly distinguished.

rigor.statement: We’ve seen it be successful in places like Queenstown, where fares were lowered, service frequency increased, and then patronage went up and it gave people more options to get around the Queenstown Lakes area without having to rely on their own cars.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete case (lower fares + frequency → higher patronage) to support the policy argument.

rigor.statement: the way the current Government policy statement (GPS) is set up, it sets aside the largest share of funding that’s going on new infrastructure or new projects just to be on State highways, and the vast majority of the public transport services and infrastructure budget is to maintain existing services, not to increase services.
rigor.explanation: Coherent critique that the GPS structure prevents genuine cross-modal trade-off comparison.

divination.statement: When it’s eventually done, by the end of 2027, New Zealand will have a world-leading national ticketing system.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the system will be world-leading and complete by end-2027; IT rollouts frequently slip, and 'world-leading' is hard to verify.

divination.statement: the latest, as of March 2026, is: 211 homes delivered of the Budget 2024 social housing; 228 from the Budget 2025 social housing, which was specifically for Auckland. I’m told that, since November 2023, 2,600 net new social houses have been added in Auckland, and we are on track to meet the commitment for an additional increase of 3,000 by the end of November 2026.
divination.explanation: Predicts hitting 3,000 additional homes by November 2026; on-track claim, outcome still pending.

divination.statement: In terms of Air New Zealand, they have provided me with reassurances consistently that the changes they are making to their routes right now are temporary to address the current fuel crisis... maintaining regional connectivity is our number one priority.
divination.explanation: Implicit prediction that route changes are temporary; depends on the fuel crisis easing, uncertain.

civility.statement: What the Prime Minister understands is that, actually, a failed policy that ended oil and gas exploration puts this country at huge risk, drives up energy prices, and actually puts huge pain and suffering on low and middle income working people.
civility.explanation: Harsh criticism of a policy rather than a person, but leans on emotive hyperbole ('huge pain and suffering').

civility.statement: We haven't cranked up spending by 84 percent, driven inflation to 32-year highs, had 13 increases in interest rates, put the economy into recession where people have lost their jobs—we're doing the reverse of that. We are disciplined spenders. We've lowered inflation, we've brought interest rates down nine times, we have an economy that's growing, and we've created 15,000 new jobs in the last quarter.
civility.explanation: Partisan contrast with the previous government but focused on economic record rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: Look, I just want to reassure the member: we're in phase 1. We've got plenty of fuel. Don't worry about it, son. It's all good.
civility.explanation: Condescending and dismissive; calling the Leader of the Opposition 'son' is a belittling personal touch.

civility.statement: I really appreciate the member's anxiety in the question he's raising. I've noticed his scaremongering about the supplies of fuel that are within New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Patronising ('anxiety') and accuses the questioner of 'scaremongering' rather than engaging the question's substance.

civility.statement: Look, I appreciate the member has had experience running a crisis in the past, but we have taken the mistakes of his management and we are doing it differently. The reason, very simply, is that we are a Government that will work with industry.
civility.explanation: A dig about 'the mistakes of his management', but aimed at conduct/record rather than the person.

civility.statement: Is our country more or less exposed to imported inflation because of his decision to spend at least $1 billion of taxpayer money on a liquefied natural gas (LNG) import facility?
civility.explanation: Pointed, embeds a contested cost figure, but is a substantive policy question rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: In part of that lesson, I will take her through the history, which is that under her Government, inflation was higher and, Lord alive, if another Labour-led Government was elected, you betcha, inflation will be higher again, borrowing will be higher again, and taxes will be higher again, too.
civility.explanation: Partisan and a touch mocking ('a lesson on inflation'), but aimed at party policy.

civility.statement: Others may talk big about splashing the cash. We are taking a responsible approach.
civility.explanation: Mild partisan contrast; criticises opponents' approach without personal attack.

civility.statement: I reject not only the characterisation of that question but its intent and its meaning.
civility.explanation: Firmly rebuts a loaded, accusatory question without resorting to a personal insult of his own.

civility.statement: Well, I don't think there is a massive chasm, but its election year and there's always going to be a bit of kicking and screaming in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive ('kicking and screaming') but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: So is the Minister's position that an Indian chef coming here under the Indian free-trade agreement (FTA) will have fewer rights than a Chinese chef coming in under the China - New Zealand FTA; in other words, that an Indian chef is worth less to the National Party than a Chinese chef?
civility.explanation: Reframes a visa-terms difference as the National Party valuing Indians less—an inflammatory, racialised imputation.

civility.statement: If that's the case, has the Minister or the Prime Minister directly and explicitly informed their Indian counterparts that they intend to implement the India temporary employment entry (TEE) visa scheme in a way that treats Indians worse than Chinese, Thais, and the Vietnamese; and, if so, what was the reaction from Prime Minister Modi and trade Minister Goyal to the admission of this planned discrimination against Indian citizens?
civility.explanation: Loaded, accusatory framing ('planned discrimination', 'treats Indians worse') embedded as a presupposition.

civility.statement: Why does the India FTA include an investment clause with a completely unrealistic and unachievable $34 billion target over 15 years, when no previous New Zealand FTA has ever done so?
civility.explanation: Harsh ('completely unrealistic and unachievable') but directed at a policy clause, not a person.

civility.statement: That question absolutely demonstrates the lack of awareness of parties opposite about what's actually going on in Auckland, and I recommend they take a flight and get up there and see what's happening.
civility.explanation: Dismissive personal swipe ('lack of awareness', 'take a flight') rather than engaging the 33% capacity-cut claim.

civility.statement: I say, once again, I most certainly will not emulate anything to do with Labour, given the tragic outcomes at the Marsden Point refinery.
civility.explanation: Partisan jab tying Labour to the 'tragic' refinery closure rather than engaging the policy question.

civility.statement: This is not a time for reckless assertions, adventurous language—and I only wish that the member showed passion, zest, and advocacy, rather than acquiesce to the closure of the refinery at Marsden Point.
civility.explanation: Personal characterisation of the member's conduct and a blame imputation rather than addressing the stockholding/reporting question.

civility.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, it would appear by the member's references to question No. 1 and question No. 2 that she is not thinking for herself, but simply reading off a sheet, and the next question that might be asked is: who wrote this stuff?
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on the questioner's competence and autonomy rather than engaging the Treaty question.

civility.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, no, but I think we're seeing a very good example of what happens when you give a job to the wrong person.
civility.explanation: Personal denigration of the member as 'the wrong person' for the job.

civility.statement: Maybe they think that young Māori reading and writing doesn't matter. Certainly, from the results they got in Government, it seems that's exactly what they think.
civility.explanation: Imputes that opponents don't care about young Māori literacy—a motive smear.

civility.statement: I think she might be having a few issues; she may need some medical help
civility.explanation: Personal aspersion on the Minister's mental health; he later withdrew it.

civility.statement: Two months after the fuel crisis started, why can't he tell New Zealanders who critical customers are, how they will access fuel, what the role of the fuel companies is going to be, and when we might get to that point—what the criteria are for if we do get to that point?
civility.explanation: Pointed accountability question; sharp but focused on policy substance, not personal attack.

civility.statement: Why did she promise Kiwis to "help bring down food prices", "get food prices under control", and that they would "pay less for home-grown food at the checkout" when she had no intention of keeping those promises?
civility.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own pledges but the 'no intention of keeping' framing imputes bad faith rather than just challenging the record.

veracity.statement: What the Prime Minister understands is that, actually, a failed policy that ended oil and gas exploration puts this country at huge risk, drives up energy prices, and actually puts huge pain and suffering on low and middle income working people.
veracity.explanation: Causal claim that ending oil/gas exploration drove up energy prices is contested; the ban's near-term price effect was limited, so the framing is misleading.

veracity.statement: We've got a renewables boom like we've never seen before; we've got emissions the lowest it's been since 2010; and we've got an "and, and, and" policy where we are going to continue to invest and have fossil fuel in this country in order to lower the dry-year risk.
veracity.explanation: 'Emissions the lowest since 2010' is a checkable factual claim; plausible but unverified and sensitive to which measure is used.

veracity.statement: We haven't cranked up spending by 84 percent, driven inflation to 32-year highs, had 13 increases in interest rates, put the economy into recession where people have lost their jobs—we're doing the reverse of that. We are disciplined spenders. We've lowered inflation, we've brought interest rates down nine times, we have an economy that's growing, and we've created 15,000 new jobs in the last quarter.
veracity.explanation: Several figures appear exaggerated or selectively attributed to the prior government (e.g. '32-year highs', '84 percent'), mixing accurate and misleading claims.

veracity.statement: I also want to reassure the House: we're not going to go borrow another $44 billion or increase taxes by $90 billion.
veracity.explanation: The large round figures are partisan framing of a hypothetical and are not substantiated in the exchange.

veracity.statement: At the beginning of this year, before conflict began in the Middle East, the IMF was forecasting global growth of 3.3 percent in 2026; it's now forecasting that growth to fall to 3.1 percent. In 2027, the IMF is forecasting global growth of 3.2 percent... For New Zealand, the IMF is forecasting growth of 2.1 percent in 2026 and 2.4 percent in 2027.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific, attributable IMF forecasts; presented as sourced data.

veracity.statement: While the impacts of the conflict are still very uncertain, I would observe that oil prices are currently around 35 percent higher than they were before the conflict began—so, well south of some of the IMF's more dire predictions.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable price claim presented with appropriate caveat about uncertainty.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister made that statement in July 2024. At that time, the most recently available data showed that food prices had actually fallen for the year by 0.3 percent... in the year to March 2023, food prices rose 12.1 percent, and in the year to March 2026, they rose 3.4 percent.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures, though the choice of the July 2024 reference point is favourable framing.

veracity.statement: Here are the inflation percentage changes for quarters in the period March 2022 through September 2023: 6.9, 7.3, 7.2, 7.2, 6.7, 6, 5.6. Here is the record since we were elected: 4.74, 3.3, 2.2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.73, 3.1, 3.1. You don't need to be a mathematician to realise that food price inflation has dropped dramatically under our Government when compared to the last.
veracity.explanation: Detailed data, though conflates headline and food inflation and attributes the trend to government policy.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has secured tariff-free access for lamb, wool, coal, leather, forestry, most industrial products, infant formula, and seafood; and reductions of duty rates for our wine, as an example, from 150 percent to as low as 25 percent. For the first time in any India FTA, New Zealand has secured preferential access for apples, mānuka honey, and a tariff-free quota for kiwifruit, almost four times what we currently sell them.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable claims about the FTA terms presented as fact.

veracity.statement: This Government has invested $41 million in their professionalisation through Budget 2025... Harm within youth justice and care and protection residences has seen a 14 percent decrease since 2024... with $22 million for repairs and upgrades to Oranga Tamariki residences and $33 million in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable spending and harm-reduction figures presented as fact.

veracity.statement: Yes, we're concerned about security and quality, but that's why I'm pleased to see some softening in the rental market, which allows tenants more choice, and pleased to see credible measures such as the Stats New Zealand rental price index showing flattening rent prices.
veracity.explanation: Appeals to an official index for 'flattening rents'; directionally plausible but unquantified.

veracity.statement: I have also been advised that, globally, we consume 100 million barrels of crude oil per day. Twenty million barrels was previously going through the strait; 2.6 million barrels of that volume came from Kuwait, and less than 10 percent of that crude oil makes its way to South-east Asia.
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced ('advised') figures presented as fact.

veracity.statement: the number of Māori new entrants who are at or above expectations was 25 percent... In the couple of years we've been in, we've got it up to 43 percent. We've nearly doubled the number of young Māori new entrants who are meeting expectations for critical skills.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim, but the metric and timeframe are uncorroborated in the text and causal attribution is asserted.

rigor.statement: What the Prime Minister understands is that, actually, a failed policy that ended oil and gas exploration puts this country at huge risk, drives up energy prices, and actually puts huge pain and suffering on low and middle income working people.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal chain (ban → risk → higher prices → suffering) without supporting evidence; appeal to emotion.

rigor.statement: While the impacts of the conflict are still very uncertain, I would observe that oil prices are currently around 35 percent higher than they were before the conflict began—so, well south of some of the IMF's more dire predictions.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from current data against the modelled adverse scenarios with stated uncertainty.

rigor.statement: Here are the inflation percentage changes for quarters in the period March 2022 through September 2023: 6.9, 7.3, 7.2, 7.2, 6.7, 6, 5.6. Here is the record since we were elected: 4.74, 3.3, 2.2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.73, 3.1, 3.1. You don't need to be a mathematician to realise that food price inflation has dropped dramatically under our Government when compared to the last.
rigor.explanation: Marshals data but draws a strong causal conclusion from a before/after comparison without controlling for global inflation cycles.

rigor.statement: In part of that lesson, I will take her through the history, which is that under her Government, inflation was higher and, Lord alive, if another Labour-led Government was elected, you betcha, inflation will be higher again, borrowing will be higher again, and taxes will be higher again, too.
rigor.explanation: Asserts future outcomes from past correlation with no mechanism; partisan extrapolation.

rigor.statement: Well, no, that's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is our commitment is to promote. It is very clear in the advice the Government's received and in the text of the agreement: New Zealand must promote investment. That is the obligation that the Government has taken on.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes a commitment to 'promote' from a commitment to 'invest', citing the text and advice.

rigor.statement: So is the Minister's position that an Indian chef coming here under the Indian free-trade agreement (FTA) will have fewer rights than a Chinese chef coming in under the China - New Zealand FTA; in other words, that an Indian chef is worth less to the National Party than a Chinese chef?
rigor.explanation: Strawman/false equivalence: leaps from differing visa provisions to a claim about relative human worth.

rigor.statement: If that's the case, has the Minister or the Prime Minister directly and explicitly informed their Indian counterparts that they intend to implement the India temporary employment entry (TEE) visa scheme in a way that treats Indians worse than Chinese, Thais, and the Vietnamese; and, if so, what was the reaction from Prime Minister Modi and trade Minister Goyal to the admission of this planned discrimination against Indian citizens?
rigor.explanation: Complex question presuming a contested premise ('discrimination') that the Minister has not conceded.

rigor.statement: Why does the India FTA include an investment clause with a completely unrealistic and unachievable $34 billion target over 15 years, when no previous New Zealand FTA has ever done so?
rigor.explanation: Raises a specific, comparative concern (no prior FTA did this) but asserts unachievability as given rather than demonstrating it.

rigor.statement: I think the implication in the question was that skipping meals is a direct result of the flattening of the rental market across New Zealand. I think that is very disingenuous and has no legitimate connection.
rigor.explanation: Reasonably distinguishes correlation from causation, but uses it to deflect rather than engage the affordability data.

rigor.statement: Maybe they think that young Māori reading and writing doesn't matter. Certainly, from the results they got in Government, it seems that's exactly what they think.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: infers indifference to literacy from education results, a non-sequitur.

specificity.statement: We have a huge boom in renewables. We're opening up. We've got a strategic coal reserve sitting beside Huntly. We want to make sure that we've got as much optionality as possible so we can lower the dry-year risk, keep power bills cheaper for people.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (strategic coal reserve at Huntly) but gives no figures, timeframes, or scale for the 'boom'.

specificity.statement: We've got a renewables boom like we've never seen before; we've got emissions the lowest it's been since 2010; and we've got an "and, and, and" policy where we are going to continue to invest and have fossil fuel in this country in order to lower the dry-year risk.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dated benchmark (since 2010) but the policy description ('and, and, and') is largely a slogan.

specificity.statement: We haven't cranked up spending by 84 percent, driven inflation to 32-year highs, had 13 increases in interest rates, put the economy into recession where people have lost their jobs—we're doing the reverse of that. We are disciplined spenders. We've lowered inflation, we've brought interest rates down nine times, we have an economy that's growing, and we've created 15,000 new jobs in the last quarter.
specificity.explanation: Dense with figures: 84%, 32-year highs, 13 rises, nine cuts, 15,000 jobs.

specificity.statement: I also want to reassure the House: we're not going to go borrow another $44 billion or increase taxes by $90 billion.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise figures ($44b, $90b) but as a contrast claim rather than a costed plan.

specificity.statement: At the beginning of this year, before conflict began in the Middle East, the IMF was forecasting global growth of 3.3 percent in 2026; it's now forecasting that growth to fall to 3.1 percent. In 2027, the IMF is forecasting global growth of 3.2 percent... For New Zealand, the IMF is forecasting growth of 2.1 percent in 2026 and 2.4 percent in 2027.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures with years and revisions for both global and NZ growth.

specificity.statement: While the impacts of the conflict are still very uncertain, I would observe that oil prices are currently around 35 percent higher than they were before the conflict began—so, well south of some of the IMF's more dire predictions.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (35% higher) and frames it against the IMF's 80%/100% scenarios.

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister made that statement in July 2024. At that time, the most recently available data showed that food prices had actually fallen for the year by 0.3 percent... in the year to March 2023, food prices rose 12.1 percent, and in the year to March 2026, they rose 3.4 percent.
specificity.explanation: Multiple dated, precise figures (0.3%, 12.1%, 3.4%).

specificity.statement: Here are the inflation percentage changes for quarters in the period March 2022 through September 2023: 6.9, 7.3, 7.2, 7.2, 6.7, 6, 5.6. Here is the record since we were elected: 4.74, 3.3, 2.2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.73, 3.1, 3.1. You don't need to be a mathematician to realise that food price inflation has dropped dramatically under our Government when compared to the last.
specificity.explanation: A full quarter-by-quarter series of figures.

specificity.statement: Others may talk big about splashing the cash. We are taking a responsible approach.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like; 'responsible approach' commits to nothing concrete.

specificity.statement: New Zealand has secured tariff-free access for lamb, wool, coal, leather, forestry, most industrial products, infant formula, and seafood; and reductions of duty rates for our wine, as an example, from 150 percent to as low as 25 percent. For the first time in any India FTA, New Zealand has secured preferential access for apples, mānuka honey, and a tariff-free quota for kiwifruit, almost four times what we currently sell them.
specificity.explanation: Names specific products, a duty cut (150%→25%), and a quantified quota increase.

specificity.statement: One of the things that we agreed with India is that, every year, 1,670 high-skilled workers... can come to New Zealand under a special visa that would be created. The visa will be for three years. At the end of that time, they would need to return home... It does not give them a right automatically to bring family members here, because that was not part of the negotiation.
specificity.explanation: Exact numbers (1,670), duration (three years), and the family-rights position.

specificity.statement: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
specificity.explanation: Exact figure (all 72) and the start date.

specificity.statement: This Government has invested $41 million in their professionalisation through Budget 2025... Harm within youth justice and care and protection residences has seen a 14 percent decrease since 2024... with $22 million for repairs and upgrades to Oranga Tamariki residences and $33 million in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures with budget years and an outcome metric.

specificity.statement: The no-cause evictions are part of a broader suite of changes that were made right across the housing system to ensure there is a higher level of supply. That flexibility, which is given to landlords and also tenants, who are now able to terminate their tenancies with three weeks' notice, is absolutely right square in the middle of a suite of changes.
specificity.explanation: Notes a concrete provision (three weeks' notice) but otherwise general about the 'suite of changes'.

specificity.statement: Yes, we're concerned about security and quality, but that's why I'm pleased to see some softening in the rental market, which allows tenants more choice, and pleased to see credible measures such as the Stats New Zealand rental price index showing flattening rent prices.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named measure (Stats NZ rental price index) but no figures.

specificity.statement: I have also been advised that, globally, we consume 100 million barrels of crude oil per day. Twenty million barrels was previously going through the strait; 2.6 million barrels of that volume came from Kuwait, and less than 10 percent of that crude oil makes its way to South-east Asia.
specificity.explanation: Concrete volumes (100m, 20m, 2.6m barrels) and a routing share.

specificity.statement: Absolutely, I stand by all of the Government's statements and actions, particularly those that have benefited Māori in the form of five charter schools, which are lifting achievement and showing real tino rangatiratanga in action, allowing communities to take charge of their destiny, with education.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (five charter schools) but the 'lifting achievement' claim is unquantified here.

specificity.statement: the number of Māori new entrants who are at or above expectations was 25 percent... In the couple of years we've been in, we've got it up to 43 percent. We've nearly doubled the number of young Māori new entrants who are meeting expectations for critical skills.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after figures (25% → 43%).

specificity.statement: One of the things that the Treaty promised was the rule of law, but the rule of law needs to be clear and accessible to all people, and that is why, as part of a coalition agreement between New Zealand First and the National Party, we are clarifying and, in some cases, removing references to the Treaty principles in law.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the coalition agreement and the action (clarifying/removing Treaty principle references) but without specific clauses.

specificity.statement: To name just a few of the commitments in the deal, we're unlocking Eden Park's ownership and operating model, and recognising Eden Park as New Zealand's national stadium. We have agreed to work together on key transport projects to unlock growth, including the second harbour crossing, the Northwest Rapid Transit, and City Rail Link level crossings.
specificity.explanation: Lists named projects (Eden Park, second harbour crossing, Northwest Rapid Transit, City Rail Link crossings).

strength.statement: We have a huge boom in renewables. We're opening up. We've got a strategic coal reserve sitting beside Huntly. We want to make sure that we've got as much optionality as possible so we can lower the dry-year risk, keep power bills cheaper for people.
strength.explanation: Claims action on energy security with a real reserve, but delivery on cheaper bills is in-progress/unclear.

strength.statement: We haven't cranked up spending by 84 percent, driven inflation to 32-year highs, had 13 increases in interest rates, put the economy into recession where people have lost their jobs—we're doing the reverse of that. We are disciplined spenders. We've lowered inflation, we've brought interest rates down nine times, we have an economy that's growing, and we've created 15,000 new jobs in the last quarter.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on inflation and jobs; some is plausibly real, but credit-claiming for macro outcomes is hard to attribute to one government.

strength.statement: New Zealand has secured tariff-free access for lamb, wool, coal, leather, forestry, most industrial products, infant formula, and seafood; and reductions of duty rates for our wine, as an example, from 150 percent to as low as 25 percent. For the first time in any India FTA, New Zealand has secured preferential access for apples, mānuka honey, and a tariff-free quota for kiwifruit, almost four times what we currently sell them.
strength.explanation: Describes a concluded/secured agreement with concrete terms, not just an aspiration.

strength.statement: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete personal follow-through (visiting every site) rather than aspiration.

strength.statement: This Government has invested $41 million in their professionalisation through Budget 2025... Harm within youth justice and care and protection residences has seen a 14 percent decrease since 2024... with $22 million for repairs and upgrades to Oranga Tamariki residences and $33 million in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences.
strength.explanation: Names funded actions and a measured improvement (14% harm decrease), indicating delivery rather than promise.

strength.statement: Absolutely, I stand by all of the Government's statements and actions, particularly those that have benefited Māori in the form of five charter schools, which are lifting achievement and showing real tino rangatiratanga in action, allowing communities to take charge of their destiny, with education.
strength.explanation: Points to an implemented policy, though the asserted benefits are stated rather than demonstrated.

strength.statement: the number of Māori new entrants who are at or above expectations was 25 percent... In the couple of years we've been in, we've got it up to 43 percent. We've nearly doubled the number of young Māori new entrants who are meeting expectations for critical skills.
strength.explanation: Claims a measurable delivered improvement and credit for it, though attribution to the policy is unverified.

strength.statement: To name just a few of the commitments in the deal, we're unlocking Eden Park's ownership and operating model, and recognising Eden Park as New Zealand's national stadium. We have agreed to work together on key transport projects to unlock growth, including the second harbour crossing, the Northwest Rapid Transit, and City Rail Link level crossings.
strength.explanation: Describes agreed commitments and intentions; delivery is prospective ('agreed to work together'), not yet realised.

forthrightness.statement: Look, I just want to reassure the member: we're in phase 1. We've got plenty of fuel. Don't worry about it, son. It's all good.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specific questions about prohibiting non-critical customers; he gives reassurance instead of any answer.

forthrightness.statement: Again, we are working that through with industry. One of the lessons out of COVID is, actually, we don't believe in a parent-child relationship where Government happens to industry; we actually work with industry. We have ongoing work as we put more definition around phases 3 and 4.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for the Government's definition of 'critical customers'; gives no definition and pivots to a process/COVID talking point.

forthrightness.statement: Look, I appreciate the member has had experience running a crisis in the past, but we have taken the mistakes of his management and we are doing it differently. The reason, very simply, is that we are a Government that will work with industry.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how petrol stations will identify critical customers; answers with a jab about the previous crisis and 'working with industry', not the mechanism asked for.

forthrightness.statement: At the beginning of this year, before conflict began in the Middle East, the IMF was forecasting global growth of 3.3 percent in 2026; it's now forecasting that growth to fall to 3.1 percent. In 2027, the IMF is forecasting global growth of 3.2 percent... For New Zealand, the IMF is forecasting growth of 2.1 percent in 2026 and 2.4 percent in 2027.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers the question about the IMF main scenario.

forthrightness.statement: The Prime Minister made that statement in July 2024. At that time, the most recently available data showed that food prices had actually fallen for the year by 0.3 percent... in the year to March 2023, food prices rose 12.1 percent, and in the year to March 2026, they rose 3.4 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question (does she agree, and the year-to-March-2026 figure) and supplies the requested number.

forthrightness.statement: Well, because this Government is determined to ensure that the prices Kiwis pay will be lower than they would have otherwise been without the policy decisions that we are taking. The issue that the member continues to forget is that the period of the highest increases in food prices happened under a previous administration's policies.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she promised to bring food prices down with 'no intention' of keeping it; deflects to an unfalsifiable counterfactual rather than addressing the promise.

forthrightness.statement: One of the things that we agreed with India is that, every year, 1,670 high-skilled workers... can come to New Zealand under a special visa that would be created. The visa will be for three years. At the end of that time, they would need to return home... It does not give them a right automatically to bring family members here, because that was not part of the negotiation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Peters' question about family entry rights: no automatic right, and explains why.

forthrightness.statement: Well, no, that's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is our commitment is to promote. It is very clear in the advice the Government's received and in the text of the agreement: New Zealand must promote investment. That is the obligation that the Government has taken on.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly denies the 'clawback' characterisation and states the actual obligation (promote, not invest).

forthrightness.statement: Well, I don't think there is a massive chasm, but its election year and there's always going to be a bit of kicking and screaming in New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to explain the gap between Indian and NZ accounts of the deal; dismisses it as election-year noise rather than addressing the substance.

forthrightness.statement: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'how many sites have you visited' with a precise count.

forthrightness.statement: I'm not going to talk to individual contract decisions. Those are operational matters. Yes, I will say I have visited Birthright, but I will not be going into operational matters.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about Birthright being forced to close; declines on 'operational matters' grounds, leaving the substance of the funding concern unaddressed.

forthrightness.statement: The no-cause evictions are part of a broader suite of changes that were made right across the housing system to ensure there is a higher level of supply. That flexibility, which is given to landlords and also tenants, who are now able to terminate their tenancies with three weeks' notice, is absolutely right square in the middle of a suite of changes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why proceed with no-cause evictions given security concerns; reframes them as part of a 'suite' for supply rather than addressing the security objection.

forthrightness.statement: That question absolutely demonstrates the lack of awareness of parties opposite about what's actually going on in Auckland, and I recommend they take a flight and get up there and see what's happening.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address the specific figure (33% cut / 600,000 homes) put to him.

forthrightness.statement: I think the implication in the question was that skipping meals is a direct result of the flattening of the rental market across New Zealand. I think that is very disingenuous and has no legitimate connection.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how housing can be 'affordable' when one in four skip meals due to housing costs; disputes the framing instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: I have also been advised that, globally, we consume 100 million barrels of crude oil per day. Twenty million barrels was previously going through the strait; 2.6 million barrels of that volume came from Kuwait, and less than 10 percent of that crude oil makes its way to South-east Asia.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the advice he has seen on the Kuwait force-majeure impact on supply.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, given the minuscule amount of the crude oil which feeds the refineries in South-east Asia, where New Zealand derives its refined fuel from, such an insignificant amount is highly unlikely to show a long-term impact, and I'm advised there is no immediate impact.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question on pump-price impact with a clear (if optimistic) assessment.

forthrightness.statement: I say, once again, I most certainly will not emulate anything to do with Labour, given the tragic outcomes at the Marsden Point refinery.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he hasn't used Labour's statutory powers and relies on voluntary cooperation; answers with a partisan refusal, not the reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: This is not a time for reckless assertions, adventurous language—and I only wish that the member showed passion, zest, and advocacy, rather than acquiesce to the closure of the refinery at Marsden Point.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to consulting on higher stockholding/reporting; deflects with rhetoric about the member.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, no, but I think we're seeing a very good example of what happens when you give a job to the wrong person.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a 'no' to whether the PM's position is convenience-driven but immediately pivots to attacking the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: One of the things that the Treaty promised was the rule of law, but the rule of law needs to be clear and accessible to all people, and that is why, as part of a coalition agreement between New Zealand First and the National Party, we are clarifying and, in some cases, removing references to the Treaty principles in law.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms standing by the vote and explains the rationale and mechanism directly.

divination.statement: In part of that lesson, I will take her through the history, which is that under her Government, inflation was higher and, Lord alive, if another Labour-led Government was elected, you betcha, inflation will be higher again, borrowing will be higher again, and taxes will be higher again, too.
divination.explanation: Predicts higher inflation/borrowing/tax under a future Labour government; partisan and not well-evidenced.

divination.statement: As I said, given the minuscule amount of the crude oil which feeds the refineries in South-east Asia, where New Zealand derives its refined fuel from, such an insignificant amount is highly unlikely to show a long-term impact, and I'm advised there is no immediate impact.
divination.explanation: Predicts no long-term price impact from the Kuwait declaration; reasoned from the small supply share but inherently uncertain.

authenticity.statement: Well, because this Government is determined to ensure that the prices Kiwis pay will be lower than they would have otherwise been without the policy decisions that we are taking. The issue that the member continues to forget is that the period of the highest increases in food prices happened under a previous administration's policies.
authenticity.explanation: Defends a commitment ('get food prices under control') against a record of rising food prices by reframing it as 'lower than otherwise'—a shift from the original pledge.

authenticity.statement: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
authenticity.explanation: Stated commitment to front-line engagement is matched by the described action of visiting all offices.

charisma.statement: I move, That this House condemn all incidents of antisemitism in New Zealand and affirm that antisemitism has no place here.
charisma.explanation: A unifying, cross-party condemnation of antisemitism that invites the whole House to affirm a common value rather than attacking opponents.

charisma.statement: Well, my thoughts absolutely go out to Jamie and others like him in the economy who are doing everything right... it sounds as if he's someone who's had the gumption to start his own business, to put his own money and time on the line, and to take risks.
charisma.explanation: Warm, empathetic acknowledgement of a named struggling business owner that humanises the response and broadens appeal.

civility.statement: I move, That this House condemn all incidents of antisemitism in New Zealand and affirm that antisemitism has no place here.
civility.explanation: Respectful, value-based motion with no personal attack; standard consensus-seeking House condemnation.

civility.statement: What we can control is our own spending, and this Government is determined to take a responsible course in which we do not add fuel to the inflation fire, as was not the case in recent history under previous Governments.
civility.explanation: Legitimate policy contrast with the prior government, though the 'fuel to the fire' jab is mildly partisan rather than purely substantive.

civility.statement: Well, because I'd put my economic management record up against his any day of the week. This is a former Prime Minister who drove up spending 84 percent, who actually drove inflation to 32-year highs, 12 or 13 interest rate rises, slowed an economy up, and created unemployment.
civility.explanation: Attacks the opponent's policy record rather than his character; harsh but largely substantive.

civility.statement: I've seen reports of Labour scaremongering about our fuel situation, and I just think that's really inappropriate for a Leader of the Opposition not to get in behind New Zealand and New Zealanders in a crisis. This country has sufficient supplies of fuel, we're managing the crisis to the very best of our ability, and we're serving New Zealanders well.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Opposition's criticism as 'scaremongering' and 'inappropriate' — a dismissive framing rather than engagement with their substance.

civility.statement: I can. I'm very proud to say we'll have a national flood plan by the end of this year. We are the first Government to do so, and we are taking action and putting investment into climate change, not just words and bumper stickers and Post-it notes.
civility.explanation: Substantive claim paired with a mild belittling jab at opponents' 'words and bumper stickers'.

civility.statement: I'd have to go back and look at the Hansard, but as I recall them, the member's questions weren't very precise, and what I'd stressed in answer to those questions was that I hadn't been presented with a forecast, which was the case.
civility.explanation: Mild deflection onto the questioner's imprecision, but no personal attack.

civility.statement: Because when people ask me whether they should have confidence in me, they need to compare themselves with the alternative, which is that member, and what she is promoting is more taxes, more spending, more borrowing, and more debt—back to the bad old COVID days.
civility.explanation: Attacks the opponent's alleged policy programme rather than her character, but the 'bad old COVID days' framing is a partisan caricature.

civility.statement: Well, my thoughts absolutely go out to Jamie and others like him in the economy who are doing everything right... it sounds as if he's someone who's had the gumption to start his own business, to put his own money and time on the line, and to take risks.
civility.explanation: Respectful and constructive, engaging the constituent's situation rather than scoring points.

civility.statement: I utterly reject the assertion made in the latter part of that question, and it's an assertion that the Labour Party dishonourably continue to make on social media. We have a plan, we have a fuel response plan, we have published that plan, we are taking all of the measures necessary.
civility.explanation: Labels the opponents' claim 'dishonourable' — a character-tinged rebuttal she later withdrew after a point of order.

civility.statement: Well, we're working through a procurement process, but on this side of the House we are focused on affordable electricity prices, keeping the lights on, and protecting jobs, and the reality is, you can't run an electricity system on hope that it will rain. That's the Opposition's strategy—
civility.explanation: The 'hope that it will rain' line caricatures the Opposition's position rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: Why should the tens of thousands of New Zealanders who have lost jobs under his leadership have confidence in him when the job that he seems most committed to fighting for is his own?
civility.explanation: Frames a personal jibe about Luxon clinging to his own job around a real jobs statistic — pointed and somewhat personal rather than purely policy-focused.

civility.statement: Why did his Government decide to cut flood protection funding at a time when extreme weather is becoming more frequent and severe, by approximately half compared to the former Government?
civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive — challenges a budget decision on policy grounds without personal attack.

civility.statement: If she truly is on the side of construction workers, then why are there 39,570 working-age jobseeker support clients as at the end of January 2026, who have declared construction, mining labourer, or trades worker as their previous occupation?
civility.explanation: The 'if she truly is on the side' framing is mildly barbed but the substance is a legitimate data-based challenge.

civility.statement: What about the smoke-free generation rules that your Government revoked and repealed? What was the economic impact on the health system as a result of the repealing of that particular piece of legislation, given the Minister's last comments?
civility.explanation: Challenges a specific government action and its fiscal consequences on substance rather than attacking the person.

veracity.statement: Stats New Zealand points out that rents rose only 1.2 percent in the year—the smallest annual increase in 16 years.
veracity.explanation: Specific, attributed statistical claim plausibly drawn from Stats NZ; selecting the most favourable figure is mild cherry-picking but the number itself is presented accurately.

veracity.statement: We know, from a previous data release, that petrol prices rose 18.6 percent in the month of March alone, following the start of the conflict... Stats NZ identified that they were the largest contributor to the quarterly inflation rate, adding one percentage point to the total.
veracity.explanation: Detailed figures attributed to Stats NZ, with the caveat that petrol fell in Jan/Feb provided rather than concealed — context-aware rather than misleading.

veracity.statement: Well, annual CPI inflation in Australia is currently 3.7 percent; in the UK, it is 3.2 percent; and the OECD average is 3.4 percent... New Zealand is starting from a somewhat stronger position than many other countries.
veracity.explanation: Comparator figures sound plausible, but the 'stronger position' framing omits that NZ's own headline rate context makes the comparison flattering rather than clear-cut.

veracity.statement: Well, because I'd put my economic management record up against his any day of the week. This is a former Prime Minister who drove up spending 84 percent, who actually drove inflation to 32-year highs, 12 or 13 interest rate rises, slowed an economy up, and created unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Mixes a real signal (inflation reaching multi-decade highs) with contestable framings like '84 percent' spending and attributing rate rises/unemployment solely to the predecessor — selective and partly misleading.

veracity.statement: I've seen reports of Labour scaremongering about our fuel situation, and I just think that's really inappropriate for a Leader of the Opposition not to get in behind New Zealand and New Zealanders in a crisis. This country has sufficient supplies of fuel, we're managing the crisis to the very best of our ability, and we're serving New Zealanders well.
veracity.explanation: The 'sufficient supplies' assurance is asserted without evidence during an acknowledged crisis; not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Well, this Government doesn't just talk words; we put action and investment to climate change. That's why this country, in the last quarter, has had less emissions produced than in any time since 2010. That's why we're investing in resilience in our roading network; that's why we're investing another $200 million into our flood protection.
veracity.explanation: The 'lowest emissions since 2010' claim is specific but unverified and potentially driven by economic slowdown rather than policy; presented as a credit.

veracity.statement: One of them was based on an extreme set of assumptions, including escalating conflict... and, critically, oil prices averaging US$180 a barrel being sustained through quarter two and quarter three. I note that if all of these assumptions did come to pass, inflation could reach over 7 percent. However... oil prices in quarter two are currently US$95 a barrel, which is around half what was assumed in the stylised scenario.
veracity.explanation: Carefully distinguishes a stylised scenario from a forecast and contrasts the $180 assumption with the current $95 — accurate and non-misleading framing.

veracity.statement: Well, because if you talk to those in the construction sector, they say one of the most important things for ensuring that there's high levels of construction activity is that interest rates are lower. And on the watch of this Government, there have been successive interest rate reductions, whereas on the watch of the previous Government, they increased at such a rapid rate that it's meant that many construction projects fell over.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate on rate movements under each government, though attributing all project failures to the previous government's rates is an oversimplification.

veracity.statement: Because the economy has been going through a challenging recovery following a period of excessively high inflation that was sustained outside of the target band for 33 months in a row, leading to a massive spike in interest rates and a very difficult economic recovery.
veracity.explanation: The '33 months outside the target band' is a specific, checkable claim presented as the cause of the difficult recovery; broadly plausible though framed to deflect blame.

veracity.statement: Westpower estimates the scheme will generate enough electricity for 12,000 homes and prevent—Chlöe Swarbrick—129,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. I'm told this is equivalent to taking 69,000 cars off the road annually.
veracity.explanation: Figures are properly attributed to Westpower and 'I'm told', framing them as estimates rather than hard facts.

veracity.statement: There are 48 referral applications that have been lodged and found compliant, and 47 substantive applications have been lodged and found complete. If they're all approved, these would authorise the construction of nearly 24,000 new houses, thousands of new retirement village units, and thousands of additional megawatts of new electricity generation.
veracity.explanation: Counts are precise, but the housing/megawatt totals are conditional on all being approved — clearly flagged with 'if they're all approved'.

veracity.statement: Well, listen up: the average number of working days for a substantive decision is 126... Auckland Port estimates their application to extend the wharf would have taken more than three years; it took five months and nine days... Green Steel... took seven months and 18 days. They say it would have taken six years under the RMA.
veracity.explanation: Concrete timings are checkable; the RMA-comparison times are attributed estimates that flatter the policy.

veracity.statement: Well, unfortunately, after the previous Government made the decision to ban oil and gas exploration, we have seen a significant reduction in gas availability in New Zealand. It is reducing faster than was expected and that is damaging jobs, it is damaging industries across our country... I can tell the member: hope is not a strategy.
veracity.explanation: Declining gas availability is real, but attributing it wholly and on this timeframe to the exploration ban is contested by analysts who cite field depletion.

veracity.statement: Annual figures show that overseas visitor arrivals reached 3.58 million in the year to February 2026, which is an increase of 229,000 people on the previous year. This puts us at 92 percent of the pre-COVID levels.
veracity.explanation: Attributed Stats NZ figures presented straightforwardly; the later '408,000… in February 2016' appears to be a misstatement but the headline annual figures are coherent.

veracity.statement: In December, we announced that 13,000 Chinese and Pacific travellers had already visited, with 24,000 total requests approved; that number is now at almost 67,000 visits. With an average visitor spend of $5,300 for Chinese visitors, that's an estimated economic injection of almost $350 million for Kiwi businesses from those who have visited.
veracity.explanation: Visit counts are concrete, but the $350m 'economic injection' is an extrapolation that assumes uniform high spend — an optimistic estimate flagged as 'estimated'.

veracity.statement: I note that the Stats New Zealand Research and Development Survey shows that employment in the sector increased from 28,200 roles in 2022 to 30,600 roles in 2024, with most of that growth in the private sector... Budget 2025 committed more than $1.8 billion to science and innovation.
veracity.explanation: Cites real-sounding R&D survey growth (2022–24), but answers a question about ~700 recent sector job losses with an earlier private-sector-led growth figure — true yet missing the context that changes its meaning.

veracity.statement: Of course, it isn't a cut; it is a reallocation of funding to the Advanced Technology Institute.
veracity.explanation: Framing the change purely as 'reallocation, not a cut' is contestable given the job losses raised; characterisation favourable to the Government rather than clearly accurate.

veracity.statement: I agree that the Treaty of Waitangi, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, in its two languages was the document signed at the founding of our contemporary nation.
veracity.explanation: The factual content — that the Treaty in two languages was signed at the nation's founding — is accurate.

veracity.statement: I have to dispute what the Hon Dr Duncan Webb's just stated, because under the Speaker's rulings the committee chair can call for a submission period proportional to the report back. I know that the committee clerk actually spoke to the Speaker about this issue, and I'm fully, as the chair of the committee, entitled to do this under the power of the committee and under the Speaker's ruling.
veracity.explanation: The proportionality entitlement claim is checkable against Standing Orders; presented confidently and plausibly but disputed by Webb.

specificity.statement: Stats New Zealand points out that rents rose only 1.2 percent in the year—the smallest annual increase in 16 years.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure (1.2%), a timeframe (the year), and a comparator (smallest in 16 years).

specificity.statement: We know, from a previous data release, that petrol prices rose 18.6 percent in the month of March alone, following the start of the conflict... Stats NZ identified that they were the largest contributor to the quarterly inflation rate, adding one percentage point to the total.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages, attribution to Stats NZ, and quantified contribution (one percentage point).
